nodes.title: Blind review F3: how it was answered
nodes.text: Fixed, model first (revision 23, ev.kieran_laura.viewing_2022_05): a shown evening inside the five weeks. On Saturday 28 May Laura views the green-doored house in Wroughton; in the porch she says he could put his boots in it; he says 'It's nice', knowing, and 'Monday, yeah' when she says she will email the adviser. Part 12 now says so: he sat through Harriet's refresher course with the card in his wallet, never told her, told Laura every number and the Hart nothing, and knew exactly where that line ran.

nodes.title: Blind review F33: disagreed, not changed
nodes.text: The review suggests ending on 'chosen' rather than 'awake', since the chapter is called Awake. I keep 'awake'. The supplied story premise frames the whole book as leaving a comfortable 'blue pill' world; 'awake' is the one word that closes that frame, and it closes on three people who chose a small corner of the map with their eyes open, which 'chosen' alone does not say. The insistence the reader heard came partly from the three-clocks paragraph just before it, which is now one sentence (F11).

nodes.title: Blind review 2, finding 1: how it was answered
nodes.text: Fixed, model first. The June telling (ev.kieran.telling.mortgage) now runs from the card: the October 2019 call, the card behind the bus pass, the farms and the Sharehouse, seventy-one thousand pounds in November 2021 while her HOUSE folder sat unopened, then January to the five weeks. Laura's own inner Event, ev.laura.learns_the_year_2022_06, records what she learns besides the deposit and keeps until August; it enables her handover, whose assessment now names the year: 'In November you had seventy-one thousand pounds on your phone. That's three deposits. I was doing extra nights for one of them, and you let me.' In Ten she answers Barbara's 'I'm the one who sent him the card' with 'I know who you are'. Re-read under its lenses, the handover's exit share rose from 0.08 to 0.32: the wound is sharper, as the review says.

nodes.title: Blind review 2, finding 12: how it was answered
nodes.text: Fixed together with F17: Kieran's 'That's four things' and her 'I can count' are cut. In their place Kieran thinks, and does not say, that a phone in your hand at three in the morning is not a fourth thing but all three at once, and that the man on the radio missed nothing: a new inner Event, ev.kieran.all_three_at_once_2020_09, realizing the deep-time-gap concept from his side.

nodes.title: Blind review 2, finding 13: answered, placed differently
nodes.text: Answered, in part not as suggested. The three clocks are planted early, but in Kieran's spare room in the summer of 2020, not in Barbara's mouth: 'There were three clocks in the spare room now: his body's, which wanted to sleep at eleven; the Hart's, which sent the file at ten and brought it back at seven; and the pools', which never stopped. He started living by the third.' A new Event, ev.kieran.fall.three_clocks_2020, realizes the deep-time-gap concept there. Giving the frame to Barbara would feed finding 17 (she already sounds like the book); the last paragraph now echoes something the reader has seen.

nodes.title: Blind review 2, finding 14: how it was answered
nodes.text: Answered in part. Cut twelve similes that were not Barbara's: the tide, the kettle, 'as if it had bitten him', 'as if the floor might go', the code on a door, the ancestors' weather, the wind with a job to do, 'the way weather goes down', the crowd at a match, 'a sound like something tearing slowly', 'as if checking that the house was really there', and telling that 'started feeling like weather'. That is roughly a third of the narrator's own (a pattern count across the text fell from 41 to 33, which also counts literal uses and new dialogue). Barbara's electrical ones stay, as the review suggests: the fuse board, the wiring diagram, checking the stone for current, the handbag like a toolbox, the form she had designed.

nodes.title: Blind review 2, finding 15: answered in part, one kept
nodes.text: Answered in part. Four kickers are gone: 'He had been past it every day for nine years' (One), 'Anyone ... can be pulled down the rabbit hole. You only have to own a phone and have a Tuesday', 'It would be much harder to leave' and 'Nobody in either room was stupid' (Six); several sections now end on a plain fact or an image (Six's go-live night ends 'It never felt like lying'; Eight ends on the Sharehouse's goodbyes). I kept 'Worse food.': it is Barbara's joke in dialogue, not the narrator closing a section, and it is the only laugh on that walk. I kept the chapter endings that close a motif the next chapters use (Two's quiz, Four's 'Do you walk?', Five's 'never been anybody's mother').

nodes.title: Blind review 2, finding 16: how it was answered
nodes.text: Fixed: 'weather' is down from six uses to two, the father's in One ('as if it were weather') and Barbara's unsaid sentence in Seven ('tents come down in weather'). The narrator's 'the way weather goes down' and 'started feeling like weather' are gone, the ancestors' weather became the three clocks, and Barbara's 'Price is just weather' is now 'Price is just noise', an electrician's word.

nodes.title: Blind review 2, finding 17: how it was answered

Old boy', which read as a reading list. The narrator no longer shares her weather (F16). Her silence in February and her visit in August are unchanged.

nodes.title: Blind review 2, finding 3: how it was answered
nodes.text: Fixed, model first (ev.kieran_laura.forty_pounds rewritten as a scene). The row is shown: the statement turned round, 'It's forty quid, Lor', 'Every number, every time. You said that. At this table', 'On the laptop. In the spare room', the man on probation; then the kitchen floor, and what 'The app shows the last login' does: 'You knew. And you let me. Every day. And you never said.' / 'I thought you were owed it.' / 'That's exactly the same thing again.' Re-read under its lenses after the change, the row reads shame 0.53 over guilt 0.44, loyalty 0.62 over voice 0.34, own voice 0.49 with silence 0.35: his penance, letting her watch without a word, is the old silence, and she names it.

nodes.title: Blind review 2, finding 4: how it was answered

nodes.title: Blind review 2, finding 5: how it was answered
nodes.text: Fixed, the review's second option, model first. ev.kieran.deposit_move: he moved the deposit in three payments of eight thousand on three days to his own account in the app, because he knew to the pound what drops a payment into the queue, having cleared it for twelve years and helped write the rules; none was flagged. A new inner Event, ev.kieran.fears_the_hart_2022_05, gives him the beat of fear on the Wednesday: waiting all morning for the fraud team to bring a printout with his name on it. Twelve now lists the three payments among what he never told Compliance. I did not take the first option (his own payment in his own queue): a building society would route a clerk's own flagged payment to someone else, so it would need another failure to be believable.

nodes.title: Blind review 3, finding 11: how it was answered
nodes.text: Paid, not cut, model first: a new Event, ev.kieran.mother_asks_2021_09. In the kitchen with the door shut his mother asks whether it is that bitcoin; he says savings; she says be careful. In Eleven her question to Laura, 'Are you all right, love?', now comes from someone who once asked him to be careful. Read under the lenses it is fear 0.76 and shame 0.63.

nodes.title: Blind review 3, finding 12: disagreed in part
nodes.text: Disagreed in part, and left mostly as it is. The clipped deadpan is the town's register, shared on purpose by the works, the unit and the Hart; flattening it out of Barbara or Laura would lose what the book says about how these people say things. What I did act on is the part the review is right about: fewer of the wise short lines are now the narrator's (the button and tic cuts under finding 14, 'They stayed. They chose it' under 15), so a short true line in Ten is more clearly Barbara's or Laura's.

The raid analogy for the Sharehouse's hold-the-line stays, and so does the guild conversation with Barbara in Eleven, which the review singles out. Model: the porch Event no longer holds the thought, and re-read without it the porch's shame-or-guilt reading moved from shame 0.42 to neither 0.58: the raid thought had been carrying the shame, so it was the author's, not his.

nodes.title: Blind review 3, finding 14: how it was answered
nodes.text: Answered. 'First' cut in five of the eight places named (her slowing, his fear of the Hart, the rota line, the game, Laura's joke), eighteen left in the text overall; 'exactly' down from eight to four (kept: 'He knew exactly what was happening', 'knew exactly where that line ran', and two in dialogue). The repeated liking is gone from Seven ('he checked it every morning before he checked the time. Every morning it was a little bigger.'). The third denial list, in Three, is rewritten. Of the man-doing-X similes, the sleeping child, the man let back in and the wiring diagram are cut; Barbara's fuse board and her form stay. Chapter buttons: Five now ends on 'She never once asked him to stop.' and Six on a plain act, going back to the spare room.

Read under the lenses it is voice 0.65, borrowed form 0.84 and fear 0.81: the staying is chosen, and chosen braced.

nodes.title: Blind review 3, finding 2: how it was answered
nodes.text: Fixed, model first. A new Event, ev.kieran.house_folder_2021_11, shows the hinge: with Laura asleep between two nights he opens the HOUSE folder to pay the electricity, sees DEPOSIT 21,200 and '3,800 TO GO', holds the phone with seventy-one thousand on it, and closes the folder the way she left it. An inner Event, ev.kieran.surprise_not_secret_2021_11, holds the specific thing he tells himself: 'At a hundred thousand it would be a surprise, and a surprise is not a secret.' Read under the lenses before I wrote it, the night is fear 0.94, shame 0.99, silence 1.00, loyalty 0.91 and bartering 0.80, with appetite only 0.29 on a lens that mostly does not fit: shame dressed as a surprise, so the scene puts the question she would ask, where it came from, ahead of the price. The confession in Nine now includes that night, and Laura's assessment in Ten names it: 'You opened my folder and saw what…

nodes.title: Blind review 3, finding 20: disagreed in part
nodes.text: Disagreed in part. Trimmed the reaching: 'three small people on the oldest road in Britain' is gone, and so are two of the callbacks the review counts ('the short bark' and 'The card was in his wallet'), with 'like a man let back in'. I kept the last clause, 'in the corner of the map they had chosen, awake': the brief frames the book as leaving the blue-pill world, which 'awake' closes, and the corner of the map closes Three's green corner of a continent. The three clocks stay too, planted in Four since blind review 2.

He knows the line is recorded, thinks of the card and the three payments and whoever might play the call back in a training room, and says it anyway; afterwards he half expects someone from Quality with a transcript for a week, and nobody comes. The Hart still does not find out, which the review asks to keep. nodes.title: Blind review 3, finding 4: how it was answered
nodes.text: Fixed, model first: a new inner Event, ev.barbara.nearly_speaks_2022_02, causes her drawn response. In Seven she nearly tells him, has the whole mechanism ready, and is stopped by the other name in it: half the money is Laura's (her own reckoning, as in her unsaid 'take Laura's half out'), Laura is not there and has not asked, and Barbara, talked about for seventeen years by men who never said it to her face, has never discussed a woman's money behind her back. Read under the lenses it is standing 0.80, silence 0.98, love 0.47: a choice, not a convenience.

Bounded continuation review through the installed MCP. Read the current p06, the HOUSE Event and the separate surprise-not-secret inner Event, plus the two historical notes and the round-9 final-text review. This is a self-review, not an independent reader assessment. The corrected year-and-a-half duration agrees with the current passage. The consequential choice is still that Kieran can cover the deposit but withholds the money to avoid explaining its source. His outward silence and his inward promised surprise belong to different processes. The enacted closing of Laura's folder expresses this more specifically than an added narrator explanation would. Keep this passage and the established consequence; the correction does not justify a new scene or a new outcome. The seven HOUSE Cut readings remain attributed historical estimates, not newly certified probabilities. Fear of exposure, wi…

Self-review of prose pass 1 in the enhancement fork. Sentence level: 16 recurring similes recast or cut; the ones that carry a character's way of seeing kept (Barbara's fuse board, the tent's guy ropes, the door code, the raid bosses). The closing gesture now answers the confession: Laura says she handed the deposit to him 'without looking'; the last paragraph has her take his hand without looking because she is sure it will be there. Scene level, from model revision 18: Barbara quotes Wilson's triad on the first walk and adds her own fourth thing, in her voice ('I can count, Kieran'); part 6 now stages the 2021 grand battle (regulator, banks, exchanges, purists against farmers, Harriet from Compliance against #war-room, both partly right) and the Sharehouse meetup through a door marked PRIVATE FUNCTION, where the hidden world turns out to look like the queue at the post office, which m…

Self-review: a full read of the rendered enhanced story (9,961 words, graph 33ee172b) as a reader would meet it. Four findings: a timeline error in Kieran's stake between parts 4 to 6, a missing email address that part 4 relies on, part 11's lessons unmodeled and needing to be placed after the drawn visit, and a small redundancy. Everything else read as consistent with the model: the dates and prices, the drawn decisions, the Mr Pritchard and plant-mug link, and each character's knowledge at each moment.

Trajectory selection (LLM under delegation). Kieran: keep candidate.3; it holds the drawn depeg explanation (belonging 0.91 with honesty 0.09 at the depeg). Discard candidate.1, whose belonging drops to 0.65 at the depeg and would no longer explain why he held. Laura: keep candidate.2; it keeps her almost silent in the second wave and after the telling (spoken 0.08 and 0.13) and her trust in Kieran about money collapsing (0.21). Discard candidate.3, whose home security of 0.41 after the loss contradicts losing the deposit. Barbara: keep candidate.3; guilt stays low on the February walk (0.20) and her care is acted on at the knock (0.79). Discard candidate.1, whose guilt of 0.39 in February comes before anything had gone wrong. The kept numbers are the lives' reference trajectories; the voice revision writes each person from them.

Self-review after the voice revision (graph 2a5fe56d): each principal's voice now comes from their modeled life, as the before-review asked. Findings per subject with the revised passages quoted from the rendered text are in data. The revision also lengthened the story from about 5,800 to about 8,400 words.

Self-review of the voices in the complete first draft (graph abe50dac, parts in nodes part.01 and part.07) before the character-voice revision. The author's dispositions work; the characters' voices are weaker than their modeled lives: Kieran's history barely shapes his present speech, Laura is almost silent even at her turning point, Barbara is strong but too aphoristic, the Sharehouse and Kieran's father barely speak. Findings and smallest repairs per subject are in data.

Initial creative agreement: the premise, approximately 11,000 words, and twelve parts were supplied by the human author; other creative settings were delegated to the model. Creative choices recorded subsequently are attributed to their actual decision maker.

Revised creative agreement: target approximately 16,000 words in twelve parts. Complete the full draft before iteration. The graph is the manuscript authority: drafts, reviews, plans and revisions belong to it; exported documents are renders. These choices supersede the earlier length and round rhythm.
Production scope was narrowed to completing and revising the graph-native story; PDF production was handled separately. The twelve-part structure and revised length target remained.

Original story specification: approximately 11,000 words in twelve parts, with remaining creative choices delegated to the model. The premise follows. Write a story about someone born into a world they know nothing about. It's a "blue pill" world: comfortable, familiar, and predictable. They know the people around them, and every week is pretty much the same, stuck in the 9-to-5 routine. Then, somewhere along the line, something strange happens. A "white rabbit" appears: a sign, a stranger, an opportunity that doesn't fit into their ordinary life. Our protagonist is faced with a difficult choice. Human curiosity is powerful, and after years of monotony, they're tired enough to follow it. They choose the unknown. The story should echo the most iconic imagery in pop culture, moments everyone recognizes, like Neo touching the liquid mirror in The Matrix or Harry discovering the wizarding w…

An enhancement branch continued from the earlier published story at graph 6e840daa and model revision 17. Model revision 18 adds the grand battle of 2021, the Sharehouse meetup behind a pub’s back-room door and Barbara’s Wilson line; the prose is enhanced part by part through graph edits.

Faye's open decision was drawn, not chosen: cut.faye.2025.daughter_app.response (faye-titcombe-life r1, 65cbe4fe) with seed 'rabbit-hole-run/faye/daughter-app/2025-09', u=0.2055, realized learn_it_beside_her (first draw, no reroll). The draw could not be recorded in a graph bound to her model because her life model has no graph of its own, so the full draw result is kept here and the continuation (ev.faye.learn_beside) carries a realizes_forecast relation in r2 (4d462a80). Remaining author-life questions and why they stay: the nine slow processes are described on their Events and opened where the causality runs through them (body and partnership in the 2022 adaptation, work in the redundancy arc); further opening would not change the voice. The weights of cut.faye.2021.pull and cut.faye.2026.why_write are the recorder's authored distributions for an invented persona, not estimates; the …

End of round 1. Made: story model r0 (deep-time frame, protagonist scaffold), story graph, brief and agreement records, author persona Faye Titcombe named and her life registered as its own model (faye-titcombe-life r0). Next, from that model's open questions: rebuild her shocks with change_arc_scaffold so they read as change arcs; model her deepest and learned wants in the construct the tool reads; give Cut-bearing moments places (Swindon, the south-coast university, the payments office, Avebury); add the long developments that enclose her life (the Swindon railway works 1843-1986, the building society and the three-day clearing cycle, the Neolithic landscape of the downs); name concepts (routine as safety, understanding as protection, the band); draw one choice of hers. Then her author model (voice), the author_reader stage, and at least three candidate worlds. Early candidate seeds, …

End of round 2. Made: Faye's life r1-r2 (change arcs, wants under an inner root, places, long developments, concepts and realizations, outlook and threat Cuts, a drawn decision: learn_it_beside_her), her author model (author.model.faye), the author_reader stage with five buttons, the candidates stage (The Exceptions Queue chosen), and names for the three principals: Kieran Hale (Kez), Barbara Ashby, Laura Russell (Lor). Next: name the building society and the chat server; the opening stage with the era marked real (documentary cutoff about 2023) and each real fact used recorded as a report with its source (the March 2020 lockdown and crash, the 2020 yield-farming summer, the November 2021 peak, the May 2022 stablecoin collapse, the June 2022 lending freezes, the November 2022 exchange collapse; the 2019 scam-reimbursement code and 2020 payee checks; banks' limits on crypto payments 2021…

Author model: Faye Titcombe, an invented persona (fictional_author), writing this novel in 2025-2026. Her life (faye-titcombe-life r2) produces six writing dispositions: band vision (offices and chat servers seen as forager bands), mechanism clarity (exact, brief explanations of how the money moves), walking beside (no warnings, no punishment, no absolution), wry comedy as a way of carrying shame, a landscape of chalk and stones with three clocks running at once, and respect for the dignity of routine. Each has a counterweight recorded with it. All basis is invented except one labelled interpretation. Composition point and reasons are recorded as basis b.composition; her life model is faye-titcombe-life revision 2 (model 4d462a80d15a0f0882d4d4926aafd99c06daff1f4fba95970e9969486919167e).

Name candidates for the invented author persona, from the random seed word 'fade' (life_story_structure_explore, name mode): Faye Titcombe, Jade Kempster, Dale Webb. Etymological remarks are ordinary English associations, not invented derivations.

Selected under delegation (LLM choice, not a human decision): the invented author persona is Faye Titcombe, born 1979 in Swindon, who publishes under that name. Reason: the name fits a working-class Swindon family in 1979, carries the seed's two private senses (fading chalk that must be scoured; betting against the crowd) without symbolism on the surface, and is not a known author's name. Jade Kempster fits the year less well; Dale Webb is flatter and fits the chosen life less.
Name candidates for the protagonist from the random seed word 'ear': Kieran Hale, Tom Earley, Ryan Hearn.

Selected under delegation (LLM choice): the protagonist is Kieran Hale, born 1990 in Swindon, called Kez by colleagues. The name is ordinary for his year and town, and the seed's sense of listening fits a man whose job is to hear a scam in a stranger's voice, without symbolism on the surface. Tom Earley reads as a pun; Ryan Hearn is flatter.
Name candidates for the retired engineer from the random seed word 'branch': Barbara Ashby, Brenda Ash, Margaret Lyne.

Selected under delegation (LLM choice): the engineer is Barbara Ashby, born 1953 in Swindon, who insists on 'Barbara, never Babs'. The name fits her year, is distinct from Kieran Hale and Faye Titcombe, and the seed's senses (bank branch, branch line, code branch, fork) are private resonances with her life, not surface symbolism.
Name candidates for Kieran's partner from the random seed word 'autumn': Laura Russell, Amber Price, Hannah Russell.

Selected under delegation (LLM choice): Kieran's partner is Laura Russell, born 1991, an intensive-care nurse; Kieran calls her Lor. Ordinary for her year and distinct from the other names; the seed's autumn stays a private resonance.
Name candidates for the chat server from the random seed word 'share': the Sharehouse, Fair Share Farmers, Share the Kill.

Selected under delegation (LLM choice): the chat server is the Sharehouse (members say 'the House'), an invented community of a few thousand anonymous yield farmers. The name reads as ordinary crypto slang; that Kieran's shared house deposit ends up serving a 'house' online is never remarked on in the prose.
Name candidates for Kieran's building society from the random seed word 'heart': the White Hart Building Society, Hearth and Home Building Society, Heartland Building Society.

Selected under delegation (LLM choice): Kieran works for the White Hart Building Society (staff say 'the Hart'), an invented mutual founded in 1868 by Swindon railwaymen meeting at a White Hart inn, head office and payments operations in west Swindon. It stands in for the town's real mutuals, which stay unnamed. A white animal sits in the old institution's name without anyone in the story remarking on it.

Completed a whole-book disclosure and physical-staging pass through the public MCP. The fourteen current prose leaves retain the exact accepted manuscript: Part Eight now separates the depeg, 2010 memory and return. Twenty-eight selected fact nodes distinguish reader disclosure from character knowledge; twelve chapter plans and thirteen stable document spans model the telling. Eight bounded native spatial Events record relative position, reach, barriers and movement already present in the prose and are explicitly rendered by their passages. No invented coordinates, reader psychology or new numerical estimates. A full voice read retained Faye’s existing prose. Fresh-reader pilot: target recovery 5/5 with the guild memory, 1/5 without; this is a five-question pilot and not whole-book quality evidence. The current model comparison reports no rewritten or retimed existing Events or changed …
Begin with practiced routine, then a call which exposes a gap in that expertise. Guild leadership is visible; the painful departure is not yet told.
Let a small carried object hold secrecy through four months of summary. The secret is disclosed to the reader, withheld from Laura and Compliance.
Contrast rapid wallet discovery with the long physical work of Laura’s night. Switch focal access explicitly: her private judgment is not Kieran’s knowledge.
Compress the summer through mechanisms, competing clocks and social recognition. Distinguish own savings from the future deposit; preserve the closed lid as an incomplete warning.
Slow to walking dialogue. Barbara controls her biography; let Kieran privately resist her grand account, leaving its authority contestable.
Alternate household fatigue, institutional action and private gains. The HOUSE folder turns a sum into an available action he does not take.
Explain enough of the peg to make risk recoverable. Separate Laura’s exhausted permission from knowledge of its mechanism; Barbara’s withheld warning creates asymmetry.
Interrupt the collapse with the 2010 raid only after the present refusal to sell. Return to professional customer care. Do not turn subjective guilt into actual accusation.
Give the reader the balance before the hopeful porch encounter. Delay Laura’s access until the statements force confession; her inward shame remains her account.
Bring Barbara physically into Laura’s kitchen, then leave Laura to stage her own handover. The hand placed beside hers invites without demanding an ending.
Let repetitive household acts carry repair, punctured by the forty-pound argument. Reinterpret the guild memory only when Kieran speaks it to Barbara; no cure is certified.
Return to the call and walking forms. Keep institutional secrecy unresolved while changing what Kieran offers a customer and where the phone is on the walk.

Barbara’s “You’re allowed” speech makes her the final authority in another woman’s exclusion; Laura can answer “I wasn’t there” while the later handover remains. The February scene names both partners, so Barbara must say “the two of you,” not Laura alone. “Laura, who had never asked for anything” overstates the character; an exchange with Jade lets us discover ordinary reciprocity and remaining awkwardness. Faye’s attention to routine dignity and wry restraint supports the small scene. These observations do not settle blame or retroactively change the February intention.

Reviewed the changed Events and the existing choices and consequences named in the local plan. Retained cast, chronology, finances, ending and numerical records; distinguish attributed interpretation from world interaction.

Enhance two existing scenes through dialogue and shared activity. Let Laura name her exclusion from the deposit decision in Barbara’s visit; give Jade a reciprocal interest in the Sunday swap. Preserve the visit, handover, slow rebuilding and existing accepted outcomes. Do not turn Barbara’s partial recognition into a settled allocation of blame. These are prospective fictional refinements, not recovered historical evidence. Follow the selected fictional author’s voice; leave other lives open unless a scene calls for more detail. No numerical values are introduced or recertified.

nodes.title: Two bounded prose changes, world model retained
nodes.text: This editorial round adopts the informed review’s two localized prose changes. Ten means ten thousand in the preceding monetary context; making the unit explicit changes no amount. The ending keeps the joke, delayed laugh, phone left in the car, wind and hand taken, while removing the repeated clocks/map explanation. It omits a destination detail without asserting a different walk or denying Kieran’s understanding. All twelve parts and existing depiction links remain. Prior reviews are historical; no numerical lens readings were rerun or declared current. The three factual model corrections in the predecessor remain an unpublished editorial candidate awaiting the author’s choice.
Barbara admits her February knowledge to Laura; Laura answers that she was not there. Barbara acknowledges that exclusion.
Barbara recounts her apprenticeship, closure, retraining and connection with Ron on their walk; her account is her chosen presentation.
Barbara offers an analogy of different historical clocks; Kieran’s disagreement with it stays private.
Kieran helps build a payment block and then routes his own payment round it.
Barbara sends a recovery phrase with fifty pounds behind it; Kieran keeps it behind his bus pass and does not declare the gift or tell Laura.
The £40 argument reveals Laura’s daily checking and Kieran’s prior knowledge of it. A CHECKED column makes this visible.
Barbara says she worked on the batch clearing system; Kieran cannot explain who could turn it off.
Savings statements force the June confession: about £290 of the deposit and £6,000 of his own tokens remain. Laura hears the hidden history.
The peg collapses; Kieran understands the mechanism but does not sell on the bounce.
Laura agrees to Kieran earning interest on the £24,000 deposit, £15,000 hers; this is not informed knowledge of the token risk.
Kieran puts £6,000 of his own holiday savings into the pools, not the shared deposit, and gains recognition as Kez.
Kieran still has not declared the customer gift to Compliance, despite greater honesty with Laura.
In May 2010 Kieran logged off a failing raid at 11.52 before his first shift; the guild later dissolved and nobody blamed him. His guilt is his interpretation.
Kieran finally tells Barbara the 2010 memory. She reframes it as going to work; he is not fully convinced.
Laura explains what the deposit and concealment meant; Kieran offers every number, every time and puts his hand next to hers without taking it.
In November Kieran has £71,000 and sees Laura’s house folder and the £3,800 shortfall; he avoids selling and explaining.
Jade asks for a Saturday in return for Laura’s Sunday; this is reciprocal help, not a rescue without needs of its own.
Kieran tells Chloe on the recorded line that it went wrong for him and asks who she will tell before releasing the payment.
On the March walk Laura takes Kieran’s hand; he left his phone in the car. This does not prove permanent recovery.
The reader sees Laura’s intensive-care work and her private easy-war judgment; she does not tell Kieran either account.
Laura interprets her exhausted delegation as her own part in the loss; this is attributed shame, not narrator-certified equal responsibility.
Kieran restores the wallet on 12 March 2020; its balance is 0.0071 BTC, then £28.14.
Kieran takes Pritchard’s loss call professionally while afraid of his own transfers being found.
Both inspect the accounts; Kieran sells his remaining £5,200 stake in September; rebuilding is household work.
Kieran reliably clears the Hart payment queue and handed his old guild to Sander when he started work.
The pools never stop; Kieran sacrifices sleep and closes his laptop when Laura comes home.
Barbara knows a failure mechanism but tells Kieran it is for him and Laura to decide; three warnings composed in her car remain unsaid.
At the May house viewing the deposit is £340 and Laura does not know; Kieran misses a chance to tell her.

nodes.title: Depleted or rested body
nodes.text: Depleted or rested body. Is {subject} made from a rested body, a tired one, or a depleted one (short of sleep, stressed for weeks, running on habit)? Why: The model holds sleep and exhaustion as processes (kieran.sleep_hours, laura.exhaustion) but no decision reads them. If depletion pushes choices towards habit and the group, then Laura's 'do what you think' on her seventh night of ten and Kieran's hold on three hours of sleep are partly the body's decisions, which changes where the story places blame and what it asks of the institutions that ran them down. Source: Stress physiology and sleep science (allostatic load: McEwen; sleep deprivation and decision-making). Over a life: A person whose consequential acts cluster in depleted weeks is being decided for by their conditions; rest restores choice.

nodes.title: Exit, voice or loyalty
nodes.text: Exit, voice or loyalty. Facing decline or harm in a group or institution they belong to, does the person answer {subject} by exit (leaving), voice (speaking up to change it) or loyalty (staying and bearing it)? Why: Kieran's loyalty to the band and Laura's silence are both loyalty without voice; Barbara exits the Hart in 2019, stays silent in February and then chooses voice in August. The lens predicts that loyalty without voice lets decline run to collapse, and that the story turns when someone moves from loyalty to voice. It also asks why Kieran exited the guild in 2010, the one exit he never forgave. Source: Albert O. Hirschman, Exit, Voice, and Loyalty (1970). Over a life: Loyalty that never finds voice ends in a late, costly exit or in collapse; learning voice is a crossing.

nodes.title: Fear or love
nodes.text: Fear or love. Is what {subject} does primarily out of fear or out of love? Why: The same kinds of fear recur across four opened readings (the five weeks, the November night, the silence toward the Hart, Laura's handover) and the same kinds of love across two (the rebuild, the desk); fixing them as the lens's children keeps every later opening on one vocabulary. Source: Round 8 openings.

nodes.title: Gift, reciprocity or market
nodes.text: Gift, reciprocity or market. Is {subject} a gift (given without price, creating a bond and an obligation), reciprocity (a mutual arrangement among members), or a market exchange (a priced transaction between strangers)? Why: Barbara's card, the rent Kieran pays his parents, the Sharehouse's three a.m. help and Barbara's lessons are gifts; the Hart was founded as reciprocity among railwaymen; the stablecoin is pure market. If the story's harm comes from treating a reciprocal thing (the shared deposit) as a market thing, and its healing from gifts (the visit, the lessons, 'pass the gravy'), the lens predicts which acts bind people and which dissolve them. Source: Marcel Mauss, The Gift (1925); Karl Polanyi, The Great Transformation (1944), on reciprocity, redistribution and exchange; David Graeber, Debt (2011). Over a life: A life or an institution that moves from reciprocity to market lo…

nodes.title: Reason, alibi or recognition
nodes.text: Reason, alibi or recognition. In {subject}, is this inner account the person's own reason (what actually moves them), an alibi (a story they tell themselves in its place, which lets them go on), or a recognition (something they come to see that they could not see before)? Why: The story's inner Events hold what moves Kieran, what he tells himself instead (at a hundred thousand it would be a surprise, and a surprise is not a secret), and later what he comes to see (the phone as all three clocks at once; the logoff as going to work). An inner lens can show the arc from alibi to recognition, and set his own reasons at the deposit (love for Laura first) against what they are doing. Compared only with other inner readings. Source: Suggested by the operator in round 7: what Kieran tells himself, read against his own reasons.

nodes.title: Script or own voice
nodes.text: Script or own voice. In {subject}, does the person speak or act in someone else's script (an institution's, a group's, a family's), in a borrowed form that carries their own words, or in their own voice? Why: Kieran's arc runs from reading scripts (the scam-check questions, the Sharehouse's chants) to asking his own questions on the last call; the confession fails because the only voice he has is the scam-line one; Laura says the unbearable thing through the handover form; Barbara never uses anyone's script but hides behind her own rule. If voice is a process, the model predicts that a person can only repair in their own voice, and that borrowed forms (the handover) are how a person who has only ever held things together finds one. Source: This story's own world (the Hart's scam-check script, the nurse's SBAR handover); kin to Bakhtin on authoritative and internally persuasive discourse…

nodes.title: Script or own voice
nodes.text: Script or own voice. Why: Kieran's arc runs from reading scripts (the scam-check questions, the Sharehouse's chants) to asking his own questions on the last call; the confession fails because the only voice he has is the scam-line one; Laura says the unbearable thing through the handover form; Barbara never uses anyone's script but hides behind her own rule. If voice is a process, the model predicts that a person can only repair in their own voice, and that borrowed forms (the handover) are how a person who has only ever held things together finds one. Revised: the first version had no answer for silence, and the silent acts (Kieran telling nobody at the Hart, Laura's two months, Barbara's Febru…

nodes.title: Shame or guilt
nodes.text: Shame or guilt. After {subject}, does the person carry it as shame (I am bad, so I must hide) or as guilt (I did something bad, so I can repair it)? Why: The model has Kieran hiding for five weeks and Barbara saying 'I didn't say it was my fault. I said what I did.' If shame and guilt are distinct processes, hiding is predicted by shame and repair by guilt, and the turning point of the story is not the confession but the conversion of shame into guilt: Barbara's visit gives Laura and Kieran the grammar of guilt. It would also predict that Kieran's first scam-line voice in the confession is shame speaking. Source: The psychology of self-conscious emotions (Helen Block Lewis; June Tangney): shame targets the self, guilt the behaviour; shame predicts concealment, guilt predicts reparation. Over a life: A person who moves from shame to guilt about the same act becomes able to repair it; one…

nodes.title: The bit that waits
nodes.text: The bit that waits. Does {subject} build in waiting before money or belief can move (a delay by design), slow it only by friction, or let it move at once? Why: Invented from Barbara's 'I wrote the bit that waits'. If waiting is a circuit breaker, the model predicts that systems which move at once fail in days (the stablecoin's spiral took four) while systems that wait fail slowly enough to be stopped, and that the old institutions' dullness is a safety feature, not only a cost. It also asks the same of people: Laura waits, Kieran cannot. Source: Invented for this story, from Barbara's line about the clearing code; kin to circuit breakers in market design and to cooling-off periods in consumer law. Over a life: A system that removes its waiting gains speed and loses its brakes.

nodes.title: Wanting, bartering or standing
nodes.text: Wanting, bartering or standing. Is {subject} done out of wanting (the child: I want it, and I get it or I don't), bartering (the adolescent: conditional, done to get a reaction, a performance for approval), or standing (the adult: acting unconditionally for what one stands for, even if disliked for it, so that setbacks make one stronger)? Why: Fear or love asks what moves an act; this asks what the act is for and on what condition. It can separate acts the model now reads alike: Kieran's reliability at the Hart and his loyalty in the Sharehouse may both be bartering for approval and belonging, which would predict that he holds in May 2022 because leaving would lose the reaction he performs for, not because he believes. nodes.title: Who can switch it off
nodes.text: Who can switch it off. Who holds the off switch of {subject}: a person, an office or board, a charismatic founder, code and whoever holds its keys, or nobody? Why: Barbara's first question to Kieran, asked of the world: the works and the plant were switched off by boards; the Hart can be; the clearing by an office; the Sharehouse by its moderators; the stablecoin by nobody, which is why its failure could not be stopped once it started; the market by nobody. Joined with Weber's types of authority and a fourth this world adds, authority by code, it predicts where the story's powerlessness comes from and why the old institutions feel both oppressive and safe. Source: Barbara Ashby's question in part 1; Max Weber's traditional, rational-legal and charismatic authority, with authority by code added for this world. Over a life: An era that moves its money from switches held by offices to swit…

nodes.title: Wonder, appetite or anxiety
nodes.text: Wonder, appetite or anxiety. Is {subject} moved by wonder (wanting to see and understand how things are), appetite (wanting more of something: money, status, the rush), or anxiety (the fear of missing out, of being left behind)? Why: The brief puts curiosity at the centre ('Human curiosity is powerful, and after years of monotony, they're tired enough to follow it'), and fear or love cannot see it: typing the twelve words in reads 31% neither. If curiosity is a process, the story's descent is wonder turning into appetite and then into anxiety, and the ending is wonder recovered without appetite (Kieran's unscripted questions on the last call, Barbara's lessons). Source: The supplied story premise; the old distinction between curiositas and studiositas (Augustine, Aquinas) and the modern psychology of fear of missing out. Over a life: A life whose wonder becomes appetite and then anxiety…

nodes.title: A model inconsistency found while answering blind review 2
nodes.text: Not in the review. The deposit process and Laura's nursing period had her fifteen thousand already saved by October 2019, while her handover and the text have it as her pandemic night shifts. Fixed in the model: about 12,000 in October 2019 (about 4,000 hers), 24,000 by January 2022 with 15,000 hers, most of it overtime from the two pandemic winters. Seven now says 'fifteen thousand of it was Laura's, most of it overtime from two pandemic winters'; her 'It was every night shift I did in the pandemic' stands as what the money means to her.

nodes.title: The story's eight decisions were drawn, not chosen
nodes.text: Every consequential choice after the white rabbit was drawn with a seed fixed in advance from weights the configured estimator (typesafe jev-1.13.0) read from the modeled states, in world order, each conditioned on the draws before it: (1) deposit consent, asks_and_she_leaves_it_to_him; (2) Barbara on the February walk, says_it_is_his_choice_and_nothing_more; (3) the depeg, holds_everything; (4) the telling, hides_it_until_the_mortgage_forces_it; (5) Laura, stays_and_holds_it_together_in_silence; (6) Barbara after the fall, the remainder, built as a new continuation: she goes to Laura herself; (7) the conversation, stay_and_rebuild_in_the_open; (8) Kieran's end, stays_at_his_desk_by_choice_with_open_eyes. The one decision not drawn is Kieran keeping the card in November 2019: the supplied story premise fixes that the protagonist chooses the unknown.

nodes.title: The drawn remainder: Barbara goes to Laura
nodes.text: The remainder of cut.barbara.2022.after meant something none of the five options held. Of the continuations her life allows, going to Laura herself is the one that (a) answers her guilt with the truth rather than money or lessons, (b) breaks her rule of never being anybody's mother in the one direction that costs her, (c) verifies the person rather than the key, and (d) is the only thing that can break Laura's drawn silence. It surprises and, read back, looks inevitable.

nodes.title: The lenses on Kieran's silence to Compliance
nodes.text: Asked of the new Compliance act (drawn: tells_nobody), the lenses read shame 0.87, fear 0.62, loyalty 0.99, rested 0.99 and standing only 0.26. The shame that turned into guilt at the kitchen table in August stays shame at work: in a rested body, by choice, he keeps one undeclared thing from the institution. That is why his crossing from bartering to standing stays partial (the ending reads wanting 0.52 and standing 0.46), and it agrees with the draw. Part 12 already carries it ('he told Laura every number, every time, and he told the Hart nothing, and he knew exactly where that line ran'), so the prose is unchanged for it.

nodes.title: Where the lenses disagree, and where I disagree with the estimator
nodes.text: Where two lenses read the same act differently. (a) Barbara's February silence: loving, standing, rested and a gift of freedom by every lens, and yet the one thing it withholds is voice (loyalty 0.81), which is what Kieran needed. Both hold: her standing was real, and it was standing for a rule that had displaced the person it was meant to protect. This opens the concept of standing into standing for a rule and standing for a person. (b) The hold: bartering (0.47) and standing (0.42) at once, loyalty (1.00), shame (0.67), depleted (0.76). It is a stand from inside and a performance from outside; the model should hold both. (c) Kieran's 2010 logoff: standing (0.93) to the lens and desertion to him. The actor-local reading (his) is operative, so it drives the hold; the external reading is true enough to be given to him later by someone he believes. (d) Laura's silence: wanting (0.91), sha…

nodes.title: The disagreement about Laura, resolved
nodes.text: Last round I disagreed with the estimator's reading of Laura as 'wanting' almost throughout and did not overwrite it. The state-free re-estimate shows that reading was an artefact of the estimator reading her last period's answer as her state; state-free, her intensive-care years read standing (0.87) and her silence bartering (0.50), which is how I read them. The other disagreements (Barbara's February silence read as virtuous by every lens; Kieran's logoff read as standing by the lens and as desertion by him) stand as recorded.

nodes.title: What the lenses found
nodes.text: Eight lenses (fear or love, wanting-bartering-standing, shame or guilt, exit-voice-loyalty, depleted or rested, gift or market, the bit that waits, who can switch it off) answered 91 records with estimator weights (13 wanting-bartering-standing records re-estimated with sharper meanings). Findings: (1) The old world waits and has an off switch; the new world does neither. The works, the Hart and the clearing wait by design (0.88-1.00) and can be switched off by an office or board (1.00); the market and the stablecoin move at once (0.96-0.99) and nobody can switch them off (0.80, 0.64). The Hart's scam-check call, a person phoning before a payment moves, is itself a bit that waits: Kieran's job is the brake. nodes.title: Who crosses, who stays stuck
nodes.text: Who crosses from bartering to standing, and what failure makes them cross? Kieran, partly and late. He barters for approval through the guild and the Hart (being needed, being reliable), barters for belonging in the Sharehouse, and the hold of May 2022 is the peak of it. The failure that makes him cross is not the loss of money but the failure of the performance: the band's reaction turns worthless ('gn frens. gn forever'), and in the confession his performed scam-line voice is the only one he has. He only reaches standing at the end (0.46 against wanting 0.52), and most clearly in an act the lens cannot see, because it has no decision Cut: the March 2023 call, where he asks a customer unscripted questions that may annoy her and then releases her payment because it is hers. Barbara never barters; she stands from 1969 on. Her crossing is inside standing, from standing for a rule (never a…

Barbara's 'I didn't say it was my fault. I said what I did' is guilt; Kieran's five weeks are shame. - Fight, flight, freeze or fawn (trauma-response literature): Kieran fawns (no trouble), Laura freezes (silence), Barbara fights. - Orders of mind (Kegan): impulsive, imperial, socialized, self-authoring, self-transforming; the socialized mind is the barter…

nodes.title: Open questions deliberately left for now

Laura's and Kieran's second estimates concentrated on the new category; Barbara's stayed uncertain (remainder 0.39) and the remainder was then drawn. nodes.title: Round 7: what I decided for each within question
nodes.text: Round 7, the within questions, macro first. Of the 29 listed at the start (39 once the finer acts were modeled), the ones that disagreed because a coarse record was misread or labelled by its end were revised: moment readings moved to the acts they were made of, the five weeks end at the evening, the porch and the rebuild say what the model already held, and two lenses were declined on a stretch they do not fit. The 31 that remain, across 16 pairs of Events, are exceptions the stretch allows, each said in the model as a relation (and one inner Event): almost all are the ending's two ledgers, home and the Hart, or the desk and the Hart, held at the same time; the rest are the late laugh on the walk, his inner reading of 2010 lagging his acts, the one crack in the silence, two concurrent change arcs, and love and a lie in one act. nodes.title: One: Blue
nodes.text: ## One: Blue The payments file left White Hart House at ten every night and came back at seven every morning with its failures sorted into a queue, and Kieran Hale had cleared that queue for nine years. Returned item, account closed. Name mismatch. Sort code retired in 2011. Fraud rule forty-one. He could read an exception the way his grandfather Ron, a fitter in the railway works until they shut, had read a boiler by the sound it made: not the words on the screen but the shape of what had gone wrong behind them. The Hart had been founded in 1868 by railwaymen pooling their wages in the back room of a White Hart inn so that each of them, one by one, could buy a house. It still had the brass hart on the door and a mural of the founders in the canteen, men with moustaches and bowler hats looking faintly surprised to find themselves on a wall in west Swindon. Kieran liked the mural. He liked most things about the Hart. That was the problem, if it was a problem. His week had one shape. The 8.12 bus from Old Town. The blue lanyard. The tea round, which went clockwise from the window and which nobody had ever agreed to and everybody kept. Cut-off at ten. Lunch at one. The Thursday quiz at the Beehive, where his team came third nearly every week. Laura's rota on the fridge, printed monthly and held up by a magnet from Weymouth: days, nights, and the twelve-and-a-half-hour shifts she …

nodes.title: Two: Rabbit
nodes.text: ## Two: Rabbit The envelope came up from the post room on Friday 1 November, addressed in blue biro capitals: MR K. HALE, PAYMENTS EXCEPTIONS, THIRD FLOOR, WHITE HART HOUSE. It was the only letter anyone on the floor had received by name in a year, and Deb whistled. "Is it a love letter? Kieran. Is it from the helicopter man?" "It's a customer thing," he said. "It's fine. Honestly. It's just a thank-you, I think." Inside was a white index card and a sheet of lined paper torn from a pad. The card had twelve words on it in the same capitals, numbered, in two columns. They were ordinary words, some of them almost a poem, and he read them twice and then again, and they stayed words. The note said: There is fifty pounds behind these. It is yours. Go and look. B.A. On the back, in smaller capitals, was an email address. He knew what the words were before he let himself know it. He had cleared enough payments to exchanges and read enough of the fraud team's bulletins. It was a recovery phrase: twelve words from a fixed list which were, in the new world, the whole of a wallet. Whoever held the words held the money. There was no branch behind them, no mural, no brass hart, no three-day cycle, no exceptions queue. Just the words. Gifts from customers had to be declared. It was in the handbook, section nine, and in the refresher course Compliance ran every October in the training room, w…

nodes.title: Three: Mirror
nodes.text: ## Three: Mirror On the evening of Thursday 12 March 2020 the news said the markets had had their worst day since 1987 and bitcoin had lost half its value in a day. Laura was on a long and would not be home until after nine. The flat smelt of the pasta bake she had left him, covered in foil, with a note that said 40 MINS 180 LOVE YOU. She had written it at six that morning with her coat on, and had known, writing it, that he would forget. Kieran stood at the kitchen table with the television on in the other room and took the card out of his wallet. He downloaded a wallet app. It asked him whether he wanted to create a new wallet or restore one. It felt like the character-select screen of a game he had not played for ten years: new, or continue. He pressed restore. It gave him twelve empty boxes, and he typed the words into them one by one. Confirm, said the screen. He put his thumb on the glass. For a moment nothing happened, and the black surface of the phone gave him back his own face, lit from below, a man in a kitchen in Old Town in a Hart fleece, tired, ordinary. Then the glass seemed to soften under his thumb, the way a puddle gives when you step in it expecting ground, and the balance rose out of nothing. 0.0071 BTC. £28.14. Half of what she had given him. The first thing the other world taught him was that it moved while you watched it. "Right," he said aloud, to nobod…

nodes.title: Four: Field
nodes.text: ## Four: Field What happened that summer happened to everyone who was there, and they all said the same thing about it afterwards, and the thing they said was: what the actual hell was that. In the middle of June a lending protocol started paying its users in a new token just for using it, and within two months there were pools, and pools of pools, and tokens named after food, and people moving money between them at three in the morning to chase yields of four hundred, nine hundred, two thousand percent a year. Kieran read the words and none of them meant anything. Liquidity. Impermanent loss. Governance. Gas. Staking. Slippage. Rug. APY, APR, TVL, LP, DAO, ape, degen, wen, ser. A new word every hour, a new protocol every day, and every protocol named after something you could eat. A sushi one. A pasta one. A pickle one. A yam, which lasted about a day and a half and then broke, and everybody laughed about it, and some people lost their houses. "Oh my God," he said to the empty spare room at two in the morning, and then, because it was two in the morning, he typed into the search bar: wtf is impermanent loss. He learned it anyway, the way he had learned the game: by doing the stupid thing first and reading the forums after. In July he put in six thousand pounds: his own savings, which were going to pay for Crete, Laura's first holiday abroad since a school trip to Calais, befo…

nodes.title: Five: Tribe
nodes.text: ## Five: Tribe They met in the car park above Avebury on a Sunday, with a hard wind coming across the downs. She was smaller than her voice, grey-haired, in a waxed jacket older than he was, with a collie that ignored him completely. She kept her hands in her pockets. She looked him up and down the way you look at a fuse board. "You're taller than you sound," she said. "Come on. She needs walking, and so do you, by the look of you." She lived at Avebury Trusloe, the far side of the village from the stones, in a cottage with a satellite dish she had put up herself. She walked faster than he did. They went up onto the Ridgeway, the chalk track white between the fields, and she told him about herself in the order she chose, in short sentences. "Rodbourne. Dad was a boilermaker in the works, Grandad before him. I wanted to be an electrician from when I was ten. Mended the wireless with a hairgrip. Nobody took it serious." A stile; she went over it without using her hands. "1969 they let me in as an apprentice. Three women on the tools in the whole works. The men called me Babs. I didn't answer to it. After about a year they stopped." "My grandad was in the works," Kieran said. "Ron Hale. He was a fitter." She stopped on the track. "Ron Hale. Boiler shop. Big hands. Whistled Elvis." For a moment she looked at him differently. "He called me Barbara from the first week. Him and about…

nodes.title: Six: Harvest
nodes.text: ## Six: Harvest In January 2021 the third lockdown sent Laura back onto the unit for the worst weeks of the whole thing. She came home in the dark and sat in the car outside the flat for twenty minutes before she came up. Kieran watched her from the spare-room window, the dome light off, her hands on the wheel, and stayed where he was, because he thought she wanted to be alone, and because he did not know what he would say if he did. When she came up she took her uniform off in the hallway and put it straight into the machine on a sixty, and stood in the shower until the hot water ran out. "How was it?" he said, when she came out. "We lost two." She was towelling her hair, not looking at him. "One was forty-one. Sats wouldn't come up. We proned him four times." She hung the towel on the radiator, square. She hung everything square. "It's fine. What did you do?" "Nothing. Work. The batch." He had made nine thousand pounds that week. He left it unsaid. It would have sounded like a different language, and it was. Later she lay on the sofa scrolling through houses in Wroughton on her phone. It was the only thing she looked at that was not a monitor. A three-bed semi with a front door painted green. A garden with a shed. "That one's got a porch," she said. "Look. You could put your boots in it." "It's nice." "It's got a front door that's ours." She said it lightly. She said all the…

nodes.title: Seven: Anchor
nodes.text: ## Seven: Anchor After November the prices went down, gradually and then all at once and then gradually again. By Christmas his seventy-one thousand was fifty. By the new year it was forty-five. His own money stayed where it was, in the farm tokens and the pools, because moving it would have meant selling at the bottom, and he did not sell at the bottom. The Sharehouse stopped talking about moons. zoom out it's a healthy correction ser anyone who sells here deserves to be poor smart money is going to safe yield, typed Dmitri. twenty percent on a dollar. it literally does not move. Safe yield was a dollar. Not a real dollar, but a token that was always worth a dollar, and a savings protocol that paid nearly twenty percent a year for holding it. The token did not keep its dollar with dollars in a vault. It kept it with a trick of arithmetic: anyone could always swap one of them for a dollar's worth of a sister token, and back, and all that swapping held the price in place like a tent held by its guy ropes. Kieran read the paper. He understood it. He understood that the ropes held only while the sister token was worth more than all the dollars tied to it, and he understood that everybody in the tent believed it would hold, and that the believing was part of what held it. It was a peg. Everything he had ever worked in was a peg, when you looked: the Hart's deposits, the three-day …

## Eight: Hole On Saturday 7 May the dollar that did not move moved. Ninety-nine cents, then back. The Sharehouse made jokes about it. lol the dollar is at 0.99 i'm literally shaking buy the dip on a dollar On Monday evening, the ninth, it was ninety-eight, then ninety-three, then eighty. Laura was on nights; the rota said so. Kieran sat at the spare-room desk with the Sharehouse open on one screen and the price on the other, and he stayed awake, and the ropes went one by one. He knew exactly what was happening. That was the worst of it. People were selling the dollar and swapping it for the sister token, and each swap made new sister tokens out of nothing, and each new sister token made the others worth less, so each swap needed more of them, and the fall fed itself like a fire in a draught. He could have drawn it on a whiteboard. He could have written the Hart's fraud team a short, excellent email about it, with a diagram. it has always come back, said the Sharehouse. do not sell. that is literally what they want we are all in this together frens. hold the line The founder's account posted that he was deploying more capital. A thousand cartoon faces reposted it. It was like the old raids, when the tank died and the healer died and twenty-five people on voice chat were shouting, and the one thing you never did, the thing people never forgave, was leave. Hold. Hold. Everybody …

By Thursday it was twenty cents, and the Hart's fraud lines filled with customers who had lost their savings, some of them through the same app Kieran had used to walk round the block he had built, and the payments team was pulled onto the phones. He was afraid of the Hart. All morning he waited for somebody from the fraud team to come down to the third floor with a printout of three payments of eight thousand pounds and his name at the top. Nobody came. They were busy with the customers. After lunch he took a call from a man in Stratton who had put in his redundancy money. "I'm sixty-one," the man said. "I was at the plant. Thirty years. They said it was a dollar. A dollar. Can you get it back? You're a bank. Can you get it back?" Stratton. The plant. Thirty years. He did not let himself think of his father. "I'm really sorry, Mr Pritchard," Kieran said. "I'm just going to take a few details, and then I'll explain what we can and can't do. Is that okay?" His own voice came out of his mouth steady and kind and professional, the voice he had used on Barbara, and the man began to cry, and Kieran said he was very sorry, and he was. After the call he sat with his headset on and the line dead and looked at the orange flags in the queue until Deb put a hand on his shoulder and asked if he wanted a tea. "No, you're alright. Thanks, Deb. I'm fine." He went home and checked a balance t…

It was the night before his first shift at the Hart. Twenty-five of them on voice chat, four minutes into the hardest fight of the expansion, the fight they had been trying for six weeks. The tank went down. Someone in Tallinn was shouting for heals. Kieran, calling it, looked at the clock on his bedroom wall in Penhill, which said 11.52, and at the shirt his mother had ironed for the morning on the back of the door, and said into the headset, "Sander, you've got it," and logged off. He never logged in again. He heard later that they wiped, and wiped again, and that by June the guild had broken up and Sander had stopped playing. Nobody blamed him. Somebody wrote on the forum: kez had a real life to go to. That was the part he could not forgive. That it had been easy. That nobody had minded. That twenty-five people had been in the dark and he had gone to bed.

nodes.title: Nine: Silent
nodes.text: ## Nine: Silent For five weeks he said nothing. He went to work and came home. He took the calls. He checked the dead balance at night; by June it was a few hundred pounds, then less. He lost weight. His right hand shook when he held his phone, so he started holding it in his left. He slept three hours a night and told Laura it was the heat. He knew how to do this. He had learned it with a white card behind a bus pass: you carried the thing everywhere, you let the week go on around it, and you told no one, and after a while the not telling was the heaviest thing in the wallet. "You look grey," she said one morning, coming in off a night. "Are you eating?" "I'm fine. Honestly. It's just work. The scam lines are mental at the moment." "Get your bloods done." She was already in the kitchen, already opening the fridge. "I mean it. You look like my Tuesday admissions." On the last Saturday in May Laura had a day off, and she had booked a viewing. It was the house from her phone, back on the market after a sale had fallen through: the three-bed semi in Wroughton with the green front door and the porch. The agent was a boy in a tight suit who called her Lauren twice. Laura walked through it touching the door frames, as she touched a patient's shoulder before she did anything to them. She opened the kitchen cupboards. She stood in the smallest bedroom and looked down at a garden with …

nodes.title: Ten: Stone
nodes.text: ## Ten: Stone On a weekday in August, while Kieran was at the Hart, Barbara Ashby took the bus into Swindon from the stop outside the Red Lion, which she had not done in two years. She had left the car at home on purpose. She sat at the front, where she could see the road, with her handbag on her knees like a toolbox. She had not asked anyone for anything since March 1986, when she had stood in the personnel office at the works and asked whether there was anything, anything at all, and been told there was not. She was not going to ask for anything now. She was going to give something, and it was not money, and she did not know how you gave it. She rehearsed nothing. Rehearsing was what she had done in February, all the way home in that car, and look where that had got everybody. In town she walked up Wood Street, past the pubs that had been banks, to the bakery Kieran had once brought her lardy cake from, and knocked on the door of the flat above it. She had worked out from what he said about the rota that Laura would be home between nights on a Tuesday. If she was wrong she would come back on the Wednesday. Laura answered in a hoodie and pyjama bottoms, between nights, with her hair tied up. This small grey woman in a waxed jacket was a stranger to her. "You're Laura," the woman said. "I'm Barbara. I'm the one who sent him the card." "I know who you are," Laura said. "Good," …

nodes.title: Eleven: Field, Again
nodes.text: ## Eleven: Field, Again In the morning Laura got up before him, on her day off, and when he came into the kitchen she had the laptop open at the bank and a pen in her hand. "Right," she said. "Show me. All of it. Every account." He sat down beside her and showed her, and she wrote down every number he read out, in a column down the side of the page, the way she wrote obs. Her hand was not quite steady. They opened one account that both of them could see. They stuck a spreadsheet on the fridge next to the rota, held by a second magnet, from Lyme Regis. It was a ledger, Kieran thought, the oldest thing there was: not the kind anyone in the world could read, like the one that had swallowed the deposit, but the kind two people could. They postponed the house by two years. In September he sold what was left of his own tokens, five thousand two hundred pounds, and paid it into the joint account, and they both watched the number arrive. Kieran deleted the apps and told Laura every number, every time, until telling her every number stopped feeling like confession and started feeling like housekeeping. He slept again: six hours, then seven. "Four hundred and twelve in the joint," he would say, coming in. "Car insurance is up." "Course it is," she would say. "Everything's up. Put the kettle on." Laura asked her friend Jade on the unit to swap so that she could have one Sunday a month of…

nodes.title: Twelve: Awake
nodes.text: ## Twelve: Awake He stayed on the payments-exceptions desk at the Hart. The routine was the same. He was not. He knew how old the machine was now, and what ran under it, and who could switch it off. He knew what the new machine had done to him in the night. He kept the card in his wallet behind his bus pass, soft as cloth now, with its 0.0071 bitcoin still behind it, which he had looked up once that spring: about a hundred and fifty pounds. He had never spent it and never would. It was not a key any more. It was a reminder, kept by choice, as his grandfather Ron had kept a brass works tally token in his pocket for fifteen years after the hooter stopped. It was also, he knew, a gift from a customer that he had never declared. In October Harriet from Compliance had run the same refresher course in the training room, with the same cartoon of the man holding the chocolates under the red cross, and he had sat through it with the card in his wallet and had not put his hand up. He never told her about the card, or the app, or the three payments of eight thousand pounds. He told Laura every number, every time, and he told the Hart nothing, and he knew exactly where that line ran. author_reader: The book comes out of Faye Titcombe's invented life: a railway-works child who learned that routine is someone else's to end, an archaeologist of the first gatherings, eighteen years inside the payments batch, a fall into decentralized finance in 2020-2022 that she understood and could not stop. She writes it in 2025-2026 beside a fifteen-year-old daughter who has just found a trading app. The story presses the fear of being left behind, the fear that a safe life is someone else's to end, the longing for more world, and the shame of knowing better.

candidates: Three candidate worlds from Faye's life: The Exceptions Queue (a Swindon payments clerk handed twelve words by an engineer who built the old machine), Twelve Words (a warehouse picker finds a stranger's wallet) and The Pension (a claims handler of fifty-eight). Chosen under delegation: The Exceptions Queue, keeping the twelve words and an older person's late wonder from the others.

opening: The chosen world opened in four successive accounts: October 2019 to March 2023 in Swindon and on the downs; Kieran Hale, Barbara Ashby and Laura Russell; the card of twelve words; the wallet first opened on the night bitcoin halved; the 2020 lockdown and yield-farming summer; the grand battle through Kieran's own working day; the house deposit in the stablecoin; the May 2022 collapse; an ending open to the model's draws. The era is real with a documentary cutoff of 31 March 2023. Two claims of the earlier accounts are revised to reconcile with documented prices.

units.title: One: Blue
units.text:
## One: Blue

The payments file left White Hart House at ten every night and came back at seven every morning with its failures sorted into a queue, and Kieran Hale had cleared that queue for nine years. Returned item, account closed. Name mismatch. Sort code retired in 2011. Fraud rule forty-one. He could read an exception the way his grandfather Ron, a fitter in the railway works until they shut, had read a boiler by the sound it made: not the words on the screen but the shape of what had gone wrong behind them.

The Hart had been founded in 1868 by railwaymen pooling their wages in the back room of a White Hart inn so that each of them, one by one, could buy a house. It still had the brass hart on the door and a mural of the founders in the canteen, men with moustaches and bowler hats looking faintly surprised to find themselves on a wall in west Swindon. Kieran liked the mural. He liked most things about the Hart. That was the problem, if it was a problem.

His week had one shape. The 8.12 bus from Old Town. The blue lanyard. The tea round, which went clockwise from the window and which nobody had ever agreed to and everybody kept. Cut-off at ten. Lunch at one. The Thursday quiz at the Beehive, where his team came third nearly every week. Laura's rota on the fridge, printed monthly and held up by a magnet from Weymouth: days, nights, and the twelve-and-a-half-hour shifts she called longs. Sunday lunch in Penhill, where his father talked about the car plant closing in 2021 as if it were weather.

"They'll find something for the good ones," his father said, carving. "Pass the gravy."

"You're one of the good ones, Dad."

"Pass the gravy, Kieran."

He was twenty-nine. He was reliable. His appraisals used the word three times. At sixteen he had run a raiding guild of forty people across six countries in an online game, set the timetables, called the pulls, known who was sulking in Lisbon and who needed carrying in Tallinn, and nobody on the third floor knew it. When he took the job at twenty he had logged off for the last time, handed the guild to a Dutch boy called Sander, and become, deliberately, no trouble to anyone.

Some Sunday evenings the week sat on his chest like a cat. He kept it to himself. It seemed an ungrateful thing to feel in a town where people had queued outside the plant gates for jobs.

On Monday 21 October 2019, at 3.40 in the afternoon, fraud rule forty-one stopped a payment of forty thousand pounds from a savings account opened in 1989 to an account at a crypto exchange, and the case dropped into his queue with a small orange flag. Deb, from the next bank of desks, leaned round her monitor. She had sat next to him for six years and had decided long ago that he was the nicest man on the floor and slightly wasted on it.

"Ooh. Forty grand to bitcoin. That's a romance scam, that is. Some bloke in Ghana with a picture of a helicopter."

"Could be," Kieran said. "Probably not. Sorry, Deb, I just need to ring her."

He rang her.

"Hello, is that Mrs Ashby? Sorry to bother you. My name's Kieran, I'm calling from the White Hart's payments team about a transfer you made earlier today. It's nothing to worry about, it's just a check we do."

"Barbara," said the voice. "Never Mrs. You've got a script, haven't you. Go on, then. Read it to me."

He read her the script. Has anyone contacted you and asked you to move your money. Have you been promised a return. Has anyone asked you to keep this conversation private. Have you been asked to download anything onto your computer.

She answered each question like a woman filling in a form she had designed herself. No. No. No. No.

"Brilliant, thank you, that's really helpful," he said, which was what you said. "I'll just make a note and then I can—"

"My turn," she said. "How old is the system you're sat in?"

"Sorry?"

"The clearing. Not your quick payments, the batch: the salaries, the direct debits, the thing that runs every night and takes three days to move money that could move in a second. How old is it?"

He found, with a small cold shock, that he did not know. "It's been updated a lot," he said. "I think."

"I updated it," said Barbara Ashby. "From 1988 to 2013, at a bureau in Reading. I wrote the bit that waits. It was built for magnetic tape, my love. It's got more patches on it than my dad's allotment shed. Do you know who could switch it off?"

"I'm not sure that's really—"

"No," she said. "You don't. Nobody on your floor does. That's not your fault. What's your surname, Kieran? And which desk is that?"

He told her: Hale, payments exceptions, third floor. Nothing in the script told him not to. He released the payment at 4.55, because nothing in the script allowed him to stop it, and he went home on the bus with the feeling of having walked past a door he had not known was in the wall.

units.title: Two: Rabbit
units.text:
## Two: Rabbit

The envelope came up from the post room on Friday 1 November, addressed in blue biro capitals: MR K. HALE, PAYMENTS EXCEPTIONS, THIRD FLOOR, WHITE HART HOUSE. It was the only letter anyone on the floor had received by name in a year, and Deb whistled.

"Is it a love letter? Kieran. Is it from the helicopter man?"

"It's a customer thing," he said. "It's fine. Honestly. It's just a thank-you, I think."

Inside was a white index card and a sheet of lined paper torn from a pad.

The card had twelve words on it in the same capitals, numbered, in two columns. They were ordinary words, some of them almost a poem, and he read them twice and then again, and they stayed words. The note said: There is fifty pounds behind these. It is yours. Go and look. B.A. On the back, in smaller capitals, was an email address.

He knew what the words were before he let himself know it. He had cleared enough payments to exchanges and read enough of the fraud team's bulletins. It was a recovery phrase: twelve words from a fixed list which were, in the new world, the whole of a wallet. Whoever held the words held the money. There was no branch behind them, no mural, no brass hart, no three-day cycle, no exceptions queue. Just the words.

Gifts from customers had to be declared. It was in the handbook, section nine, and in the refresher course Compliance ran every October in the training room, which he had sat a fortnight before: the one with the cartoon of a man holding a box of chocolates with a red cross over it. Declaring it would mean a form, and the form would mean Compliance, and Compliance would mean a note on Barbara Ashby's file. It would make her a case. It would make him a colleague who had accepted something.

In the guild there had been a rule, never written down, that you did not take loot you had not earned in front of people who had. He thought about that. Then he thought that there was nobody in front of him.

He put the card in his wallet, behind his bus pass, and did not declare it. He told nobody, not even Laura. It was the first thing in five years he had not told Laura, and all day he could feel it there behind the bus pass, a small square of weight.

He left the words alone. He looked them up once, on his phone in the third-floor toilets, confirmed what they were, and put the phone in his pocket and washed his hands. For four months the card rode in his wallet across the town and back. It softened at the corners. Every scam call he made after that had a second voice in it.

"Has anyone asked you to move your money?" he would say, and in his head Barbara said: How old is the thing you're sat in?

"Have you been promised a return?" And: Who could switch it off?

The routine stayed the same. It only began, faintly, to feel like a costume. Warm, well made, and somebody else's: the Hart fleece he wore on dress-down Fridays.

In the canteen the founders looked down from their mural with their moustaches and their surprise. He found himself wondering what the back room of the White Hart had smelt of in 1868, beer and coal smoke and wet wool, and whether any of those men had lain awake afraid that the thing they were building would not hold.

At the Thursday quiz the question was which animal Alice followed down the hole, and everyone at the table wrote rabbit, and they came third.

units.title: Three: Mirror
units.text:
## Three: Mirror

On the evening of Thursday 12 March 2020 the news said the markets had had their worst day since 1987 and bitcoin had lost half its value in a day. Laura was on a long and would not be home until after nine. The flat smelt of the pasta bake she had left him, covered in foil, with a note that said 40 MINS 180 LOVE YOU. She had written it at six that morning with her coat on, and had known, writing it, that he would forget.
