Kieran stood at the kitchen table with the television on in the other room and took the card out of his wallet.

He downloaded a wallet app. It asked him whether he wanted to create a new wallet or restore one. It felt like the character-select screen of a game he had not played for ten years: new, or continue. He pressed restore. It gave him twelve empty boxes, and he typed the words into them one by one.

Confirm, said the screen.

He put his thumb on the glass. For a moment nothing happened, and the black surface of the phone gave him back his own face, lit from below, a man in a kitchen in Old Town in a Hart fleece, tired, ordinary. Then the glass seemed to soften under his thumb, the way a puddle gives when you step in it expecting ground, and the balance rose out of nothing.

0.0071 BTC. £28.14.

Half of what she had given him. The first thing the other world taught him was that it moved while you watched it.

"Right," he said aloud, to nobody. "Okay. Right."

Then he found the explorer, the public ledger, and pasted in his address, and there was the transaction that had sent him the coins on 31 October 2019, and the one before that which had sent them to her, and behind that another, and another, branching back through thousands of hands and eleven years. There was no queue. There was no cut-off. There were no exceptions, only confirmations. Anyone could read it. Anyone in the world. He sat down on the kitchen chair so suddenly that it scraped.

It was like the moment in the old game when you rode out of the starting valley for the first time and the map, which you had thought was the world, turned out to be a green corner of a continent, with the rest of it black at the edges, waiting. New area discovered. He had forgotten that feeling.

Laura came in at twenty past nine and found him still at the table with the pasta bake cold in its foil.

"You haven't eaten," she said. "Kieran. It said forty minutes. It was on the note."

"Sorry. Sorry. I got caught up. The markets are mad."

"Everything's mad." She put her bag down very carefully, as she did after a bad shift. "They're saying it's going to be us next. Like Italy. We're rehearsing proning tomorrow." She saw his face and stopped. "It's fine. Eat your tea."

On 23 March the country locked down. Laura went onto the COVID intensive-care unit at the hospital on the edge of town and began sleeping in the day with a towel over the curtain rail. Kieran carried the queue home on a laptop and set it up in the spare room, and the Hart shrank to a screen, and the week lost its shape. What it had instead was the laptop, and the phone, and the card, and every night after the file went, the black edges of the map.

He only read. He read until three in the morning, as he had read patch notes at fifteen, and in the day he cleared the exceptions queue from the spare room with Laura asleep through the wall. When she woke they talked about the car park and the canteen and whether the Co-op had flour, because there was nothing either of them could say about their real day that would not frighten the other.

What she did not tell him about were nights like the one in the middle of April, when the unit was running at half again as many beds as it was built for, and the alarms went all night like birds in a hedge. She spent twelve and a half hours in a hood that made her own breath loud in her ears. At three in the morning she and six others turned a man of fifty-eight onto his front, on the count of the one holding his head, every line and tube gathered in their hands so that nothing pulled, because on his front his lungs might take the air the machine was pushing into them. At five she held a phone to another man's ear so that his daughter in Leeds could tell him the cat was fine, and that she loved him, and that he was not to worry about the cat. She did not cry. You did not, on the unit. You did it in the car, or not at all.

At eight she came home and found Kieran asleep at the spare-room desk with his cheek on his arm and his phone lit beside him, a green line climbing on it. She stood in the doorway in her coat and thought: at least one of us is having an easy war. Then she took her uniform off in the hall, put the towel over the curtain rail and went to bed, and she did not tell him that either.

units.title: Four: Field
units.text:
## Four: Field

What happened that summer happened to everyone who was there, and they all said the same thing about it afterwards, and the thing they said was: what the actual hell was that.

In the middle of June a lending protocol started paying its users in a new token just for using it, and within two months there were pools, and pools of pools, and tokens named after food, and people moving money between them at three in the morning to chase yields of four hundred, nine hundred, two thousand percent a year. Kieran read the words and none of them meant anything. Liquidity. Impermanent loss. Governance. Gas. Staking. Slippage. Rug. APY, APR, TVL, LP, DAO, ape, degen, wen, ser. A new word every hour, a new protocol every day, and every protocol named after something you could eat. A sushi one. A pasta one. A pickle one. A yam, which lasted about a day and a half and then broke, and everybody laughed about it, and some people lost their houses.

"Oh my God," he said to the empty spare room at two in the morning, and then, because it was two in the morning, he typed into the search bar: wtf is impermanent loss.

He learned it anyway, the way he had learned the game: by doing the stupid thing first and reading the forums after.

In July he put in six thousand pounds: his own savings, which were going to pay for Crete, Laura's first holiday abroad since a school trip to Calais, before the pandemic cancelled it. It was his money. It was not the deposit. He told himself that on the landing, with his hand on the bathroom door, and it was true.

He began to farm. That was the word. You put your seed into a field and it grew and you harvested it and replanted, and the fields were open all night, and the crop did not care what time it was in Wiltshire. He set alarms for three and five, and learned which pools would thin at which hours. There were three clocks in the spare room now: his body's, which wanted to sleep at eleven; the Hart's, which sent the file at ten and brought it back at seven; and the pools', which never stopped. He started living by the third. It did not occur to him until much later that he was not farming the tokens so much as they were farming him: that what he had planted was his own sleep, and that it was being harvested every night at three.

In August, the week the yam broke, a link in a thread about it took him to a chat server called the Sharehouse, where a few thousand anonymous people with cartoon avatars were awake in every time zone at once.

anyone awake, said the channel, at 3.14 a.m. British Summer Time.

awake ser

frens who is farming the new pool

ser the new pool is a rug

ser everything is a rug if you zoom out enough

He asked why a swap he was thinking of making would fail, and a man in Ohio with a frog for a face answered it in forty seconds, and a woman in Manila with a cat in sunglasses corrected the man in Ohio, and they argued, and in the end somebody called Dmitri with no avatar at all posted a diagram. Kieran understood the diagram. He understood it as he had understood raid bosses at fifteen: completely, and then in his sleep. The next week somebody new asked the same question, and he answered it before anyone else could.

ser you are a legend, typed the frog. who is this guy

kez, typed Dmitri. kez knows.

He sat in the blue light of the spare room with his heart going like a boy's.

The yields were real, some of them. By September his six thousand was nine.

"You're up early," Laura said once, coming in from a night at seven and finding him at the laptop in his dressing gown.

"Couldn't sleep," he said, and closed the lid, not quickly, because quickly would have meant something.

In September, the month of the rule of six, Barbara emailed him. He had written to the address on the back of her note once, in March, a single line: thank you, I looked. She wrote back: Good. Do you walk?

units.title: Five: Tribe
units.text:
## Five: Tribe

They met in the car park above Avebury on a Sunday, with a hard wind coming across the downs. She was smaller than her voice, grey-haired, in a waxed jacket older than he was, with a collie that ignored him completely. She kept her hands in her pockets. She looked him up and down the way you look at a fuse board.

"You're taller than you sound," she said. "Come on. She needs walking, and so do you, by the look of you."

She lived at Avebury Trusloe, the far side of the village from the stones, in a cottage with a satellite dish she had put up herself.

She walked faster than he did. They went up onto the Ridgeway, the chalk track white between the fields, and she told him about herself in the order she chose, in short sentences.

"Rodbourne. Dad was a boilermaker in the works, Grandad before him. I wanted to be an electrician from when I was ten. Mended the wireless with a hairgrip. Nobody took it serious." A stile; she went over it without using her hands. "1969 they let me in as an apprentice. Three women on the tools in the whole works. The men called me Babs. I didn't answer to it. After about a year they stopped."

"My grandad was in the works," Kieran said. "Ron Hale. He was a fitter."

She stopped on the track. "Ron Hale. Boiler shop. Big hands. Whistled Elvis." For a moment she looked at him differently. "He called me Barbara from the first week. Him and about two others." She set off again. "He was all right, your grandad."

"It must have been hard, though. The rest of them."

"It was a job. I was good at it. Seventeen years." She walked on. "Then March '86, and they shut the lot. Hundred and forty years, and the hooter just stops. Whole town's clock, that hooter. People who never set foot in the works set their kitchen clocks by it. And then it doesn't go, and you're thirty-three with a trade nobody wants."

"What did you do?"

"Learned computers. Nights at the tech. First in the exam." She said it flat, a meter reading, without pride. "The bureau took me on in '88. Twenty-five years keeping the clearing standing up. Nobody ever put my name on anything. That's fine. I know what I built. I know where the bodges are, too."

"And now you don't trust it."

"I watched it nearly stop in 2008." She slowed. "Money going out one end, not coming in the other, the whole thing holding its breath for a weekend. My code, waiting. I didn't know if it'd arrive. Then someone wrote nine pages about a ledger nobody can switch off, and I read it three times on the train to Reading. Bought my first coins the year I retired. Never sold one." She turned her head. "What are you in? Not coins. Don't tell me you're in the casino."

He told her about the Sharehouse, the pools, the farms, the nine thousand. She laughed: one short bark, not unkind, not kind either.

"Right," she said. "So you've swapped a bank you can't see for a hundred blokes with cartoon faces you can't see. At least the bank's got a mural."

"It's not like that. They're really good, some of them. There's this guy Dmitri, he—"

"Mind," she said, and stopped, and pointed.

Far below them the great stones stood in their circle round the village, grey and small at that distance, though some of them were taller than a double-decker, with the village inside the ring, pub and all.

"Farmers put those there," she said. "Four and a half thousand years ago. Dragged them across the downs on sledges. Forty tons, some of them. Took generations. Do you know why?"

"Religion?"

"That's what the signs say. I'll tell you what I think, for nothing." She pulled the collie's ear. "They wanted somewhere to gather. People will do almost anything to have a place to gather. That chat room of yours is the same animal. Worse food."

"I heard a man on the radio," she said. "Biologist. Ants, mostly. He said the trouble with people is we've got Palaeolithic emotions, medieval institutions and god-like technology." She looked down at the stones. "He missed one out. A phone in your hand at three in the morning."

Kieran thought that a phone in your hand at three in the morning was not a fourth thing but all three at once, and that the man on the radio had missed nothing. He let it stand. He kept the rest to himself as well: that the Sharehouse was the first band since the guild that needed him, and that when he typed and forty people answered he felt what the men in the back room of the White Hart must have felt: that he was one of them, that they were building something, that it would hold.

At the car park she opened her boot and the collie jumped in.

"Same time next month," she said. It was not a question. "Wear proper shoes."

They walked most months after that. She never once asked him to stop.

units.title: Six: Harvest
units.text:
## Six: Harvest

In January 2021 the third lockdown sent Laura back onto the unit for the worst weeks of the whole thing. She came home in the dark and sat in the car outside the flat for twenty minutes before she came up. Kieran watched her from the spare-room window, the dome light off, her hands on the wheel, and stayed where he was, because he thought she wanted to be alone, and because he did not know what he would say if he did.

When she came up she took her uniform off in the hallway and put it straight into the machine on a sixty, and stood in the shower until the hot water ran out.

"How was it?" he said, when she came out.

"We lost two." She was towelling her hair, not looking at him. "One was forty-one. Sats wouldn't come up. We proned him four times." She hung the towel on the radiator, square. She hung everything square. "It's fine. What did you do?"

"Nothing. Work. The batch." He had made nine thousand pounds that week. He left it unsaid. It would have sounded like a different language, and it was.

Later she lay on the sofa scrolling through houses in Wroughton on her phone. It was the only thing she looked at that was not a monitor. A three-bed semi with a front door painted green. A garden with a shed.

"That one's got a porch," she said. "Look. You could put your boots in it."

"It's nice."

"It's got a front door that's ours." She said it lightly. She said all the important things lightly, so they could be taken as jokes if they had to be. She had been moved on from five rented houses before she was thirteen. In six years with him she had never once asked for anything except that.

The market went up. By the Christmas just gone his six thousand had been fifteen thousand pounds; by February it was thirty-eight; then forty-five. The Sharehouse had grown to four thousand members. People asked for Kez by name.

kez is this safe

kez wen new pool

kez my mum wants to get in, what do i tell her

tell her only what she can lose, he wrote, and felt wise, and did not think about his own mother.

In June the Hart's board decided to block payments to several crypto exchanges, after the regulator's warnings and a run of scam losses, and because Kieran knew better than anyone on the floor why a payment failed, they seconded him to the project that built the block.

It was the year everybody was at war with everybody. The regulator said anyone buying crypto should be prepared to lose all their money, and the Sharehouse printed it on a T-shirt. Banks blocked exchanges, exchanges bought the fronts of football shirts, and the Sharehouse posted a tyrannosaurus in a tie with the caption have fun staying poor.

The block went live on a Thursday in July. At nine there was a call on Teams to mark it, nine faces in nine spare rooms, and Harriet from Compliance, who was new and very serious, shared her screen: a bar chart of the year's scam losses, taller every month. She told them about a widow in Highworth who had sent her savings to a man she had met on an app. "We're seeing a lot of harm," she said. "Kieran, you know what that looks like better than any of us."

His phone lay face down by his keyboard and buzzed all through the call. It was #war-room, where a sixth-former in Hull was explaining that the Hart and everything like it were legacy institutions and deserved what was coming.

"I think if we just look at the merchant category codes we'll catch most of it," Kieran said, and his project manager said, "Brilliant, Kieran, that's exactly the kind of thing."

That night a new pool opened at midnight, and he wanted two thousand pounds in it before the yield came down. His card was refused. He sat and looked at the refusal for a while, the reason code and the short polite sentence under it, which he had helped to write. Then he opened a payments app the Hart had never heard of, sent the money to himself, and from himself to the exchange, and it arrived in forty seconds. It never felt like lying.

At the end of July the car plant made its last car. His father worked the final shift and came home with his hi-vis vest and a commemorative mug and put the mug in the cupboard over the kettle and did not take it out again.

"They gave us a mug," he said at Sunday lunch.

"Dad. I'm so sorry."

"It's only a mug." He carved. "Pass the gravy."

For three months, until the union won back his father's agency years and the redundancy money came through, Kieran paid his parents' rent from his gains, by bank transfer on the first of the month, with the reference MUM AND DAD. His father thanked him once, in the car outside the Job Centre, without looking at him.

"You didn't have to."

"I wanted to."

"Well." His father looked at the Job Centre's glass door, and at his own reflection in it. "Your grandad would have liked that. Doesn't matter where it comes from, he used to say, as long as it comes."

It was the best thing the money ever did. It was also the thing that made him certain the money was real: that the game was not a game, that he had been right, that everybody who had laughed at the food tokens was wrong.

His mother asked him once, in the kitchen with the door shut, whether it was that bitcoin. He said it was savings. She said, "Well, be careful," and he said he was.

In October the Sharehouse met in Swindon. One of the regulars, a cartoon owl, turned out to live in Stratton, and she booked the back room of a pub in Old Town in the name of a darts team. You went past the toilets and through a door marked PRIVATE FUNCTION, and there it was, the hidden world, in a room that smelt of carpet and chips. Eleven of them. The owl was a dental nurse called Mandy. There was a lorry driver who had made four hundred thousand pounds and still drove the lorry, because what else would he do all day. There was a retired postman, a man from the council's parking department, and a boy who should not have been in a pub and whose mother thought he was at chess club. Nobody looked like their avatar. Nobody looked like a wizard. They looked like the queue at the post office.

"You're Kez," Mandy said, and held out her hand. "I thought you'd be older."

"Sorry."

"Don't be sorry. You saved me eleven hundred quid in the summer with that thing about slippage." She lifted her glass. "To Kez."

"To Kez," said the room, and he stood in the back room of a pub in the town where he was born and felt it: whatever the railwaymen had felt in the back room of the White Hart in 1868, whatever the farmers felt when the last stone went up. The band had faces now.

By November 2021 his screen said he was worth seventy-one thousand pounds. He liked it, more than he would have admitted. Some nights he opened the app only to look at the number, and felt it in his shoulders like a warm bath. His alarms went at three and five. The rota on the fridge said LONG, LONG, OFF, NIGHT, NIGHT, NIGHT, and he read it every morning as he read the price: to know what was coming.

Laura had a shortlist of three houses and a folder called HOUSE on the laptop they shared. He had never opened it. One night that month, with Laura asleep through the wall between two nights, he opened the laptop to pay the electricity, and there it was on the desktop where it had been for a year, and he opened it.

Three houses, each in its own folder, the listings saved. A spreadsheet of what the mortgage would be at four different rates. A document called DEPOSIT with one line in it, updated in September: 21,200. Under it, in her capitals: 3,800 TO GO.

He sat with his phone in his other hand and the number on it. He could sell in the morning and pay the deposit into the joint account three times over, and she would never do another extra night for it. He had the app open. What stopped him was not the price. It was the question she would ask, which was where it had come from, and the answer, which was a year and a half of nights she had slept through and a card behind his bus pass she had never heard of.

So he told himself the thing he went on telling himself all winter: not yet. At a hundred thousand it would be a surprise, and a surprise is not a secret.

He closed the folder the way she had left it, and paid the electricity, and went back to the spare room.

units.title: Seven: Anchor
units.text:
## Seven: Anchor

After November the prices went down, gradually and then all at once and then gradually again. By Christmas his seventy-one thousand was fifty. By the new year it was forty-five. His own money stayed where it was, in the farm tokens and the pools, because moving it would have meant selling at the bottom, and he did not sell at the bottom. The Sharehouse stopped talking about moons.

zoom out

it's a healthy correction ser

anyone who sells here deserves to be poor

smart money is going to safe yield, typed Dmitri. twenty percent on a dollar. it literally does not move.

Safe yield was a dollar. Not a real dollar, but a token that was always worth a dollar, and a savings protocol that paid nearly twenty percent a year for holding it. The token did not keep its dollar with dollars in a vault. It kept it with a trick of arithmetic: anyone could always swap one of them for a dollar's worth of a sister token, and back, and all that swapping held the price in place like a tent held by its guy ropes. Kieran read the paper. He understood it. He understood that the ropes held only while the sister token was worth more than all the dollars tied to it, and he understood that everybody in the tent believed it would hold, and that the believing was part of what held it. It was a peg. Everything he had ever worked in was a peg, when you looked: the Hart's deposits, the three-day cycle, the plant, the works. They held because everyone agreed they would.

House prices in Wroughton had gone up faster than the deposit. The deposit was twenty-four thousand pounds in a savings account at the Hart, earning nothing, and fifteen thousand of it was Laura's, most of it overtime from two pandemic winters.

On a Sunday in January he said it at the kitchen table. The rota was on the fridge behind her. She had the calendar open and was writing viewings into it in green pen.

"Lor. Can I— sorry, can I just run something past you? It's a money thing. It's boring."

"Mm."

"I want to move the deposit somewhere it'll actually earn something before we buy. Twenty percent. It's pegged to the dollar. It doesn't go up and down like the other stuff. It's basically a savings account, just— better."

She barely looked up. She had worked seven nights out of the last ten, and the green pen was running out.

"You're the one who knows about money," she said. "Do what you think."

"Are you sure? I can explain how it—"

"Kieran." She shook the pen. "I trust you. Do what you think."

He did not explain what a stablecoin was, and she did not ask.

She had meant it. When he said twenty percent and a dollar she had thought of the monitors on the unit: numbers she did not have to check, because somebody competent was watching them. For years she had been the one who held everything, the rota and the bills and her mother's bad years and the ventilated and the dying, and saying do what you think was the first time she had put anything down. For a second, at the kitchen table, with the green pen running out, it had felt like rest.

By the end of the week the twenty-four thousand pounds had left the Hart in three payments of eight thousand, on three days, to his own account in the app it had never heard of. He knew to the pound what would drop a payment into the exceptions queue: he had cleared that queue since he was twenty, and he had helped write the rules. None of the three was flagged. Then it became twenty-four thousand pounds' worth of dollars that did not move, earning twenty percent, and he checked it every morning before he checked the time. Every morning it was a little bigger.

In February he told Barbara on the Ridgeway, walking towards the long barrow, pleased with himself.

She stopped walking. She looked at the barrow for a long time, at the great sarsens of its doorway, and he waited for her to say the thing about casinos.

She nearly told him. She had the whole of it ready: the tent and the guy ropes, the sister token, the arithmetic. What stopped her was the other name in it. Half that money was Laura's, and Laura was not there and had not asked her, and Barbara, who had spent seventeen years in the works being talked about by men who never said it to her face, had never in her life discussed a woman's money behind her back.

"That's yours and Laura's to decide," she said.

"But what do you think? Honestly. You know how these things work better than—"

"I think it's yours and Laura's to decide." She clicked her tongue at the collie. "Come on. Dog's getting cold."

She said nothing else about it all afternoon. She talked about the men who had dragged the stones, and about the collie's hips, and about a programmer she had worked with in 1994 who had kept a ferret in his desk drawer. On the short drive down to Avebury Trusloe, with the collie asleep on the back seat, she composed the three sentences she could have said, clause by clause. One: a dollar held up by guy ropes is a tent, and tents come down in weather. Two: take Laura's half out tomorrow, whatever you do with your own. Three: I gave you that card, so I get a say. They were good sentences. She said none of them out loud, even to the dog, because she had never been anybody's mother and did not mean to start at sixty-eight.

## Eight: Hole

On Saturday 7 May the dollar that did not move moved. Ninety-nine cents, then back. The Sharehouse made jokes about it.

lol the dollar is at 0.99 i'm literally shaking

buy the dip on a dollar

On Monday evening, the ninth, it was ninety-eight, then ninety-three, then eighty. Laura was on nights; the rota said so. Kieran sat at the spare-room desk with the Sharehouse open on one screen and the price on the other, and he stayed awake, and the ropes went one by one.

He knew exactly what was happening. That was the worst of it. People were selling the dollar and swapping it for the sister token, and each swap made new sister tokens out of nothing, and each new sister token made the others worth less, so each swap needed more of them, and the fall fed itself like a fire in a draught. He could have drawn it on a whiteboard. He could have written the Hart's fraud team a short, excellent email about it, with a diagram.

it has always come back, said the Sharehouse.

do not sell. that is literally what they want

we are all in this together frens. hold the line

The founder's account posted that he was deploying more capital. A thousand cartoon faces reposted it. It was like the old raids, when the tank died and the healer died and twenty-five people on voice chat were shouting, and the one thing you never did, the thing people never forgave, was leave. Hold. Hold. Everybody hold.

On Tuesday it touched sixty cents and bounced to ninety and the channel roared.

TOLD YOU

few understand

He could have sold at ninety. He could have sold at sixty. He did not, because selling would make it real, and because of a night in May 2010.

It was the night before his first shift at the Hart. Twenty-five of them on voice chat, four minutes into the hardest fight of the expansion, the fight they had been trying for six weeks. The tank went down. Someone in Tallinn was shouting for heals. Kieran, calling it, looked at the clock on his bedroom wall in Penhill, which said 11.52, and at the shirt his mother had ironed for the morning on the back of the door, and said into the headset, "Sander, you've got it," and logged off. He never logged in again. He heard later that they wiped, and wiped again, and that by June the guild had broken up and Sander had stopped playing. Nobody blamed him. Somebody wrote on the forum: kez had a real life to go to. That was the part he could not forgive. That it had been easy. That nobody had minded. That twenty-five people had been in the dark and he had gone to bed.

By Thursday it was twenty cents, and the Hart's fraud lines filled with customers who had lost their savings, some of them through the same app Kieran had used to walk round the block he had built, and the payments team was pulled onto the phones. He was afraid of the Hart. All morning he waited for somebody from the fraud team to come down to the third floor with a printout of three payments of eight thousand pounds and his name at the top. Nobody came. They were busy with the customers.

After lunch he took a call from a man in Stratton who had put in his redundancy money.

"I'm sixty-one," the man said. "I was at the plant. Thirty years. They said it was a dollar. A dollar. Can you get it back? You're a bank. Can you get it back?"

Stratton. The plant. Thirty years. He did not let himself think of his father.

"I'm really sorry, Mr Pritchard," Kieran said. "I'm just going to take a few details, and then I'll explain what we can and can't do. Is that okay?"

His own voice came out of his mouth steady and kind and professional, the voice he had used on Barbara, and the man began to cry, and Kieran said he was very sorry, and he was. After the call he sat with his headset on and the line dead and looked at the orange flags in the queue until Deb put a hand on his shoulder and asked if he wanted a tea.

"No, you're alright. Thanks, Deb. I'm fine."

He went home and checked a balance that was a number and then a smaller number.

By Friday the thirteenth the deposit was worth about three thousand pounds and falling, and his own tokens, going down with everything else, were worth about ten thousand. The sister token was worth almost nothing. The Sharehouse had gone from certainty to instructions to silence to jokes to goodbyes.

it was an honour farming with you all

gn frens. gn forever

units.title: Nine: Silent
units.text:
## Nine: Silent

For five weeks he said nothing.

He went to work and came home. He took the calls. He checked the dead balance at night; by June it was a few hundred pounds, then less. He lost weight. His right hand shook when he held his phone, so he started holding it in his left. He slept three hours a night and told Laura it was the heat. He knew how to do this. He had learned it with a white card behind a bus pass: you carried the thing everywhere, you let the week go on around it, and you told no one, and after a while the not telling was the heaviest thing in the wallet.

"You look grey," she said one morning, coming in off a night. "Are you eating?"

"I'm fine. Honestly. It's just work. The scam lines are mental at the moment."

"Get your bloods done." She was already in the kitchen, already opening the fridge. "I mean it. You look like my Tuesday admissions."

On the last Saturday in May Laura had a day off, and she had booked a viewing.

It was the house from her phone, back on the market after a sale had fallen through: the three-bed semi in Wroughton with the green front door and the porch. The agent was a boy in a tight suit who called her Lauren twice. Laura walked through it touching the door frames, as she touched a patient's shoulder before she did anything to them. She opened the kitchen cupboards. She stood in the smallest bedroom and looked down at a garden with a shed and a trampoline the sellers were leaving behind.

In the porch she turned round, and her face was lit up in a way she almost never let anyone see.

"You could put your boots in here," she said.

The deposit was worth three hundred and forty pounds. He had checked it in the car.

"It's nice," Kieran said.

"It's more than nice." She turned to the agent. "How fast would we need to move?"

The agent said the sellers wanted a quick sale and were open to offers. Laura said she would email the mortgage adviser on Monday. Kieran looked at the green door and thought: now, here, in the porch, before she sends it. He said, "Monday, yeah," and held the door for the agent.

In the car she talked all the way home about where the sofa would go. At the Wroughton roundabout she put her hand on his knee, which she did perhaps twice a year, and said, "I know work's been horrible. It'll be better once we're in." He said it would. He would remember that roundabout for the rest of his life, and nobody watching from the pavement would have seen anything at all.

At the start of June Mandy messaged him privately. The owl, and then:

hiya kez sorry to bother u

i lost 11k. the dollar one

my husband doesnt know. he thinks its in the isa

should i tell him?

He sat at the spare-room desk for a long time. Then he typed: yes. tonight. before he finds out some other way. it's worse if he finds out.

thanks kez, she wrote. ur a good one x

He closed the laptop. He did not tell Laura that night, or the next, or for ten days after that.

When the mortgage adviser answered Laura's email in the middle of June, asking for their savings statements, Laura forwarded it to him with a thumbs-up and a small house.

He told her that evening at the kitchen table, with the rota on the fridge behind her. He had rehearsed it on the landing, on the bus, in the third-floor toilets, and none of the versions survived the first sentence.

"Lor. I need to tell you something and I need you to let me get to the end. Sorry. I'm sorry. I just need to get to the end."

He told her everything, from the beginning, in the order it had happened: the call in October 2019 and the card behind his bus pass; the spare room and the farms and the Sharehouse, where people called him Kez; the number in November, seventy-one thousand pounds, and the night he had opened her folder called HOUSE and closed it again the way she had left it; then January, the dollar that did not move, the ropes, the Tuesday bounce, the Friday, the five weeks. He told her how much, to the pound. His voice did the thing it did on the scam line, steady and professional, and he hated it, and he could not stop it, because it was the only voice he had that did not shake. He did not cry, because he did not think he was allowed to.

She listened. She let him get to the end. When he stopped she asked three questions, as if she were taking a history.

"How much is left?"

"Of the deposit, about two hundred and ninety pounds. Of mine, about six thousand."

"Is any of it recoverable?"

"No. I don't think so. No."

"Does anyone else know?"

"Barbara. Some of it. Not all."

"Right," Laura said. "Okay."

Then she went to bed.

In the morning she moved what was left into an account in her own name, picked up two extra shifts a week, and withdrew the mortgage enquiry with a polite email he found in the shared inbox: Due to a change in our circumstances. She did not shout. If she cried, it was in the car. She had learned on five doorsteps, watching her mother hand back keys to men who did not look at her, that you hold everything together and you say nothing, and she was very good at it, and she held.

What she felt, under the holding, was not only anger. It was the thing she had seen on her mother's face on those doorsteps. She had been asked. She had said do what you think, and she had not looked, and she had handed their front door to him the way her mother handed back keys. She could not look at the fridge. She could not have said any of it, because saying it would have meant saying her own part, and she had no words for her own part. Nobody had ever shown her what they sounded like.

The flat went quiet in a new way. Before, they had been two people with screens: hers the monitors, his the charts. Now his charts showed a dead number, and there were no more words either. The rota stayed on the fridge. He read it every morning to know when she would be asleep, awake or gone, and understood that for two years he had been reading it as a timetable of when nobody would be watching.

In July he walked with Barbara and told her the rest. She did not laugh, and she did not say anything about casinos. She walked a long way without speaking, faster than him, the collie trotting to keep up, and at the long barrow she stopped and put her hand flat on one of the great stones, as if she were checking it for current.

"I gave you a key," she said, "and not a map."

"It's not your fault."

"I didn't say it was my fault. I said what I did." She took her hand off the stone. "Those are different things. You'll learn that."

Then she said nothing else, all the way down.

units.title: Ten: Stone
units.text:
## Ten: Stone

On a weekday in August, while Kieran was at the Hart, Barbara Ashby took the bus into Swindon from the stop outside the Red Lion, which she had not done in two years. She had left the car at home on purpose. She sat at the front, where she could see the road, with her handbag on her knees like a toolbox. She had not asked anyone for anything since March 1986, when she had stood in the personnel office at the works and asked whether there was anything, anything at all, and been told there was not. She was not going to ask for anything now. She was going to give something, and it was not money, and she did not know how you gave it. She rehearsed nothing. Rehearsing was what she had done in February, all the way home in that car, and look where that had got everybody.

In town she walked up Wood Street, past the pubs that had been banks, to the bakery Kieran had once brought her lardy cake from, and knocked on the door of the flat above it. She had worked out from what he said about the rota that Laura would be home between nights on a Tuesday. If she was wrong she would come back on the Wednesday.

Laura answered in a hoodie and pyjama bottoms, between nights, with her hair tied up. This small grey woman in a waxed jacket was a stranger to her.

"You're Laura," the woman said. "I'm Barbara. I'm the one who sent him the card."

"I know who you are," Laura said.

"Good," said Barbara. "Can I come in? I won't stay. I don't sit down in other people's kitchens, so you needn't bother with the kettle."

She stayed standing, in the kitchen by the fridge with the rota on it and told Laura what she had done, in short flat sentences.

"I gave him a key without a map. I checked the key and not the person. That's the opposite of everything I believe, and I did it anyway, because I liked his voice on the phone and I thought, there's one who could see it. In February he told me where your deposit was. I knew how that thing could fail. I could have drawn it for him on the back of a car-park ticket. I said it was his choice and nothing else, because I have never been anybody's mother, and I have been very proud of that for fifty years." She looked at the rota. "That part's mine. The rest is his. I'm not here to make it better. I can't. I'm here because somebody in this should say it out loud to you, and it isn't going to be him, and by the look of you it isn't going to be you either."

Laura stood with her arms folded. "You don't know anything about me."

"No. That's fair." Barbara looked at her properly then. "I know what holding everything looks like. I held a whole works together for seventeen years, one fuse at a time, and nobody ever asked me how. You're allowed to say something. That's all. That's all I came to tell you. You're allowed."

"You knew about the deposit," Laura said.

"In February. Yes."

"And you didn't say."

"I said it was for the two of you to decide."

"I wasn't there."

Barbara opened the clasp of her handbag and closed it again.

"No," she said. "You weren't."

When she had gone, Laura sat at the kitchen table for a long time. Then she took the rota off the fridge, and looked at the months of it, the longs and the nights and the days, and put it back, square, under the magnet from Weymouth.

That evening, when Kieran came in, she was sitting at the table with a notepad, as she sat at handover.

"Sit down," she said. "I'm going to do this how I know how to do it, or I won't be able to do it at all. Don't interrupt."

He sat.

"Situation," Laura said. "Our deposit's gone. Fifteen thousand of it was mine. It was every night shift I did in the pandemic. Every one." She never looked down at the notepad. "Background. I've been moved out of five houses. The last one I was twelve and I carried my stuff to the car in a bin bag because we'd run out of boxes, and I decided, I'm never doing that again. Never. That money was a front door. That's what it was. It wasn't money." She breathed in, out, as she taught relatives to. "Assessment. You lied to me for five weeks. You went to work and came home and ate your tea and lied. And before that there were two years of nights in that room, and a year of them rich. In November you had seventy-one thousand pounds on your phone. That's three deposits. You opened my folder and saw what I still needed and closed it again, and I was doing extra nights for it, and you let me. That's worse than the money. It's so much worse than the money, Kieran. And I said do what you think. I know I did. I said it because I was so tired of being the one who holds everything that I handed it to you without looking. So that's mine. Barbara's right. That bit's mine." Her voice went, and came back. "Recommendation."

She stopped. It was the only line she had not written down.

"I don't know," she said. "I don't know. I want you to tell me what we do."

He did not answer with the scam-line voice. He did not have it any more. He reached across the table and put his hand next to hers, not on it, where she could take it or not.

"We tell each other everything," he said. "Every number. Every time. Even the boring ones. And we start again, slowly. And I'm sorry. I'm so sorry, Lor."

She did not take his hand. She did not move hers away. It was the first conversation they had had in two years that neither of them was having through a screen, and it went on until after one in the morning, and at the end of it she was the one who said, "Come to bed," and he was the one who cried.

units.title: Eleven: Field, Again
units.text:
## Eleven: Field, Again

In the morning Laura got up before him, on her day off, and when he came into the kitchen she had the laptop open at the bank and a pen in her hand.

"Right," she said. "Show me. All of it. Every account."

He sat down beside her and showed her, and she wrote down every number he read out, in a column down the side of the page, the way she wrote obs. Her hand was not quite steady.

They opened one account that both of them could see. They stuck a spreadsheet on the fridge next to the rota, held by a second magnet, from Lyme Regis. It was a ledger, Kieran thought, the oldest thing there was: not the kind anyone in the world could read, like the one that had swallowed the deposit, but the kind two people could. They postponed the house by two years. In September he sold what was left of his own tokens, five thousand two hundred pounds, and paid it into the joint account, and they both watched the number arrive. Kieran deleted the apps and told Laura every number, every time, until telling her every number stopped feeling like confession and started feeling like housekeeping. He slept again: six hours, then seven.

"Four hundred and twelve in the joint," he would say, coming in. "Car insurance is up."

"Course it is," she would say. "Everything's up. Put the kettle on."

Laura asked her friend Jade on the unit to swap so that she could have one Sunday a month off with him. They compared their phones by the lockers, with Jade's coat half on.

"I can do one," Jade said. "You take my Saturday?"

"Of course. And if there's anything else—"

"Lor. It's a swap."

They tried it again when the next rota came out. On the unit Laura had always been the one who said the true thing first, to consultants, to families, to the dying. Asking for a day off with Kieran made her feel as if she ought to explain what they would do with it. She put it in the calendar in green.

Rebuilding was slow and dull, and they chose that too. It was harvest in the old sense: the same field, the same work, every season, nothing that doubled overnight.

On the first of those Sundays they went to Penhill for lunch. His father had work now, as caretaker at the primary school at the bottom of the road, and he made the tea himself, and he made it in the plant mug: SWINDON 1992-2021 THANK YOU, in blue on white, the mug that had gone into the cupboard over the kettle on the night of the last shift and had not come out since.

"Dave Pritchard lost his redundancy on that bitcoin," his father said, carving. "Thirty years on the line with me, Dave. Put the lot in a dollar that wasn't a dollar."

Kieran put his knife down. "I know," he said, and left it there. The call was a customer's. He looked at Laura, and Laura looked back and nodded once, a nurse's nod: go on. "Dad. Mum. I need to tell you something about our deposit."

He told them. His mother, Sue, put her hand over her mouth, and then took it away and said, not to him but to Laura, "Are you all right, love? Are you?" His father listened with the carving knife in one hand and the fork in the other, and when Kieran had finished he set them down very carefully, either side of the joint.

"Your grandad," he said, "lost a week's wages on a horse once. 1961. Your nan didn't speak to him till Whitsun." He picked up the mug and drank from it and put it down. "Pass the gravy, Kieran."

It was, Laura said in the car, the most she had ever heard him say.

In October he forgot to tell her about forty pounds.

It was a game for the laptop. He had not bought one since he was twenty, and he had meant to say and hadn't. She found it on a Thursday evening, going down the statement with the green pen as she did every month now, and she put the pen on the line and turned the paper round so that he could read it.

"What's this?"

"Oh. That's a game. Sorry." He heard himself and could not stop. "It's forty quid, Lor."

"I know what forty quid is." She did not raise her voice. "Every number, every time. You said that. At this table."

"I forgot. That's all it is. I forgot."

"On the laptop," she said. "In the spare room."

It was the worst row of their eight years, and it was about forty pounds, and for an hour neither of them said what it was about. He said he could not live like a man on probation. She said nobody had asked him to. He said it felt like it. At the end of it she sat down on the kitchen floor with her back against the fridge, under the rota and the spreadsheet, and put her hands over her face.

"Every day," she said, through them. "Since August. I've checked the account behind your back every day. I hate it. I hate myself for it."

"I know," he said. "You leave the bank open on the laptop."

She took her hands away. "You knew."

"Since the first week."

"And you let me. Every day. And you never said."

"I thought you were owed it."

She stared at him. Then she began to laugh, and it was very close to crying. "That's the same thing," she said. "Kieran. That's exactly the same thing again."

He sat down on the floor next to her, with his back against the fridge as well, and after a while she leaned into him. Later they added a column to the spreadsheet on the fridge, headed CHECKED, and she ticked it every night for a month, openly, and then one night forgot to.

In November a big exchange collapsed in the background, and it turned out its customers' money had been used by its trading firm, and bitcoin fell to a quarter of its peak. Barbara's coins fell with it.

"You're very calm about it," Kieran said on the Ridgeway.

"I've seen three of these. Four, if you count 2008, and I do." She walked on. "The coins aren't the point. The point's that nobody can switch them off. Price is just noise."

She did not sell. And on the walks she began, unasked, to explain things to him. How the clearing actually worked, file by file, down to the byte. Why the bit that waits had been written to wait: because in 1988 you could not be sure the other bank existed until morning. What a key was, and what a map was, and the difference.

"A key gets you in," she said. "A map tells you where the floor stops. I gave you the one without the other. So." She tapped her head. "Map. Month by month. You'll hate it. Wear proper shoes."

The walks became lessons, and he let them. Somewhere in the second month he found that he liked it again: not the number, which he no longer looked at, but the thing itself, how the old machine and the new one actually worked, the black edges of the map coming in slowly, on foot, at Barbara's pace.

In December he told her about the guild: the raid, the clock that said 11.52, the shirt on the back of the door, Sander. He had never told anyone. She walked a long way before she answered.

"In the works," she said, "when the hooter went, a man put his tools down and went home. Middle of a job, sometimes. Nobody called it deserting." She looked at him sideways. "You went to work, Kieran. You were twenty and you went to work. That's not leaving your mates. That's the first grown-up thing you ever did."

He had told himself the story one way for twelve years. It took him most of the walk down to hear it the other way, and he was not sure, even at the car park, that he believed it. But something in him that had been holding its breath since 2010 let a little of it out.

Half the Sharehouse's channels were empty now. A few regulars still posted gm in the mornings, from Ohio and Manila and São Paulo. Dmitri had gone; his account said deleted user. Kieran looked in sometimes, and only looked. Once, when he had woken at three for no reason and gone through to the spare room out of old habit, a newcomer asked whether it was too late to get in, and Kieran wrote a long careful message about pegs and guy ropes and fires in draughts, and then deleted it, and wrote instead: ask someone who loves you to sit with you while you decide.

The newcomer replied: lol ok boomer.

He closed the laptop and went back to bed, where Laura was asleep, on a day off, next to him.

units.title: Twelve: Awake
units.text:
## Twelve: Awake

He stayed on the payments-exceptions desk at the Hart. The routine was the same. He was not.

He knew how old the machine was now, and what ran under it, and who could switch it off. He knew what the new machine had done to him in the night. He kept the card in his wallet behind his bus pass, soft as cloth now, with its 0.0071 bitcoin still behind it, which he had looked up once that spring: about a hundred and fifty pounds. He had never spent it and never would. It was not a key any more. It was a reminder, kept by choice, as his grandfather Ron had kept a brass works tally token in his pocket for fifteen years after the hooter stopped.

It was also, he knew, a gift from a customer that he had never declared. In October Harriet from Compliance had run the same refresher course in the training room, with the same cartoon of the man holding the chocolates under the red cross, and he had sat through it with the card in his wallet and had not put his hand up. He never told her about the card, or the app, or the three payments of eight thousand pounds. He told Laura every number, every time, and he told the Hart nothing, and he knew exactly where that line ran.

In March 2023 fraud rule forty-one stopped a payment of twelve thousand pounds from a saver in her twenties to one of the exchanges the block had never covered, and the case dropped into his queue with its small orange flag, and he rang her.

"Hi, is that Chloe? Sorry to bother you. My name's Kieran, I'm calling from the White Hart's payments team about a transfer you made this morning. It's just a check we do."

He read her the script. Has anyone contacted you and asked you to move your money. Have you been promised a return. Has anyone asked you to keep this conversation private.

She said no to all of it, a little impatiently. He would have, too.

"Brilliant. Thank you. That's everything I need." He looked at the flag. "Can I ask you something that isn't on the script? You can tell me to get lost."

"Go on."

"Do you know how old the thing is that you're leaving? And how new the thing is that you're going into?" He waited. "And if it goes wrong, who are you going to tell?"

There was a silence on the line. Then she said, "Have you ever bought any? Yourself?"

Nobody had asked him that at work, and every call on this line was recorded. He thought of the card behind his bus pass, and the three payments, and whoever might one day play this back in a training room. Then he said it anyway. "Yes. It went wrong. That's why I'm asking."

Another silence. "My brother, probably," she said at last. "He'd kill me."

"Tell him before," Kieran said. "Not after. That's all. Good luck, Chloe."

He understood then, with the line quiet and the flag still orange on his screen, what he was for. Barbara had written the bit that waits into the machine. He was the bit that waits in the building: a person between a saver and the speed of everything, asking her to stop for the length of a question.

He held the payment until 4.55, as long as the day would let him, and then released it, because nothing in the rules let him stop it, and because it was hers. He hoped she would ring her brother first.

For a week afterwards he half expected someone from Quality to come down to the third floor with a transcript. Nobody did.

On the Sunday the three of them walked on the Ridgeway: Barbara in front with the collie, too fast; Laura, who had never been up there, in the middle, in new boots; Kieran behind. The chalk track ran white between the fields, as it had for five thousand years. Far below them the stones stood in their circle round the village, grey and small, with smoke going up from the pub chimney.

"Why would anyone drag them all that way?" Laura asked.

"To gather," Kieran said. "People will do almost anything to have somewhere to gather."

Barbara snorted, because it was her line. "He steals everything," she said to Laura. "Watch your purse."

"I know," Laura said. "He's got my deposit."

She had not made a joke about it before. Barbara laughed, and Kieran laughed too, a beat late.

His phone was in the car.

The wind came over the downs. Laura took his hand without looking. She was sure it would be there.

unit.title: One: Blue
unit.text:
## One: Blue

The payments file left White Hart House at ten every night and came back at seven every morning with its failures sorted into a queue, and Kieran Hale had cleared that queue for nine years. Returned item, account closed. Name mismatch. Sort code retired in 2011. Fraud rule forty-one. He could read an exception the way his grandfather Ron, a fitter in the railway works until they shut, had read a boiler by the sound it made: not the words on the screen but the shape of what had gone wrong behind them.

The Hart had been founded in 1868 by railwaymen pooling their wages in the back room of a White Hart inn so that each of them, one by one, could buy a house. It still had the brass hart on the door and a mural of the founders in the canteen, men with moustaches and bowler hats looking faintly surprised to find themselves on a wall in west Swindon. Kieran liked the mural. He liked most things about the Hart. That was the problem, if it was a problem.

His week had one shape. The 8.12 bus from Old Town. The blue lanyard. The tea round, which went clockwise from the window and which nobody had ever agreed to and everybody kept. Cut-off at ten. Lunch at one. The Thursday quiz at the Beehive, where his team came third nearly every week. Laura's rota on the fridge, printed monthly and held up by a magnet from Weymouth: days, nights, and the twelve-and-a-half-hour shifts she called longs. Sunday lunch in Penhill, where his father talked about the car plant closing in 2021 as if it were weather.

"They'll find something for the good ones," his father said, carving. "Pass the gravy."

"You're one of the good ones, Dad."

"Pass the gravy, Kieran."

He was twenty-nine. He was reliable. His appraisals used the word three times. At sixteen he had run a raiding guild of forty people across six countries in an online game, set the timetables, called the pulls, known who was sulking in Lisbon and who needed carrying in Tallinn, and nobody on the third floor knew it. When he took the job at twenty he had logged off for the last time, handed the guild to a Dutch boy called Sander, and become, deliberately, no trouble to anyone.

Some Sunday evenings the week sat on his chest like a cat. He kept it to himself. It seemed an ungrateful thing to feel in a town where people had queued outside the plant gates for jobs.

On Monday 21 October 2019, at 3.40 in the afternoon, fraud rule forty-one stopped a payment of forty thousand pounds from a savings account opened in 1989 to an account at a crypto exchange, and the case dropped into his queue with a small orange flag. Deb, from the next bank of desks, leaned round her monitor. She had sat next to him for six years and had decided long ago that he was the nicest man on the floor and slightly wasted on it.

"Ooh. Forty grand to bitcoin. That's a romance scam, that is. Some bloke in Ghana with a picture of a helicopter."

"Could be," Kieran said. "Probably not. Sorry, Deb, I just need to ring her."

He rang her.

"Hello, is that Mrs Ashby? Sorry to bother you. My name's Kieran, I'm calling from the White Hart's payments team about a transfer you made earlier today. It's nothing to worry about, it's just a check we do."

"Barbara," said the voice. "Never Mrs. You've got a script, haven't you. Go on, then. Read it to me."

He read her the script. Has anyone contacted you and asked you to move your money. Have you been promised a return. Has anyone asked you to keep this conversation private. Have you been asked to download anything onto your computer.

She answered each question like a woman filling in a form she had designed herself. No. No. No. No.

"Brilliant, thank you, that's really helpful," he said, which was what you said. "I'll just make a note and then I can—"

"My turn," she said. "How old is the system you're sat in?"

"Sorry?"

"The clearing. Not your quick payments, the batch: the salaries, the direct debits, the thing that runs every night and takes three days to move money that could move in a second. How old is it?"

He found, with a small cold shock, that he did not know. "It's been updated a lot," he said. "I think."

"I updated it," said Barbara Ashby. "From 1988 to 2013, at a bureau in Reading. I wrote the bit that waits. It was built for magnetic tape, my love. It's got more patches on it than my dad's allotment shed. Do you know who could switch it off?"

"I'm not sure that's really—"

"No," she said. "You don't. Nobody on your floor does. That's not your fault. What's your surname, Kieran? And which desk is that?"

He told her: Hale, payments exceptions, third floor. Nothing in the script told him not to. He released the payment at 4.55, because nothing in the script allowed him to stop it, and he went home on the bus with the feeling of having walked past a door he had not known was in the wall.

unit.title: Two: Rabbit
unit.text:
## Two: Rabbit

The envelope came up from the post room on Friday 1 November, addressed in blue biro capitals: MR K. HALE, PAYMENTS EXCEPTIONS, THIRD FLOOR, WHITE HART HOUSE. It was the only letter anyone on the floor had received by name in a year, and Deb whistled.

"Is it a love letter? Kieran. Is it from the helicopter man?"

"It's a customer thing," he said. "It's fine. Honestly. It's just a thank-you, I think."

Inside was a white index card and a sheet of lined paper torn from a pad.

The card had twelve words on it in the same capitals, numbered, in two columns. They were ordinary words, some of them almost a poem, and he read them twice and then again, and they stayed words. The note said: There is fifty pounds behind these. It is yours. Go and look. B.A. On the back, in smaller capitals, was an email address.

He knew what the words were before he let himself know it. He had cleared enough payments to exchanges and read enough of the fraud team's bulletins. It was a recovery phrase: twelve words from a fixed list which were, in the new world, the whole of a wallet. Whoever held the words held the money. There was no branch behind them, no mural, no brass hart, no three-day cycle, no exceptions queue. Just the words.

Gifts from customers had to be declared. It was in the handbook, section nine, and in the refresher course Compliance ran every October in the training room, which he had sat a fortnight before: the one with the cartoon of a man holding a box of chocolates with a red cross over it. Declaring it would mean a form, and the form would mean Compliance, and Compliance would mean a note on Barbara Ashby's file. It would make her a case. It would make him a colleague who had accepted something.

In the guild there had been a rule, never written down, that you did not take loot you had not earned in front of people who had. He thought about that. Then he thought that there was nobody in front of him.

He put the card in his wallet, behind his bus pass, and did not declare it. He told nobody, not even Laura. It was the first thing in five years he had not told Laura, and all day he could feel it there behind the bus pass, a small square of weight.

He left the words alone. He looked them up once, on his phone in the third-floor toilets, confirmed what they were, and put the phone in his pocket and washed his hands. For four months the card rode in his wallet across the town and back. It softened at the corners. Every scam call he made after that had a second voice in it.

"Has anyone asked you to move your money?" he would say, and in his head Barbara said: How old is the thing you're sat in?

"Have you been promised a return?" And: Who could switch it off?

The routine stayed the same. It only began, faintly, to feel like a costume. Warm, well made, and somebody else's: the Hart fleece he wore on dress-down Fridays.

In the canteen the founders looked down from their mural with their moustaches and their surprise. He found himself wondering what the back room of the White Hart had smelt of in 1868, beer and coal smoke and wet wool, and whether any of those men had lain awake afraid that the thing they were building would not hold.

At the Thursday quiz the question was which animal Alice followed down the hole, and everyone at the table wrote rabbit, and they came third.

unit.title: Three: Mirror
unit.text:
## Three: Mirror

On the evening of Thursday 12 March 2020 the news said the markets had had their worst day since 1987 and bitcoin had lost half its value in a day. Laura was on a long and would not be home until after nine. The flat smelt of the pasta bake she had left him, covered in foil, with a note that said 40 MINS 180 LOVE YOU. She had written it at six that morning with her coat on, and had known, writing it, that he would forget. Kieran stood at the kitchen table with the television on in the other room and took the card out of his wallet.

He downloaded a wallet app. It asked him whether he wanted to create a new wallet or restore one. It felt like the character-select screen of a game he had not played for ten years: new, or continue. He pressed restore. It gave him twelve empty boxes, and he typed the words into them one by one.

Confirm, said the screen.

He put his thumb on the glass. For a moment nothing happened, and the black surface of the phone gave him back his own face, lit from below, a man in a kitchen in Old Town in a Hart fleece, tired, ordinary. Then the glass seemed to soften under his thumb, the way a puddle gives when you step in it expecting ground, and the balance rose out of nothing.

0.0071 BTC. £28.14.

Half of what she had given him. The first thing the other world taught him was that it moved while you watched it.

"Right," he said aloud, to nobody. "Okay. Right."

Then he found the explorer, the public ledger, and pasted in his address, and there was the transaction that had sent him the coins on 31 October 2019, and the one before that which had sent them to her, and behind that another, and another, branching back through thousands of hands and eleven years. There was no queue. There was no cut-off. There were no exceptions, only confirmations. Anyone could read it. Anyone in the world. He sat down on the kitchen chair so suddenly that it scraped.

It was like the moment in the old game when you rode out of the starting valley for the first time and the map, which you had thought was the world, turned out to be a green corner of a continent, with the rest of it black at the edges, waiting. New area discovered. He had forgotten that feeling.

Laura came in at twenty past nine and found him still at the table with the pasta bake cold in its foil.

"You haven't eaten," she said. "Kieran. It said forty minutes. It was on the note."

"Sorry. Sorry. I got caught up. The markets are mad."

"Everything's mad." She put her bag down very carefully, as she did after a bad shift. "They're saying it's going to be us next. Like Italy. We're rehearsing proning tomorrow." She saw his face and stopped. "It's fine. Eat your tea."

On 23 March the country locked down. Laura went onto the COVID intensive-care unit at the hospital on the edge of town and began sleeping in the day with a towel over the curtain rail. Kieran carried the queue home on a laptop and set it up in the spare room, and the Hart shrank to a screen, and the week lost its shape. What it had instead was the laptop, and the phone, and the card, and every night after the file went, the black edges of the map.

He only read. He read until three in the morning, as he had read patch notes at fifteen, and in the day he cleared the exceptions queue from the spare room with Laura asleep through the wall. When she woke they talked about the car park and the canteen and whether the Co-op had flour, because there was nothing either of them could say about their real day that would not frighten the other.

What she did not tell him about were nights like the one in the middle of April, when the unit was running at half again as many beds as it was built for, and the alarms went all night like birds in a hedge. She spent twelve and a half hours in a hood that made her own breath loud in her ears. At three in the morning she and six others turned a man of fifty-eight onto his front, on the count of the one holding his head, every line and tube gathered in their hands so that nothing pulled, because on his front his lungs might take the air the machine was pushing into them. At five she held a phone to another man's ear so that his daughter in Leeds could tell him the cat was fine, and that she loved him, and that he was not to worry about the cat. She did not cry. You did not, on the unit. You did it in the car, or not at all.

At eight she came home and found Kieran asleep at the spare-room desk with his cheek on his arm and his phone lit beside him, a green line climbing on it. She stood in the doorway in her coat and thought: at least one of us is having an easy war. Then she took her uniform off in the hall, put the towel over the curtain rail and went to bed, and she did not tell him that either.

unit.title: Four: Field
unit.text:
## Four: Field

What happened that summer happened to everyone who was there, and they all said the same thing about it afterwards, and the thing they said was: what the actual hell was that.

In the middle of June a lending protocol started paying its users in a new token just for using it, and within two months there were pools, and pools of pools, and tokens named after food, and people moving money between them at three in the morning to chase yields of four hundred, nine hundred, two thousand percent a year. Kieran read the words and none of them meant anything. Liquidity. Impermanent loss. Governance. Gas. Staking. Slippage. Rug. APY, APR, TVL, LP, DAO, ape, degen, wen, ser. A new word every hour, a new protocol every day, and every protocol named after something you could eat. A sushi one. A pasta one. A pickle one. A yam, which lasted about a day and a half and then broke, and everybody laughed about it, and some people lost their houses.

"Oh my God," he said to the empty spare room at two in the morning, and then, because it was two in the morning, he typed into the search bar: wtf is impermanent loss.

He learned it anyway, the way he had learned the game: by doing the stupid thing first and reading the forums after.

In July he put in six thousand pounds: his own savings, which were going to pay for Crete, Laura's first holiday abroad since a school trip to Calais, before the pandemic cancelled it. It was his money. It was not the deposit. He told himself that on the landing, with his hand on the bathroom door, and it was true.

He began to farm. That was the word. You put your seed into a field and it grew and you harvested it and replanted, and the fields were open all night, and the crop did not care what time it was in Wiltshire. He set alarms for three and five, and learned which pools would thin at which hours. There were three clocks in the spare room now: his body's, which wanted to sleep at eleven; the Hart's, which sent the file at ten and brought it back at seven; and the pools', which never stopped. He started living by the third. It did not occur to him until much later that he was not farming the tokens so much as they were farming him: that what he had planted was his own sleep, and that it was being harvested every night at three.

In August, the week the yam broke, a link in a thread about it took him to a chat server called the Sharehouse, where a few thousand anonymous people with cartoon avatars were awake in every time zone at once.

anyone awake, said the channel, at 3.14 a.m. British Summer Time.

awake ser

frens who is farming the new pool

ser the new pool is a rug

ser everything is a rug if you zoom out enough

He asked why a swap he was thinking of making would fail, and a man in Ohio with a frog for a face answered it in forty seconds, and a woman in Manila with a cat in sunglasses corrected the man in Ohio, and they argued, and in the end somebody called Dmitri with no avatar at all posted a diagram. Kieran understood the diagram. He understood it as he had understood raid bosses at fifteen: completely, and then in his sleep. The next week somebody new asked the same question, and he answered it before anyone else could.

ser you are a legend, typed the frog. who is this guy

kez, typed Dmitri. kez knows.

He sat in the blue light of the spare room with his heart going like a boy's.

The yields were real, some of them. By September his six thousand was nine.

"You're up early," Laura said once, coming in from a night at seven and finding him at the laptop in his dressing gown.

"Couldn't sleep," he said, and closed the lid, not quickly, because quickly would have meant something.

In September, the month of the rule of six, Barbara emailed him. He had written to the address on the back of her note once, in March, a single line: thank you, I looked. She wrote back: Good. Do you walk?

unit.title: Five: Tribe
unit.text:
## Five: Tribe

They met in the car park above Avebury on a Sunday, with a hard wind coming across the downs. She was smaller than her voice, grey-haired, in a waxed jacket older than he was, with a collie that ignored him completely. She kept her hands in her pockets. She looked him up and down the way you look at a fuse board.

"You're taller than you sound," she said. "Come on. She needs walking, and so do you, by the look of you."

She lived at Avebury Trusloe, the far side of the village from the stones, in a cottage with a satellite dish she had put up herself.

She walked faster than he did. They went up onto the Ridgeway, the chalk track white between the fields, and she told him about herself in the order she chose, in short sentences.

"Rodbourne. Dad was a boilermaker in the works, Grandad before him. I wanted to be an electrician from when I was ten. Mended the wireless with a hairgrip. Nobody took it serious." A stile; she went over it without using her hands. "1969 they let me in as an apprentice. Three women on the tools in the whole works. The men called me Babs. I didn't answer to it. After about a year they stopped."

"My grandad was in the works," Kieran said. "Ron Hale. He was a fitter."

She stopped on the track. "Ron Hale. Boiler shop. Big hands. Whistled Elvis." For a moment she looked at him differently. "He called me Barbara from the first week. Him and about two others." She set off again. "He was all right, your grandad."

"It must have been hard, though. The rest of them."

"It was a job. I was good at it. Seventeen years." She walked on. "Then March '86, and they shut the lot. Hundred and forty years, and the hooter just stops. Whole town's clock, that hooter. People who never set foot in the works set their kitchen clocks by it. And then it doesn't go, and you're thirty-three with a trade nobody wants."

"What did you do?"

"Learned computers. Nights at the tech. First in the exam." She said it flat, a meter reading, without pride. "The bureau took me on in '88. Twenty-five years keeping the clearing standing up. Nobody ever put my name on anything. That's fine. I know what I built. I know where the bodges are, too."

"And now you don't trust it."

"I watched it nearly stop in 2008." She slowed. "Money going out one end, not coming in the other, the whole thing holding its breath for a weekend. My code, waiting. I didn't know if it'd arrive. Then someone wrote nine pages about a ledger nobody can switch off, and I read it three times on the train to Reading. Bought my first coins the year I retired. Never sold one." She turned her head. "What are you in? Not coins. Don't tell me you're in the casino."

He told her about the Sharehouse, the pools, the farms, the nine thousand. She laughed: one short bark, not unkind, not kind either.

"Right," she said. "So you've swapped a bank you can't see for a hundred blokes with cartoon faces you can't see. At least the bank's got a mural."

"It's not like that. They're really good, some of them. There's this guy Dmitri, he—"

"Mind," she said, and stopped, and pointed.

Far below them the great stones stood in their circle round the village, grey and small at that distance, though some of them were taller than a double-decker, with the village inside the ring, pub and all.

"Farmers put those there," she said. "Four and a half thousand years ago. Dragged them across the downs on sledges. Forty tons, some of them. Took generations. Do you know why?"

"Religion?"

"That's what the signs say. I'll tell you what I think, for nothing." She pulled the collie's ear. "They wanted somewhere to gather. People will do almost anything to have a place to gather. That chat room of yours is the same animal. Worse food."

"I heard a man on the radio," she said. "Biologist. Ants, mostly. He said the trouble with people is we've got Palaeolithic emotions, medieval institutions and god-like technology." She looked down at the stones. "He missed one out. A phone in your hand at three in the morning."

Kieran thought that a phone in your hand at three in the morning was not a fourth thing but all three at once, and that the man on the radio had missed nothing. He let it stand. He kept the rest to himself as well: that the Sharehouse was the first band since the guild that needed him, and that when he typed and forty people answered he felt what the men in the back room of the White Hart must have felt: that he was one of them, that they were building something, that it would hold.

At the car park she opened her boot and the collie jumped in.

"Same time next month," she said. It was not a question. "Wear proper shoes."

They walked most months after that. She never once asked him to stop.

unit.title: Six: Harvest
unit.text:
## Six: Harvest

In January 2021 the third lockdown sent Laura back onto the unit for the worst weeks of the whole thing. She came home in the dark and sat in the car outside the flat for twenty minutes before she came up. Kieran watched her from the spare-room window, the dome light off, her hands on the wheel, and stayed where he was, because he thought she wanted to be alone, and because he did not know what he would say if he did.

When she came up she took her uniform off in the hallway and put it straight into the machine on a sixty, and stood in the shower until the hot water ran out.

"How was it?" he said, when she came out.

"We lost two." She was towelling her hair, not looking at him. "One was forty-one. Sats wouldn't come up. We proned him four times." She hung the towel on the radiator, square. She hung everything square. "It's fine. What did you do?"

"Nothing. Work. The batch." He had made nine thousand pounds that week. He left it unsaid. It would have sounded like a different language, and it was.

Later she lay on the sofa scrolling through houses in Wroughton on her phone. It was the only thing she looked at that was not a monitor. A three-bed semi with a front door painted green. A garden with a shed.

"That one's got a porch," she said. "Look. You could put your boots in it."

"It's nice."

"It's got a front door that's ours." She said it lightly. She said all the important things lightly, so they could be taken as jokes if they had to be. She had been moved on from five rented houses before she was thirteen. In six years with him she had never once asked for anything except that.

The market went up. By the Christmas just gone his six thousand had been fifteen thousand pounds; by February it was thirty-eight; then forty-five. The Sharehouse had grown to four thousand members. People asked for Kez by name.

kez is this safe

kez wen new pool

kez my mum wants to get in, what do i tell her

tell her only what she can lose, he wrote, and felt wise, and did not think about his own mother.

In June the Hart's board decided to block payments to several crypto exchanges, after the regulator's warnings and a run of scam losses, and because Kieran knew better than anyone on the floor why a payment failed, they seconded him to the project that built the block.

It was the year everybody was at war with everybody. The regulator said anyone buying crypto should be prepared to lose all their money, and the Sharehouse printed it on a T-shirt. Banks blocked exchanges, exchanges bought the fronts of football shirts, and the Sharehouse posted a tyrannosaurus in a tie with the caption have fun staying poor.

The block went live on a Thursday in July.
