## Ten: Stone

On a weekday in August, while Kieran was at the Hart, Barbara Ashby took the bus into Swindon from the stop outside the Red Lion, which she had not done in two years. She had left the car at home on purpose. She sat at the front, where she could see the road, with her handbag on her knees like a toolbox. She had not asked anyone for anything since March 1986, when she had stood in the personnel office at the works and asked whether there was anything, anything at all, and been told there was not. She was not going to ask for anything now. She was going to give something, and it was not money, and she did not know how you gave it. She rehearsed nothing. Rehearsing was what she had done in February, all the way home in that car, and look where that had got everybody.

In town she walked up Wood Street, past the pubs that had been banks, to the bakery Kieran had once brought her lardy cake from, and knocked on the door of the flat above it. She had worked out from what he said about the rota that Laura would be home between nights on a Tuesday. If she was wrong she would come back on the Wednesday.

Laura answered in a hoodie and pyjama bottoms, between nights, with her hair tied up. This small grey woman in a waxed jacket was a stranger to her.

"You're Laura," the woman said. "I'm Barbara. I'm the one who sent him the card."

"I know who you are," Laura said.

"Good," said Barbara. "Can I come in? I won't stay. I don't sit down in other people's kitchens, so you needn't bother with the kettle."

She stayed standing, in the kitchen by the fridge with the rota on it and told Laura what she had done, in short flat sentences.

"I gave him a key without a map. I checked the key and not the person. That's the opposite of everything I believe, and I did it anyway, because I liked his voice on the phone and I thought, there's one who could see it. In February he told me where your deposit was. I knew how that thing could fail. I could have drawn it for him on the back of a car-park ticket. I said it was his choice and nothing else, because I have never been anybody's mother, and I have been very proud of that for fifty years." She looked at the rota. "That part's mine. The rest is his. I'm not here to make it better. I can't. I'm here because somebody in this should say it out loud to you, and it isn't going to be him, and by the look of you it isn't going to be you either."

Laura stood with her arms folded. "You don't know anything about me."

"No. That's fair." Barbara looked at her properly then. "I know what holding everything looks like. I held a whole works together for seventeen years, one fuse at a time, and nobody ever asked me how. You're allowed to say something. That's all. That's all I came to tell you. You're allowed."

"You knew about the deposit," Laura said.

"In February. Yes."

"And you didn't say."

"I said it was for the two of you to decide."

"I wasn't there."

Barbara opened the clasp of her handbag and closed it again.

"No," she said. "You weren't."

When she had gone, Laura sat at the kitchen table for a long time. Then she took the rota off the fridge, and looked at the months of it, the longs and the nights and the days, and put it back, square, under the magnet from Weymouth.

That evening, when Kieran came in, she was sitting at the table with a notepad, as she sat at handover.

"Sit down," she said. "I'm going to do this how I know how to do it, or I won't be able to do it at all. Don't interrupt."

He sat.

"Situation," Laura said. "Our deposit's gone. Fifteen thousand of it was mine. It was every night shift I did in the pandemic. Every one." She never looked down at the notepad. "Background. I've been moved out of five houses. The last one I was twelve and I carried my stuff to the car in a bin bag because we'd run out of boxes, and I decided, I'm never doing that again. Never. That money was a front door. That's what it was. It wasn't money." She breathed in, out, as she taught relatives to. "Assessment. You lied to me for five weeks. You went to work and came home and ate your tea and lied. And before that there were two years of nights in that room, and a year of them rich. In November you had seventy-one thousand pounds on your phone. That's three deposits. You opened my folder and saw what I still needed and closed it again, and I was doing extra nights for it, and you let me. That's worse than the money. It's so much worse than the money, Kieran. And I said do what you think. I know I did. I said it because I was so tired of being the one who holds everything that I handed it to you without looking. So that's mine. Barbara's right. That bit's mine." Her voice went, and came back. "Recommendation."

She stopped. It was the only line she had not written down.

"I don't know," she said. "I don't know. I want you to tell me what we do."

He did not answer with the scam-line voice. He did not have it any more. He reached across the table and put his hand next to hers, not on it, where she could take it or not.

"We tell each other everything," he said. "Every number. Every time. Even the boring ones. And we start again, slowly. And I'm sorry. I'm so sorry, Lor."

She did not take his hand. She did not move hers away. It was the first conversation they had had in two years that neither of them was having through a screen, and it went on until after one in the morning, and at the end of it she was the one who said, "Come to bed," and he was the one who cried.

## Eleven: Field, Again

In the morning Laura got up before him, on her day off, and when he came into the kitchen she had the laptop open at the bank and a pen in her hand.

"Right," she said. "Show me. All of it. Every account."

He sat down beside her and showed her, and she wrote down every number he read out, in a column down the side of the page, the way she wrote obs. Her hand was not quite steady.

They opened one account that both of them could see. They stuck a spreadsheet on the fridge next to the rota, held by a second magnet, from Lyme Regis. It was a ledger, Kieran thought, the oldest thing there was: not the kind anyone in the world could read, like the one that had swallowed the deposit, but the kind two people could. They postponed the house by two years. In September he sold what was left of his own tokens, five thousand two hundred pounds, and paid it into the joint account, and they both watched the number arrive. Kieran deleted the apps and told Laura every number, every time, until telling her every number stopped feeling like confession and started feeling like housekeeping. He slept again: six hours, then seven.

"Four hundred and twelve in the joint," he would say, coming in. "Car insurance is up."

"Course it is," she would say. "Everything's up. Put the kettle on."

Laura asked her friend Jade on the unit to swap so that she could have one Sunday a month off with him. They compared their phones by the lockers, with Jade's coat half on.

"I can do one," Jade said. "You take my Saturday?"

"Of course. And if there's anything else—"

"Lor. It's a swap."

They tried it again when the next rota came out. On the unit Laura had always been the one who said the true thing first, to consultants, to families, to the dying. Asking for a day off with Kieran made her feel as if she ought to explain what they would do with it. She put it in the calendar in green.

Rebuilding was slow and dull, and they chose that too. It was harvest in the old sense: the same field, the same work, every season, nothing that doubled overnight.

On the first of those Sundays they went to Penhill for lunch. His father had work now, as caretaker at the primary school at the bottom of the road, and he made the tea himself, and he made it in the plant mug: SWINDON 1992-2021 THANK YOU, in blue on white, the mug that had gone into the cupboard over the kettle on the night of the last shift and had not come out since.

"Dave Pritchard lost his redundancy on that bitcoin," his father said, carving. "Thirty years on the line with me, Dave. Put the lot in a dollar that wasn't a dollar."

Kieran put his knife down. "I know," he said, and left it there. The call was a customer's. He looked at Laura, and Laura looked back and nodded once, a nurse's nod: go on. "Dad. Mum. I need to tell you something about our deposit."

He told them. His mother, Sue, put her hand over her mouth, and then took it away and said, not to him but to Laura, "Are you all right, love? Are you?" His father listened with the carving knife in one hand and the fork in the other, and when Kieran had finished he set them down very carefully, either side of the joint.

"Your grandad," he said, "lost a week's wages on a horse once. 1961. Your nan didn't speak to him till Whitsun." He picked up the mug and drank from it and put it down. "Pass the gravy, Kieran."

It was, Laura said in the car, the most she had ever heard him say.

In October he forgot to tell her about forty pounds.

It was a game for the laptop. He had not bought one since he was twenty, and he had meant to say and hadn't. She found it on a Thursday evening, going down the statement with the green pen as she did every month now, and she put the pen on the line and turned the paper round so that he could read it.

"What's this?"

"Oh. That's a game. Sorry." He heard himself and could not stop. "It's forty quid, Lor."

"I know what forty quid is." She did not raise her voice. "Every number, every time. You said that. At this table."

"I forgot. That's all it is. I forgot."

"On the laptop," she said. "In the spare room."

It was the worst row of their eight years, and it was about forty pounds, and for an hour neither of them said what it was about. He said he could not live like a man on probation. She said nobody had asked him to. He said it felt like it. At the end of it she sat down on the kitchen floor with her back against the fridge, under the rota and the spreadsheet, and put her hands over her face.

"Every day," she said, through them. "Since August. I've checked the account behind your back every day. I hate it. I hate myself for it."

"I know," he said. "You leave the bank open on the laptop."

She took her hands away. "You knew."

"Since the first week."

"And you let me. Every day. And you never said."

"I thought you were owed it."

She stared at him. Then she began to laugh, and it was very close to crying. "That's the same thing," she said. "Kieran. That's exactly the same thing again."

He sat down on the floor next to her, with his back against the fridge as well, and after a while she leaned into him. Later they added a column to the spreadsheet on the fridge, headed CHECKED, and she ticked it every night for a month, openly, and then one night forgot to.

In November a big exchange collapsed in the background, and it turned out its customers' money had been used by its trading firm, and bitcoin fell to a quarter of its peak. Barbara's coins fell with it.

"You're very calm about it," Kieran said on the Ridgeway.

"I've seen three of these. Four, if you count 2008, and I do." She walked on. "The coins aren't the point. The point's that nobody can switch them off. Price is just noise."

She did not sell. And on the walks she began, unasked, to explain things to him. How the clearing actually worked, file by file, down to the byte. Why the bit that waits had been written to wait: because in 1988 you could not be sure the other bank existed until morning. What a key was, and what a map was, and the difference.

"A key gets you in," she said. "A map tells you where the floor stops. I gave you the one without the other. So." She tapped her head. "Map. Month by month. You'll hate it. Wear proper shoes."

The walks became lessons, and he let them. Somewhere in the second month he found that he liked it again: not the number, which he no longer looked at, but the thing itself, how the old machine and the new one actually worked, the black edges of the map coming in slowly, on foot, at Barbara's pace.

In December he told her about the guild: the raid, the clock that said 11.52, the shirt on the back of the door, Sander. He had never told anyone. She walked a long way before she answered.

"In the works," she said, "when the hooter went, a man put his tools down and went home. Middle of a job, sometimes. Nobody called it deserting." She looked at him sideways. "You went to work, Kieran. You were twenty and you went to work. That's not leaving your mates. That's the first grown-up thing you ever did."

He had told himself the story one way for twelve years. It took him most of the walk down to hear it the other way, and he was not sure, even at the car park, that he believed it. But something in him that had been holding its breath since 2010 let a little of it out.

Half the Sharehouse's channels were empty now. A few regulars still posted gm in the mornings, from Ohio and Manila and São Paulo. Dmitri had gone; his account said deleted user. Kieran looked in sometimes, and only looked. Once, when he had woken at three for no reason and gone through to the spare room out of old habit, a newcomer asked whether it was too late to get in, and Kieran wrote a long careful message about pegs and guy ropes and fires in draughts, and then deleted it, and wrote instead: ask someone who loves you to sit with you while you decide.

The newcomer replied: lol ok boomer.

He closed the laptop and went back to bed, where Laura was asleep, on a day off, next to him.

## Twelve: Awake

He stayed on the payments-exceptions desk at the Hart. The routine was the same. He was not.

He knew how old the machine was now, and what ran under it, and who could switch it off. He knew what the new machine had done to him in the night. He kept the card in his wallet behind his bus pass, soft as cloth now, with its 0.0071 bitcoin still behind it, which he had looked up once that spring: about a hundred and fifty pounds. He had never spent it and never would. It was not a key any more. It was a reminder, kept by choice, as his grandfather Ron had kept a brass works tally token in his pocket for fifteen years after the hooter stopped.

It was also, he knew, a gift from a customer that he had never declared. In October Harriet from Compliance had run the same refresher course in the training room, with the same cartoon of the man holding the chocolates under the red cross, and he had sat through it with the card in his wallet and had not put his hand up. He never told her about the card, or the app, or the three payments of eight thousand pounds. He told Laura every number, every time, and he told the Hart nothing, and he knew exactly where that line ran.

In March 2023 fraud rule forty-one stopped a payment of twelve thousand pounds from a saver in her twenties to one of the exchanges the block had never covered, and the case dropped into his queue with its small orange flag, and he rang her.

"Hi, is that Chloe? Sorry to bother you. My name's Kieran, I'm calling from the White Hart's payments team about a transfer you made this morning. It's just a check we do."

He read her the script. Has anyone contacted you and asked you to move your money. Have you been promised a return. Has anyone asked you to keep this conversation private.

She said no to all of it, a little impatiently. He would have, too.

"Brilliant. Thank you. That's everything I need." He looked at the flag. "Can I ask you something that isn't on the script? You can tell me to get lost."

"Go on."

"Do you know how old the thing is that you're leaving? And how new the thing is that you're going into?" He waited. "And if it goes wrong, who are you going to tell?"

There was a silence on the line. Then she said, "Have you ever bought any? Yourself?"

Nobody had asked him that at work, and every call on this line was recorded. He thought of the card behind his bus pass, and the three payments, and whoever might one day play this back in a training room. Then he said it anyway. "Yes. It went wrong. That's why I'm asking."

Another silence. "My brother, probably," she said at last. "He'd kill me."

"Tell him before," Kieran said. "Not after. That's all. Good luck, Chloe."

He understood then, with the line quiet and the flag still orange on his screen, what he was for. Barbara had written the bit that waits into the machine. He was the bit that waits in the building: a person between a saver and the speed of everything, asking her to stop for the length of a question.

He held the payment until 4.55, as long as the day would let him, and then released it, because nothing in the rules let him stop it, and because it was hers. He hoped she would ring her brother first.

For a week afterwards he half expected someone from Quality to come down to the third floor with a transcript. Nobody did.

On the Sunday the three of them walked on the Ridgeway: Barbara in front with the collie, too fast; Laura, who had never been up there, in the middle, in new boots; Kieran behind. The chalk track ran white between the fields, as it had for five thousand years. Far below them the stones stood in their circle round the village, grey and small, with smoke going up from the pub chimney.

"Why would anyone drag them all that way?" Laura asked.

"To gather," Kieran said. "People will do almost anything to have somewhere to gather."

Barbara snorted, because it was her line. "He steals everything," she said to Laura. "Watch your purse."

"I know," Laura said. "He's got my deposit."

She had not made a joke about it before. Barbara laughed, and Kieran laughed too, a beat late.

His phone was in the car.

The wind came over the downs. Laura took his hand without looking. She was sure it would be there.

## One: Blue

The payments file left White Hart House at ten every night and came back at seven every morning with its failures sorted into a queue, and Kieran Hale had cleared that queue for nine years. Closed account. Name mismatch. Sort code retired in 2011. Fraud rule forty-one. He could read an exception the way his grandfather Ron, a fitter in the railway works until they shut, had read a boiler by the sound of it.

The Hart had been founded in 1868 by railwaymen pooling their wages in the back room of a White Hart inn so that each of them, one by one, could buy a house. It still had the brass hart on the door and a mural of the founders in the canteen, men with moustaches and bowler hats looking faintly surprised to find themselves on a wall in west Swindon. Kieran liked the mural. He liked most things about the Hart. That was the problem, if it was a problem.

His week had one shape. The 8.12 bus from Old Town. The lanyard. The tea round, which went clockwise from the window and which nobody had ever agreed to and everybody kept. Cut-off at ten. Lunch at one. The Thursday quiz at the Beehive, where his team came third with the regularity of a tide. Laura's rota on the fridge, printed monthly, held up by a magnet from Weymouth: days, nights, the long days she called longs. Sunday lunch in Penhill, where his father talked about the car plant closing in 2021 as if it were weather, something that would come in over the downs whether you minded or not.

He was twenty-nine. He was reliable. His appraisals used the word. At sixteen he had led a raiding guild of forty people across six countries in an online game, set their timetables, known who was sulking in Lisbon and who needed carrying in Tallinn, and nobody on the third floor knew it. When he took the job at twenty he had logged off for the last time, given the guild to a Dutch boy called Sander, and become, deliberately, no trouble to anyone.

Some Sunday evenings the week sat on his chest like a cat. He did not mention it. It seemed an ungrateful thing to feel.

On Monday 21 October 2019, at 3.40 in the afternoon, fraud rule forty-one stopped a payment of forty thousand pounds from a savings account opened in 1989 to an account at a crypto exchange, and the system put the case in his queue, and he rang the customer.

"Mrs Ashby? My name's Kieran, I'm calling from the White Hart's payments team about a transfer you've made today."

"Barbara," said the voice. "Never Mrs. Go on, read me the script."

He read her the script. Has anyone contacted you and asked you to move your money. Have you been promised a return. Has anyone asked you to keep this conversation private. Are you being asked to download anything onto your computer.

She answered each question exactly, like a woman filling in a form she had designed. No. No. No. No. Then she said, "My turn. How old is the system you're sitting in?"

"I'm sorry?"

"The clearing. The thing that runs every night and waits three days to move money that could move in a second. How old is it?"

He found that he did not know. "It's been updated," he said.

"I updated it," said Barbara Ashby. "From 1988 to 2013, at a bureau in Reading. I wrote the bit that waits. It was designed for magnetic tape, Kieran. Do you know who could switch it off?"

He did not know that either. He released the payment at 4.55, because nothing in the script allowed him to stop it, and went home on the bus with the feeling of having walked past a door he had not known was in the wall.

## Two: Rabbit

The envelope came up from the post room on Friday 1 November, addressed in blue capitals: MR K. HALE, PAYMENTS EXCEPTIONS, THIRD FLOOR, WHITE HART HOUSE. It was the only letter anyone on the floor had received by name in a year, and Deb from the next bank of desks made a noise like a kettle.

Inside was a white index card and a sheet of lined paper torn from a pad.

The card had twelve words on it in the same capitals, numbered, in two columns. They were ordinary words. Some of them were almost a poem. He read them twice and then again, and they did not become a sentence.

The note said: There is fifty pounds behind these. It is yours. Go and look. B.A.

He knew what the words were before he let himself know it. He had processed enough payments to exchanges and read enough of the fraud team's bulletins. It was a recovery phrase: twelve words from a fixed list that were, in the new world, the whole of a wallet. Whoever held the words held the money. There was no bank behind them, no branch, no mural, no brass hart. Just the words.

Gifts from customers had to be declared. It was in the handbook, section nine, and in the online course he did every March. Declaring it would mean a form, and the form would mean compliance, and compliance would mean a note on Barbara Ashby's file that said the kind of thing that notes on files said. It would make her a case. It would make him a colleague who had accepted something.

He put the card in his wallet, behind his bus pass, and did not declare it, and did not tell Laura, which was the first thing in five years he had not told Laura.

He did not type the words in. He looked them up once, on his phone in the toilets, and confirmed what they were, and put the phone away as if it had bitten him. For four months the card rode in his wallet across the town and back. It softened at the corners. Every scam call he made after that had a second voice in it, asking him how old the thing was that he was sitting in. The routine did not change at all. It began, faintly, to feel like a costume.

In the canteen the founders looked down from their mural with their moustaches and their surprise, and he found himself wondering what the back room of the White Hart had smelt of in 1868, and whether any of those men had lain awake afraid that the thing they were building would not hold.

## Three: Mirror

On the evening of Thursday 12 March 2020 the news said the markets had had their worst day since 1987 and bitcoin had lost half its value in a day. Laura was on a long and would not be home until after nine. Kieran stood at the kitchen table with the television on in the other room and took the card out of his wallet.

He downloaded a wallet app. It asked him whether he wanted to create a new wallet or restore one. He pressed restore. It gave him twelve empty boxes, and he typed the words into them one by one, the way you would enter a code on a door you were not sure you were allowed to open.

Confirm, said the screen.

He put his thumb on the glass. For a moment nothing happened, and the black surface of the phone gave him back his own face, lit from below, a man in a kitchen in Old Swindon in a Hart fleece. Then the glass seemed to soften under his thumb, the way a puddle gives when you step in it expecting ground, and the balance rose out of nothing.

0.0071 BTC. £28.14.

Half of what she had given him. The first thing the other world taught him was that it moved while you watched it.

Then he found the explorer, the public ledger, and pasted in his address, and there was the transaction that had sent him the coins on 31 October 2019, and the one before that which had sent them to her, and behind that another, and another, a chain running back through thousands of hands to January 2009. Anyone could read it. Anyone in the world. He sat down.

It was like the moment in the old game when you left the starting valley for the first time and the map, which you had thought was the world, turned out to be a green corner of a continent, with the rest of it black at the edges and waiting. He had forgotten that feeling. It had not forgotten him.

On 23 March the country locked down. Laura went onto the COVID intensive-care unit at the hospital on the edge of town and began sleeping in the day with a towel over the curtain rail. Kieran carried the batch home on a laptop and set it up in the spare room, and the Hart shrank to a screen, and the week lost its shape. There was no bus, no tea round, no quiz. There was the laptop, and the phone, and the card, and every night after the file went, the black edges of the map.

He did not trade. He read. He read until three in the morning, the way he had at fifteen, and in the day he cleared the exceptions queue from the spare room with Laura asleep through the wall, and neither of them said much, because there was nothing either of them could say about their day that would not frighten the other.

## Four: Field

What happened that summer happened to everyone who was there, and they all said the same thing about it, and the thing they said was: what the actual hell is this.

In the middle of June a lending protocol started paying its users in a new token for using it, and within a fortnight there were pools, and pools of pools, and tokens called after food, and people moving money between them at three in the morning to chase yields of four hundred, nine hundred, two thousand percent a year. Kieran read the words and none of them meant anything. Liquidity. Impermanent loss. Governance. Gas. Staking. Slippage. Rug. APY, APR, TVL, LP, DAO, ape, degen, wen, ser, gm. A new word every hour, and a new protocol every day, and every protocol named after something you could eat.

He learned it anyway. He learned it the way he had learned the game, by doing the stupid thing first and reading the forums after. A link in a thread about a token named after a vegetable took him to a chat server called the Sharehouse, where a few thousand anonymous people with cartoon avatars were awake in every time zone at once.

They answered his questions at three in the morning. They called him Kez, after the name on his wallet. When he explained, in his first week, why a transaction had failed, a man in Ohio with a frog for a face typed ser you are a legend, and Kieran sat in the blue light of the spare room with his heart going like a boy's.

In July he put in six thousand pounds: his half of a holiday fund the pandemic had cancelled. It was his money. It was not the deposit. He told himself that, and it was true.

He began to farm. That was the word. You put your seed into a field and it grew and you harvested it and replanted, and the fields were open all night, and the crop did not care what time it was in Wiltshire. He set alarms for three and five. He knew which pools would thin at which hours, the way his grandfather's grandfather must have known the weather over the downs. It did not occur to him until much later that he was not farming the tokens so much as they were farming him: that the thing he had planted was himself, and it was being harvested every night at three.

The yields were real, some of them. By Christmas his six thousand was fifteen. By February it was thirty-eight.

In September, when people were allowed to meet outdoors in sixes, Barbara emailed him from the address on her letter, which he had answered in March with a single line, and asked if he walked.

## Five: Tribe

They met in the car park above Avebury on a Sunday with the wind coming across the downs like something with a job to do. She was smaller than her voice, grey-haired, in a waxed jacket older than he was, with a collie that ignored him. She walked faster than he did.

They went up onto the Ridgeway, the chalk track white between the fields, and she told him about herself in the order she chose. A Rodbourne girl, her father a boilermaker in the works. An apprentice electrician there from 1969, one of three women in the whole place, and the men called her Babs and she answered only to Barbara. Seventeen years of it. Then March 1986, and the works closing after a hundred and forty years, and the town's clock stopping, and her thirty-three with a trade nobody wanted.

"So I learned computers," she said. "Nights at the tech. First in the exam. The bureau took me on in '88 and I spent twenty-five years keeping the clearing standing up. Nobody ever put my name on anything. That's fine. I know what I built."

"And now you don't trust it."

"I watched it nearly stop in 2008," she said. "The money waited and I didn't know if it would arrive. Then someone wrote nine pages describing a ledger nobody could switch off, and I read it three times on the train. I bought my first coins the year I retired. I never sell." She looked at him sideways. "What are you in? Not coins. Tell me you're not in the casino."

He told her about the Sharehouse, and the farms, and the fifteen thousand. She laughed, not kindly.

"It's the old casino in a new costume," she said. "You've swapped a bank you can't see for a hundred blokes with cartoon faces you can't see. At least the bank has a mural."

Below them the great stones stood in their circle round the village, grey and leaning, and she stopped to look at them the way you might look at an old colleague.

"Farmers put those there," she said. "Four and a half thousand years ago. Dragged them across the downs on sledges, stones of forty tons, generation after generation. Do you know why?"

"Religion?"

"To gather," she said. "People will do almost anything to have somewhere to gather. That chat room of yours is the same animal. Worse food."

He did not tell her that she was wrong, because she was not, exactly. He did not tell her either that the Sharehouse was the first band since the guild that needed him, or that when he typed and forty people answered he felt what the men in the back room of the White Hart must have felt: that he was one of them, and they were building something, and it would hold.

They walked most months after that. She never asked him to stop. She had never been anybody's mother and did not mean to start.

## Six: Harvest

In January 2021 the third lockdown sent Laura back onto the unit for the worst weeks of the whole thing. She came home in the dark and sat in the car outside the flat for twenty minutes before she came up, and Kieran watched her from the spare-room window and did not go down, because he thought she wanted to be alone, and because he did not know what he would say.

When she did come up she took her uniform off in the hallway and put it straight in the machine and stood in the shower until the hot water ran out, and later she lay on the sofa scrolling through houses in Wroughton on her phone. It was the only thing she looked at that was not a monitor. A house with a front door. A garden with a shed. She had been moved on from five rented houses before she was thirteen, and she had never once, in eight years with him, asked for anything except that.

The market went up. By February his six thousand was thirty-eight thousand pounds, then forty-five. The Sharehouse had grown to four thousand members. People asked for Kez by name. He answered newcomers at three in the morning with a patience he had once kept for a guild of forty, and they thanked him, and he felt like someone who mattered.

In June the Hart's board decided to block payments to several crypto exchanges, after the regulator's warnings and a run of scam losses, and because Kieran knew better than anyone on the floor why a payment failed, they seconded him to the project that built the block. He sat in meetings about it on Teams with his camera on and his lanyard round his neck. At night he walked round it through a payments app the Hart had never heard of. He did not feel he was lying. He felt, if anything, that he was the only person in both rooms.

At the end of July the car plant made its last car. His father worked the final shift and came home with his hi-vis vest and a commemorative mug and put the mug in a cupboard and did not take it out again. He was fifty-nine. He had built engines there since 1992.

For three months Kieran paid his parents' rent. He did it from his gains, by bank transfer, and his father thanked him once, in the car outside the Job Centre, without looking at him. It was the best thing the money ever did. It was also the thing that made him certain the money was real, that the game was not a game, that he had been right.

By November 2021 his screen said he was worth seventy-one thousand pounds. Laura had a shortlist of three houses. And three clocks were running in him at once, though he would not have put it like that: a body built for a band of faces on the downs, which wanted sleep and wanted to be told it was one of them; an employer built for the three-day cycle, which closed at five and remembered everything; and a phone that never closed at all, lighting the ceiling at three and five, calling him to the harvest.

## Seven: Anchor

After November the prices went down, the way weather goes down, gradually and then all at once and then gradually again. By Christmas his seventy-one thousand was fifty; by the new year, forty-five. The Sharehouse stopped talking about moons and started talking about safe yield.

Safe yield was a dollar. Not a real dollar, but a token that was always worth a dollar, and a savings protocol that paid nearly twenty percent a year for holding it. The token did not keep its dollar with dollars in a vault. It kept it with a trick of arithmetic: anyone could always swap one of them for a dollar's worth of a sister token, and back, and the swapping held the price in place like a tent held by its guy ropes. Kieran read the paper. He understood it. He understood that the ropes held only while the sister token was worth more than all the dollars tied to it. It was a peg. Everything he had ever worked in was a peg, when you looked at it: the Hart's deposits, the three-day cycle, the plant, the works. They held because everyone believed they would hold.

House prices in Wroughton had gone up faster than the deposit. The deposit was twenty-four thousand pounds in a savings account at the Hart, earning nothing, and fifteen thousand of it was Laura's overtime from two pandemic winters.

On a Sunday in January he said it at the kitchen table. The rota was on the fridge behind her. She was marking dates on the calendar for the viewings.

"I want to move the deposit somewhere it'll earn something," he said. "Twenty percent. Before we buy in the summer. It's a dollar. It doesn't move."

She did not look up for long. She had worked seven nights out of the last ten.

"You're the one who knows about money," she said. "Do what you think."

He did not explain what a stablecoin was, and she did not ask. By the end of the week the twenty-four thousand pounds had left the Hart through the app it had never heard of and become twenty-four thousand pounds' worth of dollars that did not move, earning twenty percent, and he checked it every morning like a man checking a sleeping child.

In February he told Barbara on the Ridgeway, pleased, walking towards the long barrow. She stopped. She looked at the barrow for a long time, at the great stones of its door, and he waited for her to say the thing about casinos.

"That's yours and Laura's to decide," she said.

She said nothing else about it all afternoon. She talked about the men who dragged the stones and about the dog. On the drive home she thought of three sentences she could have said, one of them about guy ropes, and said none of them, because she had never been anybody's mother and did not mean to start.

## Eight: Hole

On Saturday 7 May the dollar that did not move moved. Ninety-nine cents. Then back. The Sharehouse made jokes about it. On Monday evening, the ninth, it was ninety-eight, then ninety-three, then eighty. Laura was on nights; the rota said so.

Kieran sat at the spare-room desk with the Sharehouse open on one screen and the price on the other, and he did not sleep, and the ropes went one by one.

He knew exactly what was happening. That was the worst of it. People were selling the dollar and swapping it for the sister token, and each swap made new sister tokens out of nothing, and each new sister token made the others worth less, so each swap needed more of them, and the fall fed itself like a fire in a draught. He could have drawn it on a whiteboard. He could have explained it to the fraud team in a short, excellent email.

The Sharehouse said: it has always come back. It said: do not sell, that is what they want. It said: we are all in this together, and a thousand cartoon faces said it with him. The founder's account said he was deploying more capital. On Tuesday it touched sixty cents and bounced to ninety and the Sharehouse cheered like a crowd at a match, and he held.

He could have sold at ninety. He could have sold at sixty. He did not, because selling would make it real, and because leaving the band while it was losing was the one thing he had never forgiven himself for, since the night at twenty when he had given the guild to Sander and logged off. The oldest part of him, the part that was older than the Hart and older than the stones, knew that the worst thing that could happen to a person was to be alone outside the fire. It did not know about percentages.

By Thursday it was twenty cents. By Friday the thirteenth the deposit was worth about three thousand pounds and falling. The sister token was worth almost nothing. The Sharehouse had gone from certainty to instructions to silence to jokes to goodbyes.

That same week the Hart's fraud lines filled with customers who had lost their savings, some of them through the same apps he had used to walk round the block he had built, and the payments team was pulled onto the phones. On Wednesday he took a call from a man in Stratton who had put in his redundancy money and wanted to know if the Hart could get it back. Kieran read him the script. His own voice came out of his mouth steady and kind and professional, the voice he had used on Barbara, and the man cried, and Kieran said he was very sorry, and he was, and he went home and checked a balance that was a number and then a smaller number.

## Nine: Silence

For five weeks he said nothing.

He went to work and came home. He took the calls. He checked the dead balance at night; by June it was a few hundred pounds. He lost weight. His hand shook when he held his phone, and he started holding it in the other hand. He slept three hours a night and told Laura it was the heat.

When the mortgage adviser emailed in the middle of June for their savings statements, Laura forwarded it to him with a thumbs-up and a house emoji.

He told her that evening at the kitchen table, with the rota on the fridge behind her. He told her everything, in the order it had happened: January, the dollar that did not move, the ropes, the Tuesday bounce, the Friday, the five weeks. He told her how much, to the pound. He did not cry, because he did not think he was allowed to.

She listened. She asked three questions. How much is left. Is any of it recoverable. Does anyone else know.

Then she went to bed.

In the morning she moved their accounts into her name, picked up two extra shifts a week, and cancelled the mortgage appointment. She did not shout. She did not cry in front of him. She had learned on five doorsteps, watching her mother hand back keys, that you hold everything together and say nothing, and she was very good at it, and she held.

The flat went quiet in a new way. Before, they had been two people with screens: hers the monitors, his the charts. Now there was one screen fewer and no more words. The rota stayed on the fridge. He read it every morning to know when she would be asleep, awake or gone, and understood for the first time that he had been reading it for two years as a timetable of when no one would be watching.

In July he walked with Barbara and told her everything too. She did not laugh, and she did not say anything about casinos. She walked a long way without speaking, faster than him, and at the long barrow she said, "I gave you a key and not a map," and then nothing else, and he thought that was the end of it.

## Ten: Stone

On a weekday in August, while Kieran was at the Hart, Barbara Ashby took the bus into Swindon, which she had not done in two years, and walked up Wood Street, and knocked on the door of a flat above a shop.

Laura answered in a hoodie, between nights. She did not know who this small grey woman was.

"I'm Barbara," the woman said. "I'm the one who sent him the card. Can I come in? I won't stay."

She did not sit down. She stood in the kitchen by the fridge with the rota on it, in her waxed jacket, and told Laura what she had done. She had given Kieran a key without a map. She had checked the key and not the person, which was the opposite of everything she believed. And in February, on the Ridgeway, when he told her where the deposit was, she had known exactly how the peg could fail, she could have drawn it for him, and she had said it was his choice and nothing else, because she had never been anybody's mother and had been very proud of that for sixty-nine years.

"That part's mine," she said. "The rest is his. I'm not here to make it better. I can't. I'm here because somebody in this should say it out loud to you, and it isn't going to be him, and it's apparently not going to be you." She looked at Laura properly for the first time. "You're allowed to say something. That's all. You're allowed."

When she had gone Laura sat at the kitchen table for a long time. Then she took the rota off the fridge, and looked at the months of it, the longs and the nights and the days, and put it back.

That evening she said it. She said it all. She said it about the five houses and the boxes she had never unpacked, and about the front door, and about what fifteen thousand pounds of pandemic nights meant in a body, and about the five weeks, which were worse than the money, much worse, and about January and "do what you think," which she knew she had said, and hated that she had said, and would not let him have all of, because she had said it, because she was so tired of being the one who held everything that she had handed it to him without looking.

He listened. It was the first conversation they had had in two years that neither of them was having through a screen.

## Eleven: Field, Again

They stayed. They chose it, which is different from staying.

They opened one account that both of them could see. They stuck a spreadsheet on the fridge next to the rota, held by the magnet from Weymouth. They postponed the house by two years. Kieran deleted the apps and told Laura every number, every time, until telling her every number stopped feeling like confession and started feeling like weather: something that came over the downs whether you minded or not, and that you talked about.

Laura, who had never asked for anything, asked for Sundays off together, and got them. She was astonished by how easy it was.

Rebuilding was slow and dull and they chose that too. It was harvest in the old sense: the same field, the same work, every season.

In November a big exchange collapsed in the background, and it turned out the customers' money had been used by its trading firm, and bitcoin fell to a quarter of its peak. Barbara's coins fell with it. She said she had seen three of these. She did not sell. On the Ridgeway she began, unasked, to explain things to him. How the clearing actually worked, file by file. Why the bit that waits had been written to wait. What a key was, and what a map was, and the difference. The walks became lessons, and he let them.

Half the Sharehouse's channels were empty now. A few regulars still posted gm in the mornings, from Ohio and Lisbon and Manila. Kieran looked in sometimes. He did not trade. Once he answered a newcomer at three in the morning who wanted to know if it was too late to get in, and he wrote a long careful message about pegs, and then deleted it, and wrote: ask someone who loves you to sit with you while you decide. Then he closed the laptop and went to bed, where Laura was asleep, on a day off, next to him.

## Twelve: Awake

He stayed on the payments-exceptions desk at the Hart. The routine was the same. He was not.

He knew how old the machine was now, and what ran under it, and who could switch it off. He knew what the new machine had done to him in the night. He kept the card in his wallet behind his bus pass, soft as cloth now, with its 0.0071 bitcoin still behind it, worth about a hundred and fifty pounds that spring; he had never spent it, and did not mean to. It was not a key any more. It was a reminder, kept by choice.

In March 2023 fraud rule forty-one stopped a payment of twelve thousand pounds from a saver in her twenties to a crypto exchange, and the case came into his queue, and he rang her.

He read her the script. Has anyone contacted you and asked you to move your money. Have you been promised a return. Has anyone asked you to keep this private.

She said no to all of it, a little impatiently, the way he would have.

Then he said: "Can I ask you something that isn't on the script? Do you know how old the thing is that you're leaving? And how new the thing is that you're going into? And if it goes wrong, who are you going to tell?"

There was a silence on the line. It was not a hostile silence. He released the payment at 4.55, because nothing allowed him to stop it, and because it was hers, and he hoped she would tell someone.

On the Sunday the three of them walked on the Ridgeway: Barbara in front with the collie, too fast; Laura, who had never been up there, in the middle; Kieran behind. The chalk track ran white between the fields as it had for five thousand years. Below them the stones stood in their circle round the village, grey and leaning.

"Why would anyone drag them all that way?" Laura asked.

"To gather," Kieran said. "People will do almost anything to have somewhere to gather."

Barbara snorted, because it was her line, and did not mind.

His phone was in the car. The card was in his wallet. Three clocks were running in him still, and would be all his life: the body's, which wanted the fire and the faces; the institution's, which closed at five and waited three days; and the machine's, which never closed at all. He could hear all three. That was the difference. For most of his life he had heard only one, and thought it was the world.

The wind came over the downs. Laura took his hand without looking, the way you do when you are sure it will be there. They walked on towards the barrow, three small people on the oldest road in Britain, in the one corner of the map they had chosen, awake.

{"schema":"meaning-model-review/v1","kind":"review","text":"# Blind read 1: *Twelve Words*

Read in full, all twelve chapters (about 10,000 words), before writing anything below. I know nothing about how it was made and have not looked.

## 1. Verdict

*Twelve Words* is a twelve-chapter novella, not a novel by length, about a Swindon building-society clerk who is handed a bitcoin seed phrase by a retired programmer in 2019, finds a tribe in DeFi during the pandemic, and loses his partner's house deposit in the Terra collapse of May 2022. It works: the prose is exact, the period is right down to the day of the week and the price, the three central people are distinct and believable, and the confession-by-nursing-handover scene in chapter Ten is as good as anything of its kind I have read recently. The single thing that would most improve it is to dramatise the five weeks of lying: the book itself says the lie was "so much worse than the money," and then gives those weeks one paragraph and one exchange about looking grey. One shown evening inside them would give the ending its full weight. Separately, a money hole (Kieran's own forty-five thousand pounds vanishes from the account without a word) needs a sentence.

## 2. What works

**The sentences.** The book is written in short, weighed, concrete sentences that almost never reach for a word they cannot pay for. "He could read an exception the way his grandfather Ron ... had read a boiler by the sound it made." "Some Sunday evenings the week sat on his chest like a cat." "She answered each question exactly, like a woman filling in a form she had designed herself." The similes are drawn from the world of the people using them (fuse boards, boilers, monitors, wiring diagrams), which is how you tell a novel from a display of style.

**The period.** I checked the things a reader who lived through 2019-2023 would stop on, and they hold. 21 October 2019 was a Monday, 1 November a Friday, 12 March 2020 a Thursday and the worst market day since 1987; £50 of bitcoin on 31 October 2019 really is about 0.0071 BTC, and 0.0071 BTC really was about £28 on the evening of 12 March 2020 and about £150 in March 2023. The Terra week is right day by day: the wobble on Saturday the 7th, eighty cents Monday evening, sixty and back to ninety on Tuesday, the founder "deploying more capital," pennies by Friday the thirteenth. Honda's last car at the end of July 2021, the FCA's "prepared to lose all their money," the bank blocks in June, FTX in November 2022 with bitcoin at "a quarter of its peak," the rule of six, the third lockdown. Swindon Works closed in March 1986; the bitcoin paper is nine pages; the Wilson line is Wilson's. Nothing here embarrassed me.

**Laura's night on the unit** (chapter Three) is the best passage of pure narrative in the book, and it is what makes the deposit matter later. "The alarms went all night like birds in a hedge." Six people turning a man on the count of the one holding his head. And the line that carries the whole marriage until chapter Ten: "at least one of us is having an easy war."

**The farming inversion.** "He was not farming the tokens so much as they were farming him: that what he had planted was his own sleep." And the pub meet-up: "Nobody looked like a wizard. They looked like the queue at the post office ... You only have to own a phone and have a Tuesday."

**Barbara's three unsaid sentences** on the drive home in chapter Seven. This is the most honest thing in the book: a flaw with a cost, in the character who otherwise risks being an oracle. Then in Nine: "I didn't say it was my fault. I said what I did. Those are different things."

**Mandy's DM** in chapter Nine: he tells her "yes. tonight. before he finds out some other way" and then does not tell Laura for ten days. The irony is not underlined. Good.

**The rota** as the book's clock: "for two years he had been reading it as a timetable of when nobody would be watching."

**Chapter Ten.** Barbara's visit ("I don't sit down in other people's kitchens, so you needn't bother with the kettle") and then Laura's SBAR: "Situation ... Background ... Assessment ... Recommendation." "I don't know. I want you to tell me what we do." Giving her the handover form as the only way she can say it is exactly right for who she is, and the one line she has not written down is the emotional hinge of the book.

**The father.** Four "Pass the gravy"s, the mug that goes in the cupboard, and then "lost a week's wages on a horse once. 1961. Your nan didn't speak to him till Whitsun." That is a man drawn in under a hundred words.

**Dmitri.** The one who drew the diagram, named him Kez, sent him to "safe yield," and whose account says "deleted user." The book never says what he was. Right call.

**The last joke.** "I know," Laura said. "He's got my deposit." Earned, and the first time the deposit is anyone's to joke about.

**Structure.** Twelve words, twelve chapters; the Alice titles (Rabbit, Mirror, Hole, Awake); "Anchor" naming the protocol without naming it; the key/map figure braided with the game's black-edged map from chapter Three. The 4.55 release in chapter One mirrored in Twelve, with the payment still released. The book does not let Kieran become a preacher; it lets him ask three questions and let go.

## 3. Findings, most serious first

**F1. Error. Chapters Two, Six, Seven: how long Laura and Kieran have been together.**
Quote (Two, November 2019): "It was the first thing in five years he had not told Laura." Quote (Six, January 2021): "In eight years with him she had never once asked for anything except that." Quote (Seven, January 2022): "For eight years she had been the one who held everything."
Five years in late 2019 and eight years in early 2022 agree (together since 2014). Eight years in January 2021 does not; it should be six or seven. Fix: change the chapter Six line to "In six years with him" (or "seven").

**F2. Major. Chapters Seven to Nine: Kieran's own money disappears from the books.**
Quote (Seven): "By Christmas his seventy-one thousand was fifty. By the new year it was forty-five." Quote (Nine): "How much is left?" "About three hundred and forty pounds."
In January 2022 Kieran has forty-five thousand pounds of his own in crypto. The book then moves the twenty-four-thousand deposit into the dollar and never mentions his own stake again. If his forty-five thousand was in anything but the dollar, it was worth perhaps fifteen to twenty thousand in June 2022 and the deposit was replaceable, which means the extra shifts, the cancelled mortgage, the two-year postponement and the "every number, every time" vow do not follow. If it went into the same tent, the book needs to say so; that is also a much bigger and more characteristic act (the man who knows pegs puts everything he has behind one). Fix: one sentence in Seven, before the kitchen-table scene, such as: he moved his own forty-five thousand into the dollar in the second week of January, and it was only when it sat there for a fortnight not moving that he thought of the deposit. Then "How much is left?" covers everything.

**F3. Major. Chapter Nine: the five weeks are the moral centre and they are a paragraph.**
Quote: "For five weeks he said nothing." Laura, in Ten: "You went to work and came home and ate your tea and lied. That's worse than the money."
The book's own verdict is that the lie is the crime, and the lie is summarised: five sentences of lost weight and a shaking hand, one exchange ("You look grey"), and the Mandy DM. We never see him inside the lie with her. Fix: one shown evening between Friday 13 May and mid-June. The obvious one is already planted: in January she "was writing viewings into it in green pen." Show a viewing, or the evening after one, with the green door and the porch for his boots, and let him say "It's nice," knowing. That scene would also make her Assessment land on something the reader has watched rather than been told about. This is the single change I would make first.

**F4. Minor. Chapter Six: the chronology folds back on itself.**
Quote: "By Christmas his six thousand was fifteen thousand pounds; by February, thirty-eight; then forty-five."
The chapter opens in January 2021 (the shower, "We lost two"), then this paragraph goes back to Christmas 2020 and forward to February. A reader has to reconstruct the order. Fix: move the price paragraph ahead of the January scene, or write "By the Christmas just gone."

**F5. Minor. Chapter Eight: Wednesday arrives after Friday.**
Quote: "By Friday the thirteenth the deposit was worth about three thousand pounds ... On Wednesday he took a call from a man in Stratton."
We reach Friday, the goodbyes, then jump back to Wednesday without a signpost. Fix: "On the Wednesday of that week" or place the Pritchard call between the Tuesday bounce and Thursday.

**F6. Minor. Chapters Six and Twelve: the block Kieran built versus the payment he releases.**
Quote (Six): "the Hart's board decided to block payments to several crypto exchanges." Quote (Twelve): "a payment of twelve thousand pounds from a saver in her twenties to a crypto exchange."
If the Hart blocks exchanges and Kieran built the block, a payment to an exchange should not be sitting in his queue for release in 2023. "Several" leaves room, but the reader who remembers chapter Six stops. Fix: "to an exchange the block had never covered" or note in Twelve that the block had been quietly narrowed.

**F7. Minor. Chapter Seven: an unsignalled head-hop mid-scene.**
Quote: "'I trust you. Do what you think.' She meant it. When he said twenty percent and a dollar she thought of the monitors."
The narration is roving omniscient throughout and mostly manages its shifts (the doorway in Three, Barbara's drive in Seven, Laura's doorsteps in Nine). This one jumps into Laura's head in the middle of a beat we have been watching from his side. Fix: a line of white space, or move the Laura passage to after "He did not explain what a stablecoin was, and she did not ask."

**F8. Minor. Whole book: the "did not" sentence is the signature and by chapter Nine it is audible.**
"He did not trade. He read." "He did not tell Laura that night, or the next." "She did not shout. She did not cry in front of him." "She did not sell."
Sixty "did not"s in ten thousand words, forty of them "He did not." Definition by negation is the book's voice and often its best move (the raid, "She did not take his hand. She did not move hers away"), but the reader starts to hear the machine. Fix: keep the ones that carry weight; turn a third of the rest into plain statements.

**F9. Minor. Chapters Five, Seven and Ten: the same simile for Barbara three times.**
Quote (Five): "in short sentences, like someone reading off a wiring diagram." Quote (Ten): "in short flat sentences, like someone reading out a fault report." Also (Seven): "as she had once composed fault reports."
Fix: keep one. The wiring diagram in Five is the freshest.

**F10. Minor. Chapters Six and Eight: repeated tag lines.**
"That was the worst of it." appears in both chapters as a sentence on its own; "the first time" six times; the section-closing one-liner nearly every section ("It had not forgotten him." "Worse food." "It would be much harder to leave." "It had never heard of a peg." "and he thought that was the end of it."). Individually good; cumulatively the narrator sounds pleased with himself. Fix: let three or four sections end on an ordinary sentence and cut one "worst of it."

**F11. Minor. Chapters Five, Eight and Twelve: the thesis is stated four times.**
Quote (Eight): "knew that the worst thing that could happen to a person was to be alone outside the fire. It did not know about percentages."
Barbara gives it with Wilson and the phone at three in the morning (Five); the narrator gives it after the raid story (Eight); the "three clocks" paragraph gives it again at the end (Twelve). The raid story already does the work, and so does the walk. Fix: cut the last three sentences of the raid paragraph and reduce the three clocks to one sentence.

**F12. Minor. Chapter Four: the slang runs ahead of the calendar.**
Quote: "gm, said the channel, at 3.14 a.m. British Summer Time." Also "have fun staying poor."
"ser," "fren," "degen," "ape," "rug" and "wen" are right for summer 2020. "gm" as the universal greeting and "have fun staying poor" as a chant belong to 2021. A crypto-native reader will notice; nobody else will. Fix: hold "gm" and HFSP back to chapter Six, where "wen new pool" and "few understand" already sit correctly.

**F13. Minor. Chapter Four: summer 2020 compressed to a fortnight.**
Quote: "within a fortnight there were pools, and pools of pools, and tokens named after food."
The lending token was mid-June; the food tokens were August. Fix: "within two months."

**F14. Minor. Chapter Four: the September marker reads the wrong way.**
Quote: "In September, when people were allowed to meet outdoors in sixes, Barbara emailed him."
In England, groups of six outdoors had been allowed since June; September's "rule of six" was a tightening. As written it sounds like permission arrived in September. Fix: "In September, when the rule was six" or simply "In September."

**F15. Minor. Chapter Four: the search-bar joke shows its wiring.**
Quote: "'OMG,' he typed into a search bar at two in the morning, and then ... 'WTF is impermanent loss.'"
Nobody types "OMG" into a search bar. The second half is real (people do type that). Fix: cut "OMG."

**F16. Minor. Chapter Eleven: Kieran names a customer's call to his parents and the book does not notice.**
Quote: "'I know,' he said. 'I took his call. At the Hart.'"
A payments clerk of twelve years, whose whole self-image is reliability, tells his family he took a named customer's fraud call. Either he would not, or it is a slip that should register (a look from Laura, a beat). Fix: "I know," he said, and left it; or let it be the first thing he has ever said about work at that table and have the book know it.

**F17. Minor. Chapter Ten: the chiasmus runs the wrong way.**
Quote: "past the shops that had been banks and the banks that had been pubs."
Banks become pubs on every Wood Street in England; pubs almost never become banks. Fix: "the pubs that had been banks."

**F18. Minor. Chapter Eleven: an ICU nurse gets fixed Sundays off by asking.**
Quote: "asked for Sundays off together, and got them. She was astonished at how easy it was."
Any nurse reading this will snort. Fix: "one Sunday a month," or make it a standing swap with Jade.

**F19. Minor. Chapter Nine: a joint account cannot be moved into one name by one party.**
Quote: "she moved their accounts into her own name."
She can empty them into her own account; she cannot rename them without him. Fix: "moved what was left into an account in her own name."

**F20. Minor. Chapters Five, Seven and Ten: where does Barbara live?**
Quote (Ten): "took the bus into Swindon from the stop outside the Red Lion." Quote (Seven): "On the drive home, over the downs with the collie asleep on the back seat."
The Red Lion is the pub in Avebury; if she lives there, she would not drive home "over the downs" from the Avebury car park. If it is another Red Lion, the reader who knows Avebury has been misdirected. Fix: name her village once, in Five.

**F21. Minor. Chapter Two: the envelope knows more than she was told.**
Quote: "MR K. HALE, PAYMENTS EXCEPTIONS, THIRD FLOOR, WHITE HART HOUSE."
On the phone he said "the White Hart's payments team" and gave his surname. She had no way to know "exceptions" or "third floor." Fix: have him say it on the call, or have Deb wonder aloud how she knew.

**F22. Minor. Chapters Three and Four: he is swapping before he has put money in.**
Quote (Three): "He did not trade. He read." Quote (Four): "He asked a question about why his swap had failed."
The failed swap comes before "In July he put in six thousand pounds." Fix: "why a swap he was about to make would fail," or move the six thousand a paragraph earlier.

**F23. Note. Chapters Eight and Eleven: the Pritchard coincidence.**
The caller from Stratton turns out to be his father's line-mate of thirty years. In a book that has already made the one bank, the one plant and the one works hold everybody, it is a second lean on the same small-world device, and it exists to set up the Sunday lunch. It does not break, but a reader feels the hand. If kept, let Kieran half-register it on the call ("Stratton. Thirty years. He did not let himself think of his father").

**F24. Note. Chapter Five: Ron and Barbara were in the works at the same time and nobody says so.**
Kieran's grandfather was a fitter in the railway works until 1986; Barbara was an electrician there from 1969 to 1986. A reader waits for one of them to mention it, all the way to the last walk. One line on the first walk would cost nothing and bind the book.

**F25. Note. Chapters Six and Eleven: the mother has no name and no line.**
"did not think about his own mother" is a good beat that lands on nothing, because she is a hand over a mouth. One line at the last lunch would do.

**F26. Note. Chapter Three: a tangled measure.**
Quote: "the unit was running at half as many beds again as it had."
Fix: "half as many beds again as it was built for."

**F27. Note. Chapter Three: "Old Swindon."**
Quote: "a man in a kitchen in Old Swindon." Everywhere else it is Old Town. Fix: Old Town.

**F28. Note. Chapters Five and Twelve: the view from the Ridgeway is a composite.**
"Below them the great stones stood in their circle round the village ... with sheep grazing between them and a pub in the middle." From the Ridgeway the stones are two kilometres off; you would not see sheep between them. Put them on Waden Hill, or accept the licence.

**F29. Note. Chapter Three: "carried the batch home on a laptop."**
A building society's payment run does not go home on a laptop; he would remote in. Read as figurative it is fine; a banking reader stops. "Carried the queue home" would pass.

**F30. Note. Chapter Four: a twelve-thousand-pound Crete fund.**
"his half of a holiday fund" makes the fund twelve thousand for a week in Crete, for a nurse and a clerk saving for a deposit. "the holiday fund" (six thousand in all) is more like them.

**F31. Note. Whole book: no institutional consequence, ever.**
The undeclared gift, the block he built and walked round, Harriet from Compliance who says "We're seeing a lot of harm": all set up, none fires. That is a choice, and the book's quietness is part of its manner, but Harriet is a gun on the wall. One line in Twelve (he told her, in the end, or he never did and knew it) would close it.

**F32. Note. Chapter Seven: "seven nights out of ten" twice in three paragraphs.**
"She had worked seven nights out of the last ten" and then "It was her seventh night out of ten." The second is inside her head and reads as echo, but on the page it is repetition. Cut one.

**F33. Note. Chapter Twelve: the last word is the chapter title.**
"in the corner of the map they had chosen, awake." A touch insistent after a chapter called Awake. The sentence is better ending on "chosen."

## 4. The characters

**Kieran.** Believed, mostly. What he wants is to be needed by a band and to be no trouble to anyone, and the book understands that those are the same wish seen from two sides. Every choice follows from that: not declaring the card (nobody in front of him), the farm (forty people answering at three in the morning), building the block and walking round it (the only one who can see both rooms), and above all the hold in chapter Eight, which the raid story explains without excusing. The one choice that is under-built is the deposit itself: the house-price reason is given, but we never watch him decide, and the fate of his own forty-five thousand (F2) leaves the size of the decision unclear. My other reservation is that the book is a little kind to him. He pays his parents' rent, he never wants the number for its own sake, he is never greedy; a flicker of plain wanting (the seventy-one thousand on the screen, and liking it) would make him more like a person and less like a case. His voice is distinct: the apologetic doubled "Sorry. Sorry," the scam-line steadiness he hates.

**Laura.** Believed. She wants a front door, and the book knows why (five houses, a bin bag at twelve) before she says it. The ICU night, "at least one of us is having an easy war," "do what you think" as the first time she puts anything down, the three questions "as if she were taking a history," and then the SBAR: every choice is the choice of someone who holds. Staying follows from who she is (leaving would be a sixth doorstep) and the book is careful to call it choosing rather than forgiving. Two reservations. She is offstage for most of 2021, which is thematically the point (she is the one not watching) but means her big scene arrives after a long absence. And the five weeks she calls worse than the money are not shown from her side or his (F3).

**Barbara.** Believed as a voice, and her voice is the most distinct in the book: flat, declarative, "for nothing," "Wear proper shoes," "I can count, Kieran." The risk with her is that she is the narrator's mouthpiece and Kieran's fairy godmother, and for four chapters she is. What saves her is chapter Seven: three composed sentences she does not say, because she "had never been anybody's mother and did not mean to start at sixty-eight." That is a real flaw with a real cost, and her bus into Swindon in Ten is the direct consequence of it, which is what an arc is. Her wants (to wake one person; to keep her distance) are in tension, and the book makes her pay for the second. The refrain about mothers is used three times and the third use turns it; that works. What does not quite work is her Wilson lecture plus her stones lecture in one walk (F11): she explains the book's theme to the reader in the guise of explaining it to Kieran.

**The father.** Believed completely in under a hundred words. Gravy, mug, horse. He wants the world not to be talked about, and the one time he talks it is about 1961. Nothing to fix.

**Deb, Mandy, Dmitri, Harriet, Mr Pritchard.** All do their jobs. Deb's "helicopter man" and the hand on the shoulder are the same person. Mandy's text voice is right. Dmitri is a silhouette on purpose and better for it. Harriet is set up and not used (F31). Mr Pritchard's "A dollar. A dollar." is the book's grief in four syllables.

Nobody sounds like anybody else in dialogue. The one place voices blur is between Barbara and the narrator, whose aphoristic habit is hers.

## 5. The ending

Earned, in its main line. The mirror call with Chloe is the right final beat because the book refuses to let him save her: he asks three questions off the script, hears "the silence of somebody walking past a door they had not known was in the wall," and releases the payment at 4.55 "because it was hers." That is what he learned, stated as an action rather than a moral. The walk with three people on it, Laura in new boots, the stolen line, "He's got my deposit," and the hand taken without looking: all paid for by chapters Nine and Ten.

Two things hold it back from fully earned. The rebuild is frictionless: one August night at the kitchen table, then "They stayed. They chose it," a spreadsheet, and a joke seven months later. Nothing goes wrong on the way; there is no evening when he does not say a number, or when she checks the joint account behind him and hates herself for it. One such beat in chapter Eleven would make the walk feel like arrival rather than announcement. And the "three clocks" paragraph explains what the walk has already shown (F11); it is the one place the book does not trust its own last image. Cut it to a sentence and end on "chosen," and the ending is as good as the handover scene.

The narration is roving omniscient throughout and mostly manages its shifts (the doorway in Three, Barbara's drive in Seven, Laura's doorsteps in Nine).
