Fix: a line of white space, or move the Laura passage to after "He did not explain what a stablecoin was, and she did not ask."","quote":"'I trust you. Do what you think.' She meant it. When he said twenty percent and a dollar she thought of the monitors.","severity":"minor","category":"F7"},{"text":"F8. Whole book: the "did not" sentence is the signature and by chapter Nine it is audible. "He did not trade. He read." "He did not tell Laura that night, or the next." "She did not shout. She did not cry in front of him." "She did not sell."
Sixty "did not"s in ten thousand words, forty of them "He did not." Definition by negation is the book's voice and often its best move (the raid, "She did not take his hand. She did not move hers away"), but the reader starts to hear the machine. Fix: keep the ones that carry weight; turn a third of the rest into plain statements.","quote":"","severity":"minor","category":"F8"},{"text":"F9. Chapters Five, Seven and Ten: the same simile for Barbara three times. Quote (Five): "in short sentences, like someone reading off a wiring diagram." Quote (Ten): "in short flat sentences, like someone reading out a fault report." Also (Seven): "as she had once composed fault reports."
Fix: keep one. The wiring diagram in Five is the freshest.","quote":"in short sentences, like someone reading off a wiring diagram.","severity":"minor","category":"F9"},{"text":"F10. Chapters Six and Eight: repeated tag lines. "That was the worst of it." appears in both chapters as a sentence on its own; "the first time" six times; the section-closing one-liner nearly every section ("It had not forgotten him." "Worse food." "It would be much harder to leave." "It had never heard of a peg." "and he thought that was the end of it."). Individually good; cumulatively the narrator sounds pleased with himself. Fix: let three or four sections end on an ordinary sentence and cut one "worst of it."","quote":"","severity":"minor","category":"F10"},{"text":"F11. Chapters Five, Eight and Twelve: the thesis is stated four times. Quote (Eight): "knew that the worst thing that could happen to a person was to be alone outside the fire. It did not know about percentages."
Barbara gives it with Wilson and the phone at three in the morning (Five); the narrator gives it after the raid story (Eight); the "three clocks" paragraph gives it again at the end (Twelve). The raid story already does the work, and so does the walk. Fix: cut the last three sentences of the raid paragraph and reduce the three clocks to one sentence.","quote":"knew that the worst thing that could happen to a person was to be alone outside the fire. It did not know about percentages.","severity":"minor","category":"F11"},{"text":"F12. Chapter Four: the slang runs ahead of the calendar. Quote: "gm, said the channel, at 3.14 a.m. British Summer Time." Also "have fun staying poor."
"ser," "fren," "degen," "ape," "rug" and "wen" are right for summer 2020. "gm" as the universal greeting and "have fun staying poor" as a chant belong to 2021. A crypto-native reader will notice; nobody else will. Fix: hold "gm" and HFSP back to chapter Six, where "wen new pool" and "few understand" already sit correctly.","quote":"gm, said the channel, at 3.14 a.m. British Summer Time.","severity":"minor","category":"F12"},{"text":"F13. Chapter Four: summer 2020 compressed to a fortnight. Quote: "within a fortnight there were pools, and pools of pools, and tokens named after food."
The lending token was mid-June; the food tokens were August. Fix: "within two months."","quote":"within a fortnight there were pools, and pools of pools, and tokens named after food.","severity":"minor","category":"F13"},{"text":"F14. Chapter Four: the September marker reads the wrong way. Quote: "In September, when people were allowed to meet outdoors in sixes, Barbara emailed him."
In England, groups of six outdoors had been allowed since June; September's "rule of six" was a tightening. As written it sounds like permission arrived in September. Fix: "In September, when the rule was six" or simply "In September."","quote":"In September, when people were allowed to meet outdoors in sixes, Barbara emailed him.","severity":"minor","category":"F14"},{"text":"F15. Chapter Four: the search-bar joke shows its wiring. Quote: "'OMG,' he typed into a search bar at two in the morning, and then ... 'WTF is impermanent loss.'"
Nobody types "OMG" into a search bar. The second half is real (people do type that). Fix: cut "OMG."","quote":"'OMG,' he typed into a search bar at two in the morning, and then ... 'WTF is impermanent loss.'","severity":"minor","category":"F15"},{"text":"F16. Chapter Eleven: Kieran names a customer's call to his parents and the book does not notice. Quote: "'I know,' he said. 'I took his call. At the Hart.'"
A payments clerk of twelve years, whose whole self-image is reliability, tells his family he took a named customer's fraud call. Either he would not, or it is a slip that should register (a look from Laura, a beat). Fix: "I know," he said, and left it; or let it be the first thing he has ever said about work at that table and have the book know it.","quote":"'I know,' he said. 'I took his call. At the Hart.'","severity":"minor","category":"F16"},{"text":"F17. Chapter Ten: the chiasmus runs the wrong way. Quote: "past the shops that had been banks and the banks that had been pubs."
Banks become pubs on every Wood Street in England; pubs almost never become banks. Fix: "the pubs that had been banks."","quote":"past the shops that had been banks and the banks that had been pubs.","severity":"minor","category":"F17"},{"text":"F18. Chapter Eleven: an ICU nurse gets fixed Sundays off by asking. Quote: "asked for Sundays off together, and got them. She was astonished at how easy it was."
Any nurse reading this will snort. Fix: "one Sunday a month," or make it a standing swap with Jade.","quote":"asked for Sundays off together, and got them. She was astonished at how easy it was.","severity":"minor","category":"F18"},{"text":"F19. Chapter Nine: a joint account cannot be moved into one name by one party. Quote: "she moved their accounts into her own name."
She can empty them into her own account; she cannot rename them without him. Fix: "moved what was left into an account in her own name."","quote":"she moved their accounts into her own name.","severity":"minor","category":"F19"},{"text":"F20. Chapters Five, Seven and Ten: where does Barbara live? Quote (Ten): "took the bus into Swindon from the stop outside the Red Lion." Quote (Seven): "On the drive home, over the downs with the collie asleep on the back seat."
The Red Lion is the pub in Avebury; if she lives there, she would not drive home "over the downs" from the Avebury car park. If it is another Red Lion, the reader who knows Avebury has been misdirected. Fix: name her village once, in Five.","quote":"took the bus into Swindon from the stop outside the Red Lion.","severity":"minor","category":"F20"},{"text":"F21. Chapter Two: the envelope knows more than she was told. Quote: "MR K. HALE, PAYMENTS EXCEPTIONS, THIRD FLOOR, WHITE HART HOUSE."
On the phone he said "the White Hart's payments team" and gave his surname. She had no way to know "exceptions" or "third floor." Fix: have him say it on the call, or have Deb wonder aloud how she knew.","quote":"MR K. HALE, PAYMENTS EXCEPTIONS, THIRD FLOOR, WHITE HART HOUSE.","severity":"minor","category":"F21"},{"text":"F22. Chapters Three and Four: he is swapping before he has put money in. Quote (Three): "He did not trade. He read." Quote (Four): "He asked a question about why his swap had failed."
The failed swap comes before "In July he put in six thousand pounds." Fix: "why a swap he was about to make would fail," or move the six thousand a paragraph earlier.","quote":"He did not trade. He read.","severity":"minor","category":"F22"},{"text":"F23. Chapters Eight and Eleven: the Pritchard coincidence. The caller from Stratton turns out to be his father's line-mate of thirty years. In a book that has already made the one bank, the one plant and the one works hold everybody, it is a second lean on the same small-world device, and it exists to set up the Sunday lunch. It does not break, but a reader feels the hand. If kept, let Kieran half-register it on the call ("Stratton. Thirty years. He did not let himself think of his father").","quote":"","severity":"note","category":"F23"},{"text":"F24. Chapter Five: Ron and Barbara were in the works at the same time and nobody says so. Kieran's grandfather was a fitter in the railway works until 1986; Barbara was an electrician there from 1969 to 1986. A reader waits for one of them to mention it, all the way to the last walk. One line on the first walk would cost nothing and bind the book.","quote":"","severity":"note","category":"F24"},{"text":"F25. Chapters Six and Eleven: the mother has no name and no line. "did not think about his own mother" is a good beat that lands on nothing, because she is a hand over a mouth. One line at the last lunch would do.","quote":"","severity":"note","category":"F25"},{"text":"F26. Chapter Three: a tangled measure. Quote: "the unit was running at half as many beds again as it had."
Fix: "half as many beds again as it was built for."","quote":"the unit was running at half as many beds again as it had.","severity":"note","category":"F26"},{"text":"F27. Chapter Three: "Old Swindon." Quote: "a man in a kitchen in Old Swindon." Everywhere else it is Old Town. Fix: Old Town.","quote":"a man in a kitchen in Old Swindon.","severity":"note","category":"F27"},{"text":"F28. Chapters Five and Twelve: the view from the Ridgeway is a composite. "Below them the great stones stood in their circle round the village ... with sheep grazing between them and a pub in the middle." From the Ridgeway the stones are two kilometres off; you would not see sheep between them. Put them on Waden Hill, or accept the licence.","quote":"","severity":"note","category":"F28"},{"text":"F29. Chapter Three: "carried the batch home on a laptop." A building society's payment run does not go home on a laptop; he would remote in. Read as figurative it is fine; a banking reader stops. "Carried the queue home" would pass.","quote":"","severity":"note","category":"F29"},{"text":"F30. Chapter Four: a twelve-thousand-pound Crete fund. "his half of a holiday fund" makes the fund twelve thousand for a week in Crete, for a nurse and a clerk saving for a deposit. "the holiday fund" (six thousand in all) is more like them.","quote":"","severity":"note","category":"F30"},{"text":"F31. Whole book: no institutional consequence, ever. The undeclared gift, the block he built and walked round, Harriet from Compliance who says "We're seeing a lot of harm": all set up, none fires. That is a choice, and the book's quietness is part of its manner, but Harriet is a gun on the wall. One line in Twelve (he told her, in the end, or he never did and knew it) would close it.","quote":"","severity":"note","category":"F31"},{"text":"F32. Chapter Seven: "seven nights out of ten" twice in three paragraphs. "She had worked seven nights out of the last ten" and then "It was her seventh night out of ten." The second is inside her head and reads as echo, but on the page it is repetition. Cut one.","quote":"","severity":"note","category":"F32"},{"text":"F33. Chapter Twelve: the last word is the chapter title. "in the corner of the map they had chosen, awake." A touch insistent after a chapter called Awake. The sentence is better ending on "chosen."","quote":"","severity":"note","category":"F33"}]}}

{"schema":"meaning-model-review/v1","kind":"review","text":"# Blind read: *Twelve Words*

Read in full, start to finish (twelve chapters, about 11,100 words), knowing nothing about how it was made.

## 1. Verdict

*Twelve Words* is a short novel about Kieran Hale, a payments-exceptions clerk at a Swindon building society, who is handed a bitcoin seed phrase by a retired mainframe programmer in 2019, goes down the DeFi hole in lockdown, puts his and his nurse partner's house deposit into a "dollar that did not move" in January 2022, and loses it in the May 2022 collapse. It works: the real-world dates and mechanics check out almost to the day and the pound, the three principals are distinct on the page, and the domestic scenes (the viewing in the porch, the SBAR speech, "Pass the gravy") carry more weight than the crypto ones, which is the right way round. The single thing that would most improve it is to let Laura learn, on the page, the whole story and not just the last five months: the confession in chapter Nine explicitly starts at "January", so she is never shown finding out that he sat on seventy-one thousand pounds in November 2021 while she scrolled Wroughton semis, and her reckoning in Ten never touches it. That is the sharper wound, the book has planted it, and it leaves it unpaid.

## 2. What works

- The research is worn lightly and is right. 12 March 2020 as the markets' worst day since 1987; the lending protocol paying a token "in the middle of June"; the yam that "lasted about a day and a half"; the rule of six; the last car "at the end of July"; the Saturday wobble to ninety-nine cents, the Tuesday bounce to ninety, "Friday the thirteenth"; the founder "deploying more capital"; the November exchange whose "customers' money had been used by its trading firm". Even the arithmetic holds: 0.0071 BTC is fifty pounds on 31 October 2019, £28.14 on the evening of 12 March 2020, and "about a hundred and fifty pounds" in spring 2023.
- The explanations are the clearest I have read in fiction. The peg: "all that swapping held the price in place like a tent held by its guy ropes." The collapse: "each swap needed more of them, and the fall fed itself like a fire in a draught." A reader who knows nothing will understand, and a reader who knows everything will not wince.
- Laura's April 2020 night is the best passage in the book and it is only one paragraph: "the alarms went all night like birds in a hedge", the six of them turning the man on the count of the one holding his head, and then "at least one of us is having an easy war."
- The small true things: the rota as "a timetable of when nobody would be watching"; the agent who "called her Lauren twice"; the father who "put the mug in the cupboard over the kettle and did not take it out again"; Mandy told to tell her husband tonight, and Kieran then not telling Laura "for ten days after that".
- Barbara's lines earn their keep: "So you've swapped a bank you can't see for a hundred blokes with cartoon faces you can't see." "I gave you a key and not a map." "I didn't say it was my fault. I said what I did. Those are different things."
- The SBAR speech is the novel's best structural idea: a nurse who can only say the unsayable in the format she uses at handover, and then "Recommendation." followed by "I don't know. I want you to tell me what we do."
- The Wroughton roundabout: "nobody watching from the pavement would have seen anything at all." And the last joke, "He's got my deposit", which is the first thing Laura says that tells you they will be all right.
- The moral ending is not tidy: he keeps the undeclared gift, sits through the compliance course, "and he knew exactly where that line ran."

## 3. Findings, most serious first

**1. Major. Nine, Ten, Eleven. "He told her everything, in the order it had happened: January, the dollar that did not move, the ropes".** The confession starts in January 2022. Laura is never shown learning about the card (2019), the farming (2020-21), the Sharehouse, or the November 2021 peak of seventy-one thousand pounds, reached while she kept "a folder called HOUSE on the laptop they shared, which he never opened". Yet in Ten she does not react to "I'm the one who sent him the card", and her SBAR speech, the book's reckoning, never mentions that he had three deposits' worth for a year and said nothing. The reader knows; Laura apparently does not; the book does not notice the gap. Fix: begin the confession at the card, and give Laura one line in the SBAR about November 2021. It is a bigger betrayal than the deposit and the novel has already set it up.

**2. Major. Six. "That was the year everybody was at war with everybody."** 2021 arrives as a year-in-review essay: the regulator, the football shirts, the tyrannosaurus in a tie, "Nobody in either room was stupid." It is the year Kieran becomes Kez, is seconded to build the block and walks round it at night, and pays his parents' rent, and each of those is a sentence of summary. Fix: cut the two "war" paragraphs to a few lines and dramatise one thing. Harriet saying "We're seeing a lot of harm" on Teams while #war-room buzzes on his phone, or the first night he routes money round his own block, would do the work the essay is doing.

**3. Major. Eleven. "It was the worst row of their eight years, and it was about forty pounds."** The rebuild is a montage. The one scene in it that tests the new rule ("every number, every time") is told in three sentences, and the kitchen-floor aftermath is half a scene. The Sunday lunch confession and the spreadsheet on the fridge are good and brief. Fix: show the row. What he says when she finds the forty pounds on the statement, and what "He said he knew. The app showed the last login" does to her face.

**4. Error. Two versus Twelve. "the online course he did every March" against "In October Harriet from Compliance had run the refresher course in the training room".** The gifts course changes month and format, and the Twelve scene depends on it being the same course with the same cartoon. Fix: make it an October classroom session in Two, or make Twelve's an extra refresher and say so.

**5. Minor. Seven, Eight. "some of them through the same apps Kieran had used to walk round the block he had built".** A Hart employee seconded to the crypto block empties a Hart savings account of twenty-four thousand pounds to a fintech to dodge that block. A payment that size from a savings account would plausibly land in the very queue he clears (forty thousand did in One), and the fraud team later recognises those apps, yet nobody at the Hart notices and Kieran never once fears it. Fix: either let the transfer land in the queue (Deb sees the flag; he releases his own payment, which would be a very good scene) or spend one line on why it does not, and give him one beat of fear in May.

**6. Minor. Six. "For three months Kieran paid his parents' rent, from his gains".** His father has just left thirty years at a plant whose closure came with redundancy money (Dave Pritchard "put in his redundancy money"). Why the family needs the son's rent three months later is not said, and the reader stops on it. Fix: one clause. The payout had not come, or was being kept for something, or the father would not touch it.

**7. Minor. Eight. "By Friday the thirteenth the deposit was worth about three thousand pounds" then "On the Wednesday of that week, the day after the bounce".** The chapter runs Saturday, Monday, Tuesday, Thursday, Friday, then backtracks to Wednesday for the Pritchard call. The reader reorients, but stops. Fix: put the call between the Tuesday bounce and Thursday.

**8. Minor. Eleven. "In November a big exchange collapsed" then "Somewhere in the second month" then "In November he told her about the guild".** The lessons begin in November, run into a second month, and the guild conversation is dated November again. Fix: date the guild talk December, or drop "second month".

**9. Minor. Nine. "by June it was a few hundred pounds, then less" against "about three hundred and forty pounds" in mid-June.** The deposit is three hundred and forty on the last Saturday in May, "then less" by June, and three hundred and forty again when he confesses. Fix: make the June figure lower, or drop "then less".

**10. Minor. Nine. "cancelled the mortgage appointment with a polite email".** No appointment was made; the adviser had answered an email asking for statements. Fix: "withdrew the mortgage enquiry" or "told the adviser".

**11. Minor. Three. "the unit was running at half as many beds again as it was built for".** Correct English, parsed twice. Fix: "half again as many beds as it was built for".

**12. Minor. Five. "That's four things." / "I can count, Kieran."** Barbara has just deliberately added a fourth item to the biologist's three, so Kieran's objection is to arithmetic she made on purpose, and the exchange reads as a misfire rather than a joke. Fix: cut Kieran's line, or let him object to something else.

**13. Minor. Twelve. "He could hear all three clocks now, the body's and the institution's and the machine's".** "Three clocks" arrives in the last paragraph as if it had been the book's frame all along. The material is there (the hooter as "Whole town's clock", the alarms at three and five, the three-day cycle) but nothing earlier names it. Fix: plant the phrase once, most naturally in Barbara's mouth on the Ridgeway, or cut it and trust the images.

**14. Note. Throughout. Simile density.** The "X, the way Y does Z" and "like a Z" shape appears in almost every paragraph: "like a woman filling in a form she had designed herself", "like someone reading off a wiring diagram", "handbag on her knees like a toolbox", "as if she were checking it for current". Most are good on their own; together they become a mannerism. Fix: cut a third, and keep the electrical ones for Barbara, where they characterise.

**15. Note. Throughout. Kickers.** Nearly every section ends on an epigram: "Worse food." "It would be much harder to leave." "You only have to own a phone and have a Tuesday." "Nobody in either room was stupid." By Six the reader can hear it coming. Fix: let some sections end on a plain fact or an image.

**16. Note. Throughout. "Weather".** At least six times as metaphor: "as if it were weather", "the way weather goes down", "started feeling like weather", "Price is just weather", "tents come down in weather". A motif tipping into a tic. Fix: keep two, the father's and Barbara's.

**17. Note. Five, Seven, Eleven. Barbara and the narrator share an instrument.** When the narration says "the way weather goes down" and Barbara says "Price is just weather", she starts to sound like the book rather than a person, and her every line is quotable. "There's a biologist at Harvard. Old boy. Ants, mostly." reads as the author's reading list. Her silence in February and the visit in August rescue her; a second thing she is plainly wrong about would rescue her further.

**18. Note. Eight. "Forty of them on voice chat" in May 2010.** If the unnamed game is the obvious one, raids were twenty-five by 2010; forty-man raids ended in 2007. Harmless because the game is never named, but a player will blink at forty appearing both for the guild at sixteen and the raid at twenty. Fix: "twenty-five of them", or keep forty as guild size only.

**19. Note. Four. "gm" in a July 2020 channel.** About a year ahead of its popularity (2021). "ser", "wen", "frens", "ape", "degen" are right for the summer.

**20. Note. One, Eight, Eleven. Lisbon and Tallinn.** They are the guild's cities in One ("sulking in Lisbon", "carrying in Tallinn") and Eight ("Someone in Tallinn was shouting for heals"), and then the Sharehouse's ("from Ohio and Lisbon and Manila"). If it is an echo, one clause could own it; otherwise it reads as recycled geography.

**21. Note. Eleven. "Once, at three in the morning, a newcomer asked".** After the rebuild Kieran is still awake at three on the Sharehouse, with the CHECKED column on the fridge, and the book does not remark on it. Either it is a relapse and should be felt, or it should happen at lunchtime.

**22. Note. Seven. "For eight years she had been the one who held everything" (January 2022).** Elsewhere the relationship is five years in November 2019, six in January 2021 and eight in October 2022, which is consistent with an autumn 2014 start. This "eight" reads as the relationship and would be seven. Fix: "For years".

**23. Note. Three. "a chain running back through thousands of hands to January 2009".** Coin history fans out rather than forming a single chain, and the first coins cannot move. A fair simplification for a first look at a block explorer; a crypto-literate reader will pause.

**24. Note. Eleven. "a game for his phone, the first he had bought in twelve years" at forty pounds.** Phone games rarely cost that. A console game makes the sum natural and the row the same.

**25. Note. Twelve. The Chloe call mirrors One almost beat for beat.** The script, "a door they had not known was in the wall", the release "at 4.55". The symmetry is the point, but the near-verbatim reuse makes it feel engineered. Fix: vary one element. Let her ask him something, or let the time be different.

**26. Note. Three. Point of view.** After two chapters locked to Kieran, the narration steps into Laura's April night, and later into Barbara's car and Laura's kitchen. These dips are among the best writing, but the first is abrupt. An earlier small step outside Kieran (Deb, or the note on the pasta bake seen from Laura's side) would prepare the widening.

That is one error, three major, nine minor and thirteen notes. The single error is a small one, and I looked hard for real-world mistakes and found none: the dates, the mechanisms, the pub names and the NHS vocabulary are all right.

## 4. The characters

**Kieran.** Believed. What he wants is to be needed by a band and to be "no trouble to anyone", and the book understands that these are the same wish seen from two sides. Every choice follows: not declaring the card because declaring would "make her a case"; putting in the Crete money and not the deposit "on the landing, with his hand on the bathroom door"; moving the deposit into the "safe" thing because it was the safe money; not selling at ninety because of Sander and the clock at 11.52; the five weeks, learned "with a white card behind a bus pass". His pleasure in the number ("felt it in his shoulders like a warm bath") is admitted once and could be admitted twice. His professional exposure is the one thing about him the book does not want to look at (finding 5).

**Laura.** Believed, and the best-written. She wants a front door that is hers, and to put something down once. "Do what you think" is properly motivated (the monitors, "somebody competent was watching them") and the book is honest that it was also her choice. Her doorstep history explains both why she stays and why she cannot say anything until someone tells her she is allowed. The SBAR speech is exactly who she is. Two gaps: she never asks how much of his money there had been, which is in character, but the book never returns to it (finding 1); and her turn from silence to speech happens in a single day after Barbara's visit, which the permission framing just about carries.

**Barbara.** Vivid and the novel's engine. She wants to be known for what she built ("Nobody ever put my name on anything. That's fine. I know what I built"), to hand someone a way of seeing, and never to be anybody's mother. Her choices follow, including the one that damns her: the three sentences composed in the car and not said. Her walk to Wood Street is the right move for the character and the book. The risk is oracle-ness (finding 17): she is right about everything except the thing she chose not to say, and her cadence is the narrator's.

**Kieran's father.** Three lines a chapter and all of them land. "Pass the gravy, Kieran", the mug in the cupboard, the horse in 1961. He is the book's model for how men of the works say things, and Barbara's reading of the guild ("You went to work") belongs to the same world.

**Deb, Mandy, Dmitri, Harriet, Chloe, Sander.** Functional and distinct enough. Mandy's "ur a good one x" and Dmitri's "kez knows" are good ears for the register. Nobody sounds like anybody else; the one blur is between Barbara and the narration.

## 5. The ending

Earned, with one unpaid debt. The rebuild does its work in the right key: a spreadsheet next to the rota, "Four hundred and twelve in the joint", the CHECKED column ticked "openly, and then one night forgot to", the parents told over the plant mug, Barbara's reframing of the night in 2010. The Chloe call gives Kieran a vocation that the book has prepared through "the bit that waits", and leaving the gift undeclared keeps the last chapter from being clean. The final walk, with Laura in new boots and "He's got my deposit", is the right image and the right joke.

What it has not paid for is Laura's knowledge (finding 1). The reconciliation stands on "We tell each other everything", and the reader is left holding one thing Laura was never told. The "three clocks" sentence (finding 13) and the near-verbatim mirror of chapter One (finding 25) make the last pages feel slightly more arranged than the rest of a book whose great strength is that nothing in it feels arranged.

{"schema":"meaning-model-review/v1","kind":"review","text":"# Blind read 3: *Twelve Words*

Read in full, start to finish, before writing a word of this. Nothing else consulted.

## 1. Verdict

*Twelve Words* is a tight novella (about 11,600 words in twelve chapters) about a Swindon building-society clerk who is handed a bitcoin seed phrase by a retired payments programmer, farms his way through the 2020 yield craze, and loses his partner's house deposit in the May 2022 stablecoin collapse; underneath the crypto it is a book about three people who "hold everything" and say nothing, and about what it costs each of them to say something. It works: the voice is controlled, the real-world scaffolding (dates, prices, the peg mechanism, the ICU, the Works, the car plant) is unusually accurate, and the marital reckoning, written as a nurse's SBAR handover, is the best structural idea in it. The single thing that would most improve it is to dramatize the hinge the book currently summarizes: November 2021, when Kieran is worth seventy-one thousand pounds and Laura's folder called HOUSE sits unopened on the laptop they share. Laura's central accusation ("That's three deposits. I was doing extra nights for one of them, and you let me") is the moral centre of the novel, and it lands on something the reader was told in two sentences rather than shown.

## 2. What works

- The opening register, which gives the whole book its way of seeing: he could read an exception "the way his grandfather Ron... had read a boiler by the sound it made: not the words on the screen but the shape of what had gone wrong behind them." Everything after is a man learning the shape of what has gone wrong behind his own screen.
- Barbara's voice is the best in the book and never slips: "It was built for magnetic tape, my love. It's got more patches on it than my dad's allotment shed." And: "So you've swapped a bank you can't see for a hundred blokes with cartoon faces you can't see. At least the bank's got a mural."
- The ICU night in Three is the strongest passage of prose. The proning ("every line and tube gathered in their hands so that nothing pulled"), the phone held to a dying man's ear so his daughter can say the cat is fine, and the button: "at least one of us is having an easy war." It gives Laura a life the book then has the discipline not to over-explain.
- The mechanics are made into metaphor without cheating. The tent and guy ropes for the peg; "he was not farming the tokens so much as they were farming him"; "Everything he had ever worked in was a peg, when you looked... They held because everyone agreed they would." A reader who knows nothing about Terra will understand the collapse; a reader who does will find nothing wrong.
- The Sharehouse chorus is exactly right, from "ser everything is a rug if you zoom out enough" to "gn frens. gn forever" to the last word the book gives it, "lol ok boomer".
- The rota. Set up as timetable in One, read "as he read the price" in Six, and turned in Nine: "for two years he had been reading it as a timetable of when nobody would be watching." That is the best single sentence about the marriage.
- The SBAR scene in Ten. "Situation... Background... Assessment... Recommendation." and then the only line she had not written down: "I don't know. I want you to tell me what we do."
- The forty-pound row in Eleven, which is where the reconciliation is actually earned: "I thought you were owed it." / "That's the same thing... That's exactly the same thing again."
- Barbara's refusal to take the easy absolution: "I didn't say it was my fault. I said what I did. Those are different things. You'll learn that."
- Small true things: the agent who "called her Lauren twice"; the men in the pub who "looked like the queue at the post office"; "It's only a mug." / "Pass the gravy."; the founders on the mural "looking faintly surprised to find themselves on a wall in west Swindon."
- The book's honesty about what does not get resolved: "He told Laura every number, every time, and he told the Hart nothing, and he knew exactly where that line ran."
- The design of the titles: twelve chapters, twelve single words, with "Field" used twice ("Eleven: Field, Again") the way a seed phrase can repeat a word. Most readers will not notice; the ones who do will smile.

## 3. Findings, most serious first

**1. Error (continuity). Part Nine.** "It was the house from her phone: the three-bed semi in Wroughton with the green front door and the porch."
Laura found that house on her phone in January 2021 (Six). The viewing is the last Saturday in May 2022, sixteen months later, in the middle of the fastest UK housing market in a generation, and the sellers "wanted a quick sale". Either it is a different house or it came back on the market; the text asserts identity and explains nothing, and the "You could put your boots in here" echo, the emotional peak of the chapter, is balanced on it. Fix: one clause ("it had come back on; the chain had fallen through") or make it "a house like the one from her phone".

**2. Major (summarized where it should be shown). Part Six, November 2021.** "Laura had a shortlist of three houses and a folder called HOUSE on the laptop they shared, which he never opened."
This is the hinge of the whole novel: the month he could have cashed out three deposits and bought her the front door, and instead kept the number "in his shoulders like a warm bath". It gets two sentences of summary. Everything downstream (Laura's "you let me", the rota-as-timetable line, the "before that there was a year") asks the reader to feel the weight of a choice they never watched him make. One scene would do it: Kieran at the laptop, the HOUSE folder there, the number there, Laura asleep through the wall, and the specific thing he tells himself. The book is good at exactly this kind of scene (the landing with his hand on the bathroom door in Four); it just skips the one that matters most.

**3. Major (contradiction). Part Twelve.** "Nobody had asked him that at work. 'Yes,' he said. 'It went wrong. That's why I'm asking.'"
One paragraph earlier the narrator has told us, with some ceremony, that Kieran "told the Hart nothing, and he knew exactly where that line ran." Then he tells a customer, on a recorded fraud line, that he bought crypto and lost. That is telling the Hart, and the man who structured three payments of eight thousand to stay under his own rules would know it. Either this is the moment he stops hiding, in which case the book should let him feel the line being crossed and let it cost something, or it is a slip. As written it is neither, and a reader stops on it at the worst possible moment.

**4. Minor (motive). Part Seven.** "'That's yours and Laura's to decide.'"
Barbara volunteers scorn freely in Five ("Don't tell me you're in the casino"; "Worse food") but withholds the one warning that matters. The book's explanation, that she "had never been anybody's mother and did not mean to start", covers restraint in general but not the switch from open contempt for the Sharehouse to silence about the peg. Ten admits it ("That's the opposite of everything I believe, and I did it anyway"), which helps, but the admission arrives after the reader has already had to swallow it. A line in Seven showing her *decide* to be quiet (she nearly speaks, and the thing that stops her is that it is Laura's money and Laura is not there) would make it a choice rather than a plot convenience.

**5. Minor (continuity, arithmetic). Parts One and Seven.** "had cleared that queue for nine years" (October 2019) and "he had cleared that queue for twelve years" (January 2022).
Twenty-seven months add three years. From a May 2010 start the true figures are nine and a half and eleven and two-thirds; one is rounded down, the other up. "Eleven years" in Seven fixes it, or drop the number.

**6. Minor (continuity). Part Ten.** "'You lied to me for five weeks. ... And before that there was a year.'"
The narrator says "for two years he had been reading it as a timetable" (Nine) and "the first conversation they had had in two years" (Ten); the card was November 2019, the farms July 2020. Laura may be counting only the rich year, but nothing tells us so, and the two figures sit in adjacent chapters.

**7. Minor (sequence). Part Four.** "A link in a thread about a token named after a vegetable took him to a chat server called the Sharehouse... In July he put in six thousand pounds."
The vegetable tokens (the yam that "lasted about a day and a half") belong to August 2020, but the paragraph order puts his Sharehouse apprenticeship, and "kez knows", before the July money. Either date the join or move "In July" to before the Sharehouse.

**8. Minor (real-world plausibility). Part Eleven.** "'I know,' he said. 'The app shows the last login.'"
This is the pivot of the best scene in the last third, and it rests on a feature most readers will not recognise: a joint account app that shows one holder when the other logged in. If a specific app does this, name the mechanism (a login alert, an email); otherwise let him know some other way (she leaves the tab open; the "last viewed" on the spreadsheet).

**9. Minor (real-world). Part Five.** "1969 they let me in as an apprentice. Three women in the whole works."
Swindon Works employed a great many women, in the trimming shop, the offices, the laundry. Barbara is entitled to exaggerate, but a Swindon reader will stop. "Three women on the tools" says what she means and is true.

**10. Minor (plausibility, unexplained). Part Six.** "For three months, until the redundancy money came through, Kieran paid his parents' rent."
A man with thirty years at the plant would normally be paid his package on leaving, and the plant's packages were famously generous. If the money was late, one clause saying why (a dispute; a staged payment) stops the reader asking. The scene the delay buys, in the car outside the Job Centre, is worth keeping.

**11. Minor (dangling implication). Part Six.** "tell her only what she can lose, he wrote, and felt wise, and did not think about his own mother."
This promises something about Sue, or about Kieran's family and money, that never arrives; Sue appears once, in Eleven, to ask Laura if she is all right. Either pay it (Sue asks him about "the bitcoin" and he deflects) or cut the last clause.

**12. Minor (characters sounding alike). Part Ten, across the book.** Barbara: "That part's mine. The rest is his." Laura, hours later: "So that's mine. Barbara's right. That bit's mine."
The echo is deliberate, and it works as an inheritance. But it exposes something wider: Barbara, Laura, Kieran's father and the narrator all speak in the same deadpan clipped understatement ("It's only a mug." "Everything's up." "It never felt like lying."). It is a good house voice, but by Ten it is sometimes hard to tell whether a wise short line is Barbara's, Laura's, or the author's. Kieran is the one voice that is distinct (the apologising, the scam-line steadiness), and that is a point in the book's favour; the women could be told apart more by rhythm than by content.

**13. Minor (over-explanation). Parts Eight, Nine, Eleven.** "since the night at twenty when he had handed the guild to Sander and logged off in the middle of a raid."
The raid as the reason he cannot sell is stated in Eight, restated in the same chapter at paragraph length, invoked again in Nine ("He thought of twenty-five people in the dark"), and told to Barbara in Eleven. The Eight paragraph is excellent ("kez had a real life to go to. That was the part he could not forgive."); the summaries around it are scaffolding that can come down. A single origin wound explaining a financial decision is already a neat device; repeating it makes it look neater than life.

**14. Minor (repeated constructions).** Across the book.
- "the first thing in five years he had not told Laura"; "For the first time she slowed"; "For the first time in twelve years he was afraid"; "understood for the first time"; "the first conversation they had had in two years"; "the first he had bought in twelve years"; "the first band since the guild"; "It was the first time she had made a joke". Eight "first"s is a tic.
- "He liked it, more than he would have admitted" (Six) and "he liked that more than he would have said" (Seven), one chapter apart, about the same feeling.
- The anaphoric denial list: "no branch behind them, no mural, no brass hart, no three-day cycle, no exceptions queue"; "There was no queue. There was no cut-off. There were no exceptions"; "There was no bus, no tea round, no quiz." Three in three chapters.
- Similes of the form "like a man/woman doing X": "like a woman filling in a form she had designed herself", "like a man checking a sleeping child", "like a man let back in", "like someone reading off a wiring diagram", "the way you look at a fuse board". Individually good; as a set they announce the author.
- "exactly" is leaned on: "answered each question exactly", "He remembered it exactly", "composed the three sentences... exactly, clause by clause", "He knew exactly what was happening", "knew exactly where that line ran".
- Nearly every chapter closes on a one-line button ("and they came third." / "and she did not tell him that either." / "gn forever" / "and he was the one who cried."). Most land; the pattern becomes audible by Nine.

**15. Minor (asserted rather than shown). Part Eleven.** "They stayed. They chose it, which is different from staying."
The choosing is not on the page; the one-in-the-morning conversation in Ten is summarized after its key lines. The book does earn the staying, but in the forty-pound row later in Eleven, not here. Trust that scene and cut the assertion, or give the assertion one concrete beat (what Laura says in the morning).

**16. Note (confusing). Part Nine.** "Now there was one screen fewer and no more words."
Whose screen? He still checks "the dead balance at night" and does not delete the apps until September. If the line means his charts have stopped mattering, say that.

**17. Note (convenience). Part Ten.** "knocked on the door of a flat above a shop."
Barbara knows Kieran's address and arrives on a day Laura is home between nights; neither is set up. She also takes the bus although she drives (she drove him to Avebury Trusloe in Seven), and the book flags the bus as significant ("which she had not done in two years") without saying why. A half-line of each would do.

**18. Note (real-world timing). Part Eight.** "On the Wednesday, the day after the bounce, the Hart's fraud lines filled with customers who had lost their savings."
On the real Wednesday the peg was still swinging between thirty and eighty cents; ordinary savers ringing a building society in numbers fits Thursday or Friday better. The rest of that week's dates and prices (Saturday the seventh, Monday the ninth, the sixty-cent bounce on the Tuesday, twenty cents by Thursday, "Friday the thirteenth") are correct, which makes this small slip more visible.

**19. Note (titles).** "One: Blue" is the only chapter title with no anchor in its chapter (the blue biro is in Two; the blue light is in Four); every other title is earned inside its part. And if the twelve titles are meant to read as a seed phrase (the count and the repeated Field suggest they are), "Silence" is, as far as I remember the standard list, not on it; "Silent" is. Worth checking, since a reader who catches the conceit will check.

**20. Note (last sentence). Part Twelve.** "three small people on the oldest road in Britain, in the corner of the map they had chosen, awake."
Three reaching phrases in a row, and "awake" is doing title work. The sentence before it, "Laura took his hand without looking. She was sure it would be there.", is the ending; it pays Ten's "She did not take his hand" exactly and needs nothing after it.

**21. Note (phrasing). Part Ten.** "I have never been anybody's mother, and I have been very proud of that for sixty-nine years."
Nobody is proud of childlessness at two. It is in character as dryness, but it reads as a slip in counting rather than a joke. (Her ages otherwise check: thirty-three in March 1986, sixty-eight in February 2022, sixty-nine in August 2022 all fit one birthday.)

**22. Note (the Hart's two speeds). Parts One and Six.** "takes three days to move money that could move in a second."
By 2019 most consumer transfers already moved in seconds, and the Hart itself later sends Kieran's money to his app in "forty seconds". Barbara is being polemical about the overnight batch, which is fair, but the novel never squares the three-day relic with the forty-second sender, and a reader who banks will notice.

**23. Note (small inconsistency). Part Twelve.** "not the number, which he no longer looked at" (Eleven) against "worth about a hundred and fifty pounds that spring."
He knows what the card is worth. One "he had looked it up once" fixes it.

**24. Note (what I did not find).** I looked hard for real-world errors in the 2019 to 2023 material and found none I would stake anything on. The 12 March 2020 crash and its "worst day since 1987"; the 23 March lockdown; the June 2020 lending-token launch and the food tokens; the rule of six; the January 2021 lockdown; the regulator's "prepared to lose all their money"; the mid-2021 exchange blocks and shirt sponsorships; the plant's last car at the end of July 2021 and the 1992 start date on the mug; the November 2021 peak; the twenty-percent dollar; the exchange collapse in November 2022 and bitcoin at a quarter of its peak; the nine-page paper; the ant biologist's line; the Works closing in March 1986 and the hooter; the fifty pounds becoming 0.0071 bitcoin becoming £28.14 becoming about £150 in spring 2023: all of it checks. Even the weekdays are right. That care is one of the book's real virtues and should be protected in revision.

## 4. The characters

**Kieran.** Believed him. He wants, for most of the book, only negatives: not to be trouble, not to be the one who leaves, not to make Barbara a case, not to make the loss real by selling. The book knows this ("become, deliberately, no trouble to anyone") and builds him out of it: the apologising, the scam-line voice he cannot switch off, the reading of the rota. His choices follow. Not declaring the card follows from the handbook cartoon and from the guild's loot rule ("there was nobody in front of him"). Structuring the three payments follows from a man who knows the rules to the pound. Not selling at ninety cents follows from Sander. The one choice the book asks us to take on trust is the one in November 2021 (finding 2). What he finally wants, in Twelve, is stated well: to be "the bit that waits in the building". I believed that too, with the reservation in finding 3.

**Laura.** Believed her, and she is better written than a supporting spouse usually is. She wants a front door that is hers, and the book gives that want a history (five doorsteps, the bin bag at twelve) without leaning on it. Her "do what you think" follows: seven nights out of ten, the green pen running out, and the one paragraph of interiority in Seven that makes it rest rather than negligence. Her silence after the confession, the extra shifts, the polite withdrawal email, the daily secret checking of the account: all of a piece with a woman who "held". The SBAR is the choice that most follows from who she is; she can only say it in the form she uses at work. The one thing I did not quite get is why she stays, as opposed to how; the book asserts it (finding 15) and then earns it later, in the row.

**Barbara.** Believed her from the first line she speaks. She wants, as she says, to give something that is not money, and she has never learned how, because she has never asked anyone for anything since the personnel office in 1986. Her contempt for the Sharehouse, her walking too fast, her refusal to sit in other people's kitchens, her lessons "month by month. You'll hate it." all cohere. The one choice that does not fully follow is her silence in February (finding 4). The book's fix, having her own it in Ten, is the right instinct and mostly works. The line about Kieran going to work at twenty being "the first grown-up thing you ever did" is the truest thing anyone says to him and could only have come from her.

**Kieran's father.** A sketch, but a good one, held together by "Pass the gravy" and the mug in the cupboard. The 1961 horse story is exactly the right size for him. Sue barely exists; her one line to Laura is well chosen.

**Deb, Mandy, Dmitri, Harriet, Chloe.** Deb and Mandy are alive in a few lines each; Mandy's "my husband doesnt know. he thinks its in the isa" is the book's irony at its cleanest. Dmitri is meant to be a name and an absence, and is. Harriet and Chloe are functions and fine as such.

## 5. The ending

Earned, mostly, and earned in the right place: not in the reconciliation scene in Ten, which is affecting but summarizes its own second half, but in the forty-pound row and the CHECKED column in Eleven, where the book shows the marriage relapsing into its old pattern, naming it ("That's exactly the same thing again"), and then letting Laura forget to tick the box. That is a real ending and it is quiet in the way the material wants.

Two reservations. First, the Chloe call (finding 3): it is the right scene, the right mirror of One, and the right sentence to end his arc on ("He was the bit that waits in the building"), but it needs to notice that he has just crossed the line the previous paragraph drew. Second, the last two pages tie every bow: the three clocks, "to gather", the short bark, the card behind the bus pass, 4.55, "awake". The book has been so disciplined about motifs that the final accounting of all of them at once feels like the author checking a list. Cut two of the callbacks and end on "She was sure it would be there."

The refusal to let the Hart find out is the ending's bravest choice and I would not change it. The book says plainly that he never declared the card, never told Compliance, and still holds an undeclared gift in his wallet, and it does not pretend that is clean. That honesty is what keeps the serenity of the walk from being cheap.
