nodes.text: {"schema":"meaning-model-story-author-record/v1","kind":"world","text":"The book comes out of Faye Titcombe's invented life: a railway-works child who learned that routine is someone else's to end, an archaeologist of the first gatherings, eighteen years inside the payments batch, a fall into decentralized finance in 2020-2022 that she understood and could not stop. She writes it in 2025-2026 beside a fifteen-year-old daughter who has just found a trading app. The story presses the fear of being left behind, the fear that a safe life is someone else's to end, the longing for more world, and the shame of knowing better.","data":{"schema":"meaning-model-story-world/v1","stage":"author_reader","author":{"personId":"referent.profile.faye.person.faye","name":"Faye Titcombe","mode":"invented","lifeModelHash":"66335be7f45c1ab93c7e59fe604b1edab462ca7340c309b9eca269f1e7c7f5c6","authorModelNodeId":"author.model.faye","livesIn":"this_world","writing":"She writes in autumn 2025 to autumn 2026 about 2019-2023, three to six years after the events. She knows how the 2021 boom and the 2022 collapses ended, so the novel can let the reader feel the protagonist's hope while knowing more than they do. She lived a version of these years but the protagonist is not her: she gives the fall to someone younger and more ordinary than herself, in the town she knows, and keeps the real markets, prices and laws in the background.","whyThisStory":"Her daughter's trading app sent her back to her own fall. She chose to learn it beside her (the drawn decision), and she needs to understand what she is walking beside: why a careful person who understood the mechanism still went in and stayed. Her motivational attention while writing goes mostly to understanding and to her daughter (cut.faye.2026.why_write).","teach":"Nothing she would call a lesson. She wants to show that the pull down the rabbit hole is ancient and human, not a private stupidity, and that the institutions and the machines it runs through are younger than they look.","figuringOut":"Whether an old mind can live in a fast world without hiding in the routine or drowning in the new game; whether understanding can ever govern feeling, which her own 1986 lesson promised and 2022 broke; and whether walking beside her daughter is love or abdication.","lifeRecords":["event:event.profile.works_closure.change_arc","event:ev.faye.p2.study","event:ev.faye.p3.ledger","event:ev.faye.p4.rabbit_hole","event:event.profile.collapse_2022.change_arc","cut:cut.faye.2022.holding","cut:cut.faye.2026.why_write","event:ev.faye.learn_beside","event:ev.macro.downs"]},"reader":null,"buttons":[{"id":"btn.left_behind","button":"Everyone else found the real game and I am still in the tutorial.","presses":"Show the protagonist's ordinary life as one small corner of a map, then open the map; let the others seem to be further in.","learns":"That the fear of being left behind is the band's fear of exile, far older than money, and can be felt without being obeyed.","readerRecords":[]},{"id":"btn.someone_elses_routine","button":"My safe life belongs to someone who could end it.","presses":"Make the routine loving and specific, then show the machinery under it: whose rules, how old, who can switch it off.","learns":"That the institutions they trust are young and man-made, which is frightening and also freeing.","readerRecords":[]},{"id":"btn.more_world","button":"There has to be more than this.","presses":"Give the white rabbit real wonder: the hidden world is genuinely astonishing before it is dangerous.","learns":"That curiosity is not a defect to be trained out, and that it needs company, not a cage.","readerRecords":[]},{"id":"btn.knew_better","button":"I knew better and did it anyway.","presses":"Let the protagonist understand the danger clearly and still be carried by the group and the feeling.","learns":"That knowing and feeling run on different clocks, and that a fall is not a verdict on one's intelligence.","readerRecords":[]},{"id":"btn.watching_them_go","button":"Someone I love is about to go down the same hole.","presses":"Give the protagonist someone who watches them go, and who must choose between forbidding and following.","learns":"That the choice between holding someone back and walking beside them is real and costly either way.","readerRecords":[]}]},"authoringClock":{"rootId":"story.understanding.c478361e6869af25970682a2","unit":"authoring_step","at":6}}

nodes.text: {"schema":"meaning-model-story-author-record/v1","kind":"world","text":"Three candidate worlds from Faye's life: The Exceptions Queue (a Swindon payments clerk handed twelve words by an engineer who built the old machine), Twelve Words (a warehouse picker finds a stranger's wallet) and The Pension (a claims handler of fifty-eight). Chosen under delegation: The Exceptions Queue, keeping the twelve words and an older person's late wonder from the others.","data":{"schema":"meaning-model-story-world/v1","stage":"candidates","authorReaderNodeId":"world.author_reader","form":{"targetWords":11000,"parts":12},"candidates":[{"id":"cand.exceptions","title":"The Exceptions Queue","world":"Swindon and the Wiltshire downs, autumn 2019 to spring 2023, in our real world: a building society's payments operations floor, a pandemic, the 2020-2021 crypto boom and the 2022 collapses.","account":"A payments clerk of about thirty works the exceptions queue at a Swindon building society, the kind of job where every week is the same and the systems date from the 1960s. Part of the job is phoning customers whose large transfers look like scams. One customer, a retired engineer in her late sixties who once wrote code for the clearing system itself, is not being scammed: she is moving her savings out of the old machine on purpose, and she leaves the clerk a card with twelve words and fifty pounds of bitcoin behind them. In the 2020 lockdown the clerk follows the words down the rabbit hole into decentralized finance, finds a band in a chat server, farms yields through the night, and moves the house deposit they share with their partner, an intensive-care nurse working the pandemic wards. By day the clerk enforces the building society's new blocks on crypto payments; by night they route around them. In May 2022 the stablecoin their deposit sits in loses its peg. The costs fall on the partnership, on the engineer's trust, and on the clerk's idea of who they are; the ending is open to the model's draws.","premise":"The person whose job is to stop other people going down rabbit holes is handed the key to one by a stranger who knows the old machine better than anyone.","emotionalCore":"The ache of a small, safe, repetitive life and the joy of discovering the map is enormous; then the old fear of the band's exile keeping you in the game after you know it is rigged.","question":"Can a mind built for a band of a hundred and fifty faces live in a world of three-day batches and twelve-second blocks without either hiding in the routine or drowning in the game?","presses":[{"buttonId":"btn.left_behind","how":"The chat server and the price charts make everyone else seem further in."},{"buttonId":"btn.someone_elses_routine","how":"The engineer shows the clerk how old and man-made the clearing system is."},{"buttonId":"btn.more_world","how":"The first transaction, the block explorer and the chat server are genuinely wondrous."},{"buttonId":"btn.knew_better","how":"The clerk understands the peg's weakness and stays because the band stays."},{"buttonId":"btn.watching_them_go","how":"The partner must choose between forbidding and following."}],"authorStake":"Faye's eighteen years on the payments floor, her own fall in 2022 and her father's works: she gives her fall to someone younger, in the town she knows, and puts beside them the choice she faced with her daughter.","longTermProcesses":["the forager mind and its band size, over three hundred thousand years","the clearing system and the three-day cycle since the late 1960s","the Swindon railway works and the town's routines, 1840s to 1986","the building society as an institution and its response to crypto","the crypto market regime from the 2020 crash through the 2021 boom to the 2022 collapses","the pandemic's pressure on hospital staff 2020-2021","the partnership and its shared house deposit","the engineer's career from the railway works to the clearing code to bitcoin"],"centralShock":"The May 2022 stablecoin collapse that takes most of the shared house deposit, arriving while the clerk's own employer is blocking the payments they used to get in.","principals":[{"name":"the clerk (to be named)","wants":"To matter and to see the whole map; and to be no trouble to anyone, which their life taught them as a way to be safe. The two wants split when the rabbit hole offers mattering at the price of trouble.","interest":"Their loyalty to whichever band they are in is what makes them a good colleague and what keeps them in the game after they know better.","readingOfShock":"As a betrayal by the band and a verdict on themselves, then slowly as something done to them by a machine built for faster minds."},{"name":"the engineer (to be named)","wants":"To be believed at last about systems she built and was never credited for; to leave something that outlasts her; and not to be anyone's mother.","interest":"She opens the door and then despises what the clerk finds behind it: a bitcoin purist who thinks decentralized finance is the old casino in a new costume.","readingOfShock":"As proof she was right about the casino, and as her own fault for handing a key to someone without a map."},{"name":"the partner (to be named)","wants":"A house of their own after years of renting and shifts; rest; to be the one who is looked after for once.","interest":"A nurse whose pandemic is bodies and breath while the clerk's is screens; strong under pressure, silent about her own needs.","readingOfShock":"Not as money but as a lie: the deposit was a shared future, and the clerk moved it without asking."}],"costs":"Following the rabbit costs the clerk sleep, the truth with their partner and finally the deposit; the partner pays with the house and her trust; the engineer pays with her belief that she can hand the future to someone else; staying in the routine would have cost the clerk the only year they felt alive.","outcome":"Open: decided by drawn decisions at the model's jumps (the confession, the partnership, what the clerk does with what is left)."},{"id":"cand.twelve_words","title":"Twelve Words","world":"The M4 distribution belt outside Swindon, 2021-2022: a gamified warehouse where handheld scanners direct every step.","account":"A night-shift picker whose every movement is set by a scanner finds, in a returned parcel, a hardware wallet and a card of twelve words. The collapse of 2022 halves the fortune while she decides whether to give it back.","premise":"A worker whose life is already a video game run by an algorithm finds the key to a different game.","emotionalCore":"The humiliation of being managed by a machine and the vertigo of suddenly holding power over a stranger.","question":"Is a key you found yours to use?","presses":[{"buttonId":"btn.more_world","how":"The wallet opens a world of wealth she never saw."},{"buttonId":"btn.someone_elses_routine","how":"The scanner's routine belongs to the company."},{"buttonId":"btn.knew_better","how":"She knows the money is not hers."}],"authorStake":"Faye's knowledge of how keys and ledgers work; less of her own life.","longTermProcesses":["algorithmic management of warehouse labour","the crypto market 2021-2022","property law for digital assets"],"centralShock":"Opening the stranger's wallet.","principals":[{"name":"the picker","wants":"Dignity and money, which conflict when the money is stolen.","interest":"Scrupulous and angry at once.","readingOfShock":"As luck owed to her."},{"name":"the owner","wants":"His key back and to not look stupid online.","interest":"Rich and helpless.","readingOfShock":"As theft."}],"costs":"Her honesty or her fortune; his pride.","outcome":"A trade between them."},{"id":"cand.pension","title":"The Pension","world":"A Swindon insurance office and a bungalow in a village under the downs, 2020-2022.","account":"A claims handler of fifty-eight, forty years at the same insurer, counts the weeks to his pension. His grandson shows him crypto on a phone at Sunday lunch. He moves his tax-free lump sum in 2021, becomes briefly the family's genius, and loses most of it in 2022. His wife learns from the bank statement.","premise":"Anyone can be pulled down the rabbit hole, even the man who has never missed a day.","emotionalCore":"Late-life wonder and late-life humiliation; a man's last chance to matter.","question":"Is it ever too late to wake up?","presses":[{"buttonId":"btn.left_behind","how":"His grandson's generation seems to own the future."},{"buttonId":"btn.more_world","how":"At fifty-eight the world opens."},{"buttonId":"btn.knew_better","how":"He has processed a thousand fraud claims."}],"authorStake":"Faye's father after the works closed: a man whose routine ended; the clerk is right that the world is bigger.","premiseInterest":"High: the gatekeeper of the old machine handed a key to the new one by its own ghost; the brief's echoes (mirror, hidden world, man behind the curtain) fall naturally into it.","readerPull":"A reader who has ever refreshed a price at 3 a.m. or lived a routine week would pick it up; the video-game realization and the OMG, WTF overwhelm fit a younger mind better.","readerPull":"Moving for older readers; less pull for the brief's broad 'anyone can be pulled down'.","verdict":"workable"}],"selection":{"chosenId":"cand.exceptions","reasons":"It is the only candidate in which every element of the brief is load-bearing: the blue pill world is literally the old machine (the clearing batch), the white rabbit is a stranger who does not fit (an engineer who built that machine), the choice is a real conflict with the protagonist's job, the grand battle runs through the protagonist's own day (blocking crypto payments by day, routing around them by night), and the Wilson triad maps onto three places the protagonist lives in: the band in the chat server, the medieval institution on the payments floor, the godlike technology in the phone. It comes most directly out of Faye's life and presses all five buttons. {"schema":"meaning-model-story-author-record/v1","kind":"world","text":"The chosen world opened in four successive accounts: October 2019 to March 2023 in Swindon and on the downs; Kieran Hale, Barbara Ashby and Laura Russell; the card of twelve words; the wallet first opened on the night bitcoin halved; the 2020 lockdown and yield-farming summer; the grand battle through Kieran's own working day; the house deposit in the stablecoin; the May 2022 collapse; an ending open to the model's draws. The era is real with a documentary cutoff of 31 March 2023. Two claims of the earlier accounts are revised to reconcile with documented prices.","data":{"schema":"meaning-model-story-world/v1","stage":"opening","candidatesNodeId":"world.candidates","accounts":["In October 2019 Kieran Hale, twenty-nine, clears payment exceptions on the third floor of the White Hart Building Society in west Swindon, a job where every week is the same and the systems are older than he is. A flagged forty-thousand-pound transfer brings him Barbara Ashby, sixty-six, who once wrote code for the clearing system he works inside and is moving her savings out of it on purpose. A week later she posts him a card with twelve words and fifty pounds of bitcoin behind them. He should declare the gift and does not. In the spring 2020 lockdown, alone in the flat while his partner Laura Russell works the intensive-care wards, he types the words in, and the small corner of the world he knew opens into a vast playing field: decentralized finance, a chat server called the Sharehouse, yields farmed through the night, and a battle between the old institutions and the new machines that runs straight through his own working day. By the end of 2021 he is rich on paper; in January 2022 their shared house deposit goes into a stablecoin paying nearly twenty percent; in May 2022 the stablecoin breaks. What he does then, and what it costs him, Laura and Barbara, is decided by the model's draws.","Kieran's world is safe and repetitive and older than it looks. His grandfather worked in the railway works until they closed in 1986; his father has built engines at the car plant on the old airfield since 1992 and is waiting for it to close, as announced, in 2021. Kieran joined the Hart at twenty, gave up the online game he had been good at as a teenager, and became the person who knows why a payment failed: every file runs overnight, every exception must be cleared before the cut-off, and a payment takes three working days because it did in 1968. His life is a band of known faces, the tea round, the Thursday quiz, Sunday lunch at his parents', Laura's shift pattern stuck to the fridge. Barbara breaks into it twice: first as a voice on the phone who laughs at his scam-check script and tells him he is standing inside a machine he has never seen, then as a letter addressed to him by name at the exceptions desk. The card is a key he is not allowed to hold. Keeping it is the first secret of his adult life.

The lockdown shrinks his routine to one room and a laptop, and that is where the other world opens: the balance appears when he types the words, the public ledger shows every transaction anyone has ever made, and the summer of 2020 turns money into a game with no closing time. Kieran is good at it. He farms tokens named after food, learns a new language in a week, finds in the Sharehouse the first group since his game that treats him as someone who matters. By day the Hart makes him the expert on its new blocks on payments to crypto exchanges; by night he routes around them. Barbara, whom he finally meets on the downs at Avebury, is a bitcoin purist who calls all of this the old casino in a new costume. Laura, exhausted by two waves of the pandemic, wants a house. In 2021 his father's plant closes, Kieran pays his parents' rent for three months from his gains, and in January 2022 the deposit goes into the stablecoin. In May 2022 it breaks in four days. The old mind that kept him loyal to every band he belonged to keeps him in the game after he understands exactly how it is failing.","October 2019 to March 2020. The blue pill is not a lie; it is a routine that works. Kieran Hale is twenty-nine, reliable, liked, no trouble to anyone, on the exceptions desk of the Hart, a mutual founded by railwaymen in 1868 in a pub. His grandfather's works closed before he was born and the town still keeps its hours. On Monday 21 October 2019 a transfer of forty thousand pounds from a long-standing saver to a crypto exchange trips the scam rules and Kieran makes the call he has made a hundred times. Barbara Ashby, sixty-six, a former railway-works electrician who retrained as a programmer and spent twenty-five years writing software for the interbank clearing, answers his questions with her own: does he know how old the thing he works on is, and who can switch it off? On Friday 1 November a letter arrives addressed to Mr K. Hale, Payments Exceptions, Third Floor. Inside is a card of twelve words and a note: there is fifty pounds behind these; it is yours; go and look. Gifts from customers must be declared. He puts the card in his wallet behind his bus pass and tells no one, not even Laura.

March 2020 to December 2021. On 12 March bitcoin halves in a day; on 23 March the country locks down. Laura goes onto the COVID intensive-care unit and sleeps in the day; Kieran works the batch on a laptop in the spare room. One night in April he types the twelve words into a wallet app, touches the glass to confirm, and the balance comes up: 0.0071 bitcoin, twenty-eight pounds, and behind it a public ledger of every transaction since 2009. It is the corner of a map going dark at the edges. The summer of yield farming turns him into a farmer of tokens named after food who wakes at three to harvest; the Sharehouse, a few thousand anonymous members awake in every time zone, becomes his band. By early 2021 his six thousand pounds is thirty-eight thousand. The grand battle is everywhere: the Hart's compliance team and the regulator's warnings, Barbara's purists against the Sharehouse's gamblers, the new exchanges against the old banks, and Kieran on both sides of it, building the Hart's payment block by day and walking around it by night. Barbara becomes his friend on long walks on the Ridgeway; she tells him the stones at Avebury were dragged there by people who wanted to gather, and that the chat server is the same animal with worse food. His father's plant closes in July 2021. By November 2021 Kieran is worth seventy-one thousand pounds on a screen.

January 2022 to March 2023. As the market falls the Sharehouse moves into 'safe yield': a dollar stablecoin whose savings protocol pays nearly twenty percent. In January the house deposit, twenty-four thousand pounds, fifteen of it Laura's, goes in; how Laura came to be part of that, or not, is drawn from the model. From 9 May 2022 the stablecoin loses its peg; the Sharehouse says it has always come back; the founder's account posts that he is deploying more capital; Kieran understands the mechanism perfectly and holds. By 13 May the deposit is worth a few hundred pounds. The same week the Hart's fraud lines fill with customers who have lost their savings, and Kieran takes their calls in the voice he used on Barbara. What follows is open until drawn: whether and when he tells Laura, what she does, what Barbara does with her own guilt at having handed a key to someone without a map, and what Kieran does with the ancient, loyal, curious mind that took him in. The story ends in March 2023 on the downs, with the three clocks still running: the body's, the institution's and the machine's.","October 2019 to March 2020: the blue pill and the white rabbit. The blue pill is not a lie; it is a routine that works. Kieran Hale, twenty-nine, reliable, liked and no trouble to anyone, sits on the exceptions desk of the Hart, a mutual founded by railwaymen in a pub in 1868. The payments file runs overnight, exceptions are cleared before the ten o'clock cut-off, a payment takes three working days because it did in 1968, and the week has the same shape every week: the 8.12 bus, the tea round, the Thursday quiz at the pub, Laura's rota on the fridge, Sunday lunch at his parents' in Penhill where his father talks about the car plant closing in 2021 as if it were weather. On Monday 21 October 2019 a transfer of forty thousand pounds from a saver of thirty years' standing to a crypto exchange trips the scam rules and Kieran makes the call he has made a hundred times. Barbara Ashby, sixty-six, laughs at the script. She was an electrician in the railway works until they closed, then spent twenty-five years at a Reading bureau writing software for the interbank clearing, including, she says, the bit that waits. She asks him whether he knows how old the thing he works on is, and who could switch it off. On Friday 1 November a letter arrives addressed to Mr K. Hale, Payments Exceptions, Third Floor, White Hart House. Inside is a card of twelve words and a note: there is fifty pounds behind these; it is yours; go and look. Gifts from customers must be declared. Declaring it would make her a case and him a colleague who accepted something. He puts the card in his wallet behind his bus pass and tells no one, not even Laura.

March 2020 to December 2020: the fall and the overwhelm. On the evening of 12 March 2020 the news says bitcoin has halved in a day; Kieran remembers the card, types the twelve words into a wallet app at the kitchen table, touches the glass to confirm, and the balance rises out of nothing: 0.0071 bitcoin, twenty-eight pounds, half of what Barbara gave him, and behind it a public ledger of every transaction since 2009, readable by anyone. On 23 March the country locks down. Laura moves onto the COVID intensive-care unit and sleeps in the day; Kieran works the batch on a laptop in the spare room. The corner of the map he has lived in turns out to have edges, and past them is the biggest game he has ever seen. The summer of yield farming arrives in June: tokens named after food, pools, harvests, governance, gas, impermanent loss, a new word every hour, and his reaction is the one everyone has: what on earth is this. He learns it anyway, fast, the way he learned the game at fifteen. He puts in six thousand pounds in July. The Sharehouse, a few thousand anonymous members awake in every time zone, becomes the first band since the game that treats him as someone who matters. In September, when people may meet outdoors in sixes, Barbara takes him walking from her cottage at Avebury Trusloe up onto the Ridgeway. She is a bitcoin purist who calls decentralized finance the old casino in a new costume, and she tells him that the stones behind them were dragged across the downs by people who wanted to gather.

January 2021 to December 2021: the grand battle and the harvest. The third lockdown sends Laura back to the unit in January for the worst weeks of the pandemic; she comes home and sits in the car outside for twenty minutes before coming up. By February Kieran's six thousand pounds is thirty-eight thousand. The battle between the old world and the new runs straight through his day: the regulator's warnings, the Hart's decision in the summer to block payments to several crypto exchanges, and Kieran, the man who knows why a payment fails, seconded to build the block by day while he walks around it at night through an app the Hart has never heard of. The Sharehouse has its own wars: purists against gamblers, one chain against another, the founders of new protocols against everyone who says they are frauds. His status rises in the band; he answers newcomers at three in the morning; he checks the farm the way his ancestors checked the fields. In July his father's plant closes and Kieran pays his parents' rent for three months from his gains, the best thing the money ever does. By November 2021 he is worth seventy-one thousand pounds on a screen, Laura has started looking at houses in Wroughton, and three clocks are running in him at once: a body built for a band on the downs, an employer built for the three-day batch, and a phone that never closes.

January 2022 to March 2023: the break and the reckoning. As prices fall, the Sharehouse moves into what it calls safe yield: a dollar stablecoin whose savings protocol pays about twenty percent. In January 2022 the house deposit, twenty-four thousand pounds, fifteen of it Laura's overtime, goes in; how Laura came to be part of that, or not, is drawn from the model. From 9 May 2022 the stablecoin slips from its dollar; the Sharehouse says it has always come back; the founder's account posts that he is deploying more capital; Kieran understands the mechanism perfectly and holds, because the band holds and because selling would make it real. By 13 May the deposit is worth about three thousand pounds and falling; by June it is worth a few hundred. The same week the Hart's fraud lines fill with customers who have lost their savings, and Kieran takes their calls in the voice he used on Barbara. What follows is open until drawn: whether and when he tells Laura, what she does, what Barbara does with the guilt of having handed a key to someone without a map, and what Kieran does with the loyal, curious, ancient mind that took him in. In November 2022 a large exchange collapses in the background and Barbara's own coins fall to a quarter of their peak; she says she has seen three of these.
